HPV vaccine uptake lags in New Zealand as sexual myths hinder school rollout

New Zealand Herald October 09, 2026

The HPV vaccine was introduced in September 2008.

It has been 18 years since a cancer-preventing vaccine was rolled out in New Zealand schools. But its uptake has stalled because of damaging myths about sexual activity and schools declining to offer the vaccine, writes Eva de Jong.

Despite its cancer-preventing benefits, the HPV vaccine has struggled to achieve a high uptake in New Zealand, but medical experts say there is a chance to reverse this trend.

During the past 18 years, there has been resistance to the HPV vaccine, with some schools choosing to opt out because of damaging myths being spread about the injection.

Today, the HPV vaccination national coverage among 15-year-olds is about 60%, which falls short of Health New Zealand’s national target of 75% and the World Health Organisation’s goal of 90%.

Across the ditch, Australia is on track to become the first country to eliminate cervical cancer by 2035. New Zealand is lagging behind with an elimination target of 2040.

There are 252 schools that have not yet delivered the HPV vaccine to students this year.

Official information obtained by the Weekend Herald from Health NZ shows at least one HPV vaccination has been administered at 1227 of the 1479 schools enrolled in the immunisation programme, as of August 31, 2026.

Health NZ said that figure may increase during the remainder of the year as the school-based delivery continues and that vaccinations at some schools may have been delivered but not yet entered into the Aotearoa Immunisation Register.

Immunisation Advisory Centre principal medical adviser Nikki Turner says 252 schools in New Zealand not offering such an impactful vaccine to their pupils is “very sad”.

“I suggest there needs to be urgent dialogue with the school boards of these schools to discuss further where these concerns are coming from and how many are misunderstandings of the science behind this vaccine,” Turner says.

“Currently this means many young people are going to be left at higher risk of these horrible cancers later in life. That is very sobering.”

Health NZ prevention screening national director Alana Ewe-Snow says a targeted campaign is being developed to improve awareness of eligibility and encourage eligible young people who missed vaccination at school to catch up.

“We are also reframing our promotional approach to focus more clearly on HPV vaccination as cancer prevention for young people, rather than primarily as a vaccine for girls,” Ewe-Snow says.

Immunisation Advisory Centre senior Māori medical adviser and Onehunga GP Mamaeroa David says a number of young people have come to her clinic after they turn 18 looking to get the HPV vaccine.

“Their parents wouldn’t let them get it, but they really want it,” she says.

“If you’ve got this group of women who were denied HPV vaccinations and then have cervical cancer now, it’s horrible. Like what a horrible way to learn that lesson.

“We still do have community pockets, like our Pacific Island communities and strongly religious groups, that have entrenched ideas about only having sex with your husband, and this can come into play when understanding the vaccine.

“It’s not about promiscuity, because you could just have one partner and still get it.”

The story of the vaccination rollout in New Zealand has been a struggle to educate parents about the importance of the vaccine.

University of Otago Associate Professor Dr Peter Sykes, who works in the Department of Obstetrics and Gynaecology, was part of a recent Christchurch-led study that confirmed the HPV vaccine was highly effective at reducing cancer rates.

“The younger you’re vaccinated, the greater your protection,” Sykes says.

He has worked in this area for decades and recalls that when the vaccine burst on to the scene it took a long time for public understanding of its benefits to catch up.

“It was brought in quite quickly I feel, and to some extent there was a lack of general awareness about the importance of the vaccine,” Sykes says.

“For many of the public, it was lumped on their plate and all the anxieties that came with it.”

The HPV vaccine was first introduced in September 2008. Boys and girls are given the HPV vaccine as it protects against cervical, vaginal, vulvar, penile, anal and back of throat cancers, as well as genital warts.

Some parents and schools had fears over false narratives about girls having their hair fall out, having seizures, or fainting in response to the vaccine.

Other parents and some religious schools misunderstood the need for the delivery of the vaccine at age 9 and felt it was encouraging girls to be sexually active and thought the HPV virus was only contracted through sexual promiscuity.

Specialist obstetrician and gynaecologist Dr Jess Dunning works at Auckland City Hospital and in private practice at the Auckland Gynaecology Group.

She says some resistance came from the fact the HPV virus is contracted through sexual contact and parents felt the vaccine might be “giving their young daughters permission to have sex”.

However, the vaccine is given at a young age because it enables a greater immune response and needs to be administered before a person becomes sexually active and could be exposed to the HPV virus, Dunning says.

Infection with the HPV virus is common, with an estimated 70-80% of sexually active individuals becoming infected at some stage in their lives – even if they have had only a single sexual partner.

Vaccine hesitancy has worsened, Dunning says, and there are now social media sources and influencers that deliver incorrect information in a plausible way.

“We are not educating families properly so that they can make decisions based on correct information,” Dunning says.

“It’s a vaccine that can prevent cancer, it’s a pretty amazing thing, and we need to push harder.”

Changes made this year mean children will receive only one dose of the HPV vaccine through the school-based immunisation programme, but previously two doses were given in school.

It is also free until aged 27 from a pharmacist or GP, and a second dose will remain available through these routes.

Internationally, many countries have also struggled to dispel myths around the HPV vaccine.

In the United States, vaccination rates have dropped amid changing public health rhetoric and repeated misleading claims from Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy jnr linking childhood vaccinations to autism.

Overseas studies that have looked at the reasons behind low vaccination rates link them to a lack of medical knowledge, uncertain beliefs and ideas, and the decision-making of the primary caregiver versus the adolescent, Dunning says.

“Who gets to decide whether they get the vaccine? Should it be the parents or should it be the kids? It’s an interesting question of autonomy when you’re 12.”

In September, the Government released its Cervical Cancer Elimination Plan 2026-2040 and announced it would make cervical screening free from March next year.

Sykes says smoothing out the mechanics of the school programme and simplifying the message of the vaccine is the way to increase HPV vaccination rates.

Often it could be as simple as a missed permission slip in a child’s bag or a conversation not had with a parent that could lead to a student slipping through the cracks, he says.

Dunning says convenience and logistics always come into play for a child getting a vaccine.

Ewe-Snow says Health NZ is working to support primary care to identify and recall eligible people who have missed vaccination.

It aims to strengthen the school-based delivery, improve access through pharmacies and community providers and to use data to target follow-up where coverage is lowest.

“We know there is more work to be done to achieve elimination of cervical cancer and to implement the recommendations arising from the Cervical Screening Register Review,” she says.

The Weekend Herald asked Health NZ for the number of participating schools that provided the HPV vaccine to students for the past five years, but Health NZ said it did not hold historical information for the years requested.

A 2024 national stocktake recorded 1418 schools participating in the immunisation programme, of which 1403 offered HPV vaccinations to students.

Cancer Society head of advocacy and public affairs Rachael Neumann has worked in public health and chronic disease prevention for more than 20 years, in government and non-profit roles, across Australia and New Zealand.

Neumann says Australia’s investment in cancer services is a long way ahead of us, and it has had a clear cervical elimination strategy for some time.

She says we need to improve the consent process through the school programme and get the message across about the advantage of being vaccinated before being exposed to the HPV virus.

“We need to move the narrative away from sexual activity or protecting from STIs to cancer prevention,” Neumann says.

“You can have a nice plan, but you need funding and commitment from politicians and our health sector to bring the results to fruition.”

There is a continuing issue of equitable access to vaccinations for Māori and Pasifika families and people living in rural areas, who consistently have lower vaccination rates than Pākehā and urban-dwelling populations.

The ongoing shadow cast over vaccinations by the Covid pandemic is also having an impact, and the lack of agency felt by groups about decisions made when carrying out vaccine mandates.

“We’ve shown in the past we can vaccinate equitably, but that’s dropped off during Covid and in places like Northland – that really needs to be fixed,” Sykes says.

Turner says school-based programmes are usually effective at closing equity gaps when it comes to vaccination, but during Covid there were high absentee rates and this caused significant disruption.

She says the focus has to be on effective resourcing of the school-based programme to ensure equitable coverage.

There is a dark history in New Zealand’s past when it comes to protecting women against cervical cancer.

A study carried out by Dr Herbert Green at the National Women’s Hospital in Auckland that began in 1966 was labelled “The Unfortunate Experiment” as women involved who had abnormal cervical smear results were left untreated.

The experiment resulted in the Cartwright Inquiry into patients’ rights being carried out by the Government and led to significant reforms.

Recently, a major review found nearly one million cervical cancer screening notifications were missed or unsent by Health NZ’s national register.

Sykes was part of the expert panel that conducted the review and says he has continuing concerns that people reaching 25 aren’t being sent effective notifications for smear tests.

David says moving to a one-dose schedule is an important step to streamline delivery of the school programme, because it is easier to arrange for children to get consent for a single vaccination.

Turner says when she reflects on the fact about 60% of young people are getting vaccinated, it troubles her greatly as those children missing out could suffer in 20 years’ time.

“Personally, I think that’s a tragedy.”

But Turner also believes this is a promising story and that if New Zealand makes a concentrated effort, the elimination of cervical cancer is within reach.

She says health resources are “really tight” and despite efforts from public health nurses there have been constraints in the public health sector that have affected vaccination coverage.

Often nurses haven’t had time to repeatedly have conversations in communities and to dispel some of the myths and fears people have about the HPV vaccine.

“The myths become embedded and then it becomes a struggle to undo them.”

Turner points out small things can happen that have a ripple effect. For instance, one child fainted after being given the HPV vaccine and that spread throughout a lot of schools.

“This is nothing to do in a way with sex, it’s not a rare, nasty sexual disease. It’s normal to be exposed to HPV.”

Sykes says ultimately Government investment in the school programme should be a straightforward decision because the cost of treating cancer in an adult is expensive for the public system compared with giving a child a vaccine.

Each year, about 175 people are diagnosed with cervical cancer and 55 people die from it.

The elimination of cervical cancer will not mean having zero cases but is defined by the World Health Organisation as reducing the incidence rate to fewer than four cases per 100,000 women.

David says she hopes in the future she will no longer, as a GP, have to witness the pain that women with cervical cancer go through.

“I think the potential for us to eliminate cervical cancer is actually very high. And it’s cancer, that’s nothing short of incredible,” she says.

New Zealand Herald October 09, 2026

A man who moved a burning car away from petrol pumps at an Auckland service station says he was just doing what he thought was right.

Police were called to a car fire at a Mill Rd petrol station about 12.10pm yesterday but arrived to find the vehicle had already been moved away from the pumps.

CCTV footage showed a man calmly approaching the car and moving it to safety, prompting a police appeal to identify the “petrol station legend”.

Thames man Rob Horne told the Herald he was at the Bombay gas station when he heard yelling from across the forecourt.

“This lady’s car was sort of starting to smoke and there was a small fire underneath it.”

Horne realised the potential danger.

“I just sort of thought, oh, well, we’re all going to blow up if we leave the fire there.”

He decided to get in the burning car and take the handbrake off to move it away from the pumps.

“I sort of just looked around and saw that no one else was doing anything,” he said.

With the car safely away from the pumps, Horne said he decided to continue on with his day, figuring it was ”problem solved”.

But reflecting afterwards, he realised it was hardly an everyday occurrence.

“It was pretty casual I suppose, but when I thought about it afterwards, I thought, s***, yeah, jumped out of a flaming car today,” he said.

“It was a little, a little bit different from my day-to-day routine.”

As for those calling him a hero, Horne said while he would take the title, the act seemed like a simple decision at the time.

“I was just doing what I thought was the right thing to do.”

The fire was out when emergency services arrived, and no other damage was caused – a result officials have credited to Horne’s speedy reaction.

Police had been trying to identify the Good Samaritan after reviewing the gas station footage.

They described him as the “petrol station legend”.

“The man very calmly enters the vehicle, releases the handbrake and pushes the vehicle away from the pump while others assist with the fire,” Sergeant Mark Fleming said.

“His brave actions prevented a much more serious situation from eventuating.”

He said, “like all good heroes”, the mystery man left without recognition.

Police said they wanted to contact the man and thank him for his actions.

“Not everyone is able to jump into action in a dangerous situation, and this man deserves to be acknowledged for his courageous quick-thinking,” Fleming said.

On the road with Chris Hipkins: Palestine, food and a healthy blood pressure

New Zealand Herald October 09, 2026

Labour leader Chris Hipkins gets his blood pressure taken. Photo / Thomas Coughlan

Campaign Diary:

“Palestine” a man said, loudly, but not quite shouting, as Labour Leader Chris Hipkins arrived at Masjid Al Mustafa in Ōtāhuhu, Auckland just after midday yesterday.

He said it again, then again, and again, almost heckling Hipkins as he met members of South Auckland’s Muslim community.

“I’ll have something to say about that inside,” Hipkins said.

He was shortly escorted round the back of the mosque to a large meeting room where he addressed perhaps 50 members of the community, some of whom had brought their children to meet Hipkins and grab a selfie.

After a brief introduction, which touched on concerns about racism and social cohesion, the floor was open to questions. The first was what Hipkins would do about the situation in Gaza.

“The first thing that we are going to do is formally recognise Palestine as a state,” Hipkins said, to solid applause.

“The way we do that in New Zealand is we invite the ambassador to present their credentials so we can do that relatively quickly. We will be doing that as a matter of priority,” he said.

“The second thing is we will support sanctions against Israel because of the unfolding genocide that is taking place in Palestine at the moment,” Hipkins said.

His first questions were perhaps specific to this community. The question on Palestine was followed by one on rising racism against minorities and what the Government could do about it (Hipkins said he would sack ministers who used “inflammatory rhetoric”), another was what a Labour Government would do to improve conditions in Afghanistan (Hipkins conceded there was not much New Zealand could do).

Other questions were of the variety every politician is being asked at the moment: what can you do about the cost of living? They did not seem blown away by Hipkins rattling off his party’s promise of free GP visits or the $20 fare cap for public transport - a policy that should appeal to this part of Auckland, given its fairly solid transport connections. Some seemed a bit bored by Hipkins explaining the wholesale grocery market - one boy began eying up the food at the back of the room: a deep dish piled high with onion bhaji bites whose smell wafts over the attendees.

Naresh Perinpanayagam, a Labour list candidate, tells the Herald these are pakora, made from chickpea flour, vegetables, spices and deep fried. They were popular and very tasty.

From there, Hipkins travelled downstairs to Friday prayers, where he delivered almost the same remarks to a slightly larger crowd.

One change to his remarks, a message Hipkins described as “the most important of all” was a plea to everyone to enrol to vote.

”With the election now just four weeks away it has never been more important to make sure you are on the electoral roll so you can vote in this year’s election.

“If you are not enrolled by the time voting starts then you will not be able to enrol - you won’t be able to vote if you are not on the roll. Do it today,” Hipkins said.

As people filed out of the mosque, Labour volunteers in bright red jackets handed out enrolment forms and helped people fill them in. Hipkins later vented frustration at low enrolment for the election. He pointed the finger in part at the Electoral Commission whose outreach had been lacking, saying that Labour seemed to be doing the commission’s job.

From the mosque, Hipkins drove to the North Shore, to visit nurse trainees at AUT’s nursing campus. The visit was arranged around promoting Labour’s promise to provide domestic nursing graduates with a guaranteed job offer.

Hipkins met a class of trainees who were at different stages of study. Several approached by the Herald relayed horror stories of previous cohorts graduating into a job market in which no one was hiring. One told the Herald they were considering backup careers before graduating nursing.

One, Neve Cusens, described Labour’s policy as “wild”, saying she was very supportive of it.

She asked Hipkins whether he had read the letter that she’d written him before his visit. Hipkins said he hadn’t, but would do so later. Cusens provided the Herald with a copy of the letter, which listed the struggles and sacrifices of trainee nurses, including responding to serious mental health incidents, dealing with unwanted sexual advances from patients and being abused.

The letter warned students were being burned out before they even entered the workforce.

“We cannot continue to rely on the goodwill, resilience and unpaid clinical contributions of students without seriously considering the cost to those students and the implications for the health system,” she wrote.

She told Hipkins she was anxiously awaiting news about whether she would be offered an interview for a graduate nursing position by the time she’d finished her degree.

After grabbing some selfies, Hipkins got his blood pressure taken. He was told it was surprisingly normal for someone doing a stressful job. Then it was back across the bridge to South Auckland, Papatoetoe this time, where Hipkins finished the day with a walkabout at the night market.

The lack of any Jacindamania equivalent hangs over this campaign. There is not an obvious swelling of support for either Chris in the way there has been for previous candidates. Hipkins got quite a few selfie requests; Rakesh Naidoo, easing into his role as a politician, helped with crowd control, wrangling people who wanted to meet Hipkins.

Still, plenty of families milled about the market, keen not to let a politician come between them and their Friday meal.

Election 2026: National’s Carlos Cheung caused an upset in Mt Roskill in 2023 - now he has ministerial ambitions and isn’t afraid to raise different views

New Zealand Herald October 09, 2026

National MP Carlos Cheung with a map of Mt Roskill before the boundary changes. Photo / Jamie Ensor

Mt Roskill was considered a Labour stronghold in 2023 when National’s Carlos Cheung seemingly came from nowhere to win it off former minister Michael Wood. The Herald recently spoke with Labour’s Wood about his attempt to reclaim the seat – you can read that here – and today talks with Cheung about three years ago and ambitions for the future.

When Carlos Cheung realised he was Mt Roskill’s newest representative in 2023, he says his mind went to National’s veteran supporters in the electorate who hadn’t once tasted victory.

“You see some of your supporters start crying, especially those seniors,” Cheung told the Herald.

“This victory means something, not only to me, but to my supporters as well, to a lot of long-term supporters in this area, because finally they can see something’s changing.

“Finally, National was winning in this electorate. In a way, that day, I think it meant more to them than to myself.”

Cheung had beaten Labour’s Michael Wood, a far more familiar face, to win Mt Roskill for National for the first time since its creation at the 1999 election. Before his win, it had been held only by Wood and former Labour leader Phil Goff.

His majority was only a slim 1564 votes, and it came amid a swing towards National across the country. Wood had also faced a high-profile fall from power, resigning from his ministerial roles over a failure to sell Auckland Airport shares.

So did Cheung win the very diverse electorate himself, did he just get caught up in National’s wider success, or was he simply the beneficiary of Wood’s troubles?

The National MP doesn’t believe there is a single reason for his success in 2023.

“A lot of people say that, ‘hey Carlos, there must be the blue wave, that’s why you get taken along’. But if you look at history, if your candidate is not strong enough or not being accepted by the constituent, that’s not changing.”

He also pointed to how his candidate vote compared with the party vote in his electorate, noting that National candidates in previous elections don’t typically match the support for the party itself.

That’s partially correct. Cheung personally got 15,659 votes while National received a similar 15,828. In 2020, National’s then-candidate, Parmjeet Parmar, got 9197 votes, to National’s 9328. But going back further, the candidate did receive about 2000-4000 fewer votes than National itself.

This year, Cheung is unlikely to benefit from a surge in support for National. The party has trended downwards in the polls, though Labour itself hasn’t capitalised, only nudging slightly north since 2023.

Analysis from National pollster David Farrar suggests boundary changes in Mt Roskill help the National candidate, but the change in party vote since three years ago wipes out those gains and more, giving Wood the edge.

Cheung has confidence he can pull through.

“I think people can judge on my track record rather than slogans or just the talking. Action speaks a thousand words, and I believe the past three years I’ve been working very hard to make changes to people.”

Cheung mentioned local issues he says he has got involved in, from advocating for removing a speed bump in Hillsborough, to addressing illegal dumping issues on a stretch of grass near a school, and continuing to push for more parking for those moving into housing developments being built in the electorate.

“I’m very visible in my community as well; no matter what event, I’ll be there to support the team, but also I’m willing to listen to my constituents and try to address their local issues.”

Asked if being a new backbencher gave him time to spend in his community that a minister may not have, Cheung said it “depends on where your heart lies”.

“When your heart is with the people, no matter how busy you are, you’re still willing to listen to your constituents. You can’t just say that, ‘hey, I want to resolve the whole country’s problem’, and then you ignore your people. This is not right.”

After a term in Parliament, does he have his eyes set on ministerial office?

“Definitely,” Cheung responded.

“I never thought of it, before I become a politician, but the more I actually work in the Parliament, I can see that sometimes becoming a minister, you can actually reach out to more resources as well, and you can actually make some policy change as well.”

He offers up health when asked what areas he’s interested in, noting his background researching diabetes, as well as ethnic communities and seniors.

Cheung said his focus would be on prevention and raising awareness early to stop illnesses developing into something that has a greater impact on the healthcare system.

“When you can find the illness a little bit earlier or identify the issue earlier, then you can receive treatment earlier, so you will have a better outcome on the patient as well.

“The hospital is the end point of the healthcare system. The idea is we don’t want people to actually go to the hospital or go see the GP.”

But for now, Cheung’s influence over policy lies in the caucus room as one of National’s backbench MPs.

Asked if he’s taken a different stand from the National Government on anything, Cheung wouldn’t say there’s anything he’s “against”, but he did highlight his role to raise the views of locals who may have different views to that of his party.

“[Mt Roskill is] a marginal seat. I manage to hear voices from both sides,” Cheung said.

“Every single member of Parliament will tell you, ‘I’ve been listening to my people’. They’re not wrong. They listen. But they may listen to their own people.”

He said people in an electorate with a clear majority for one party would be “very aligned” with that party’s policy.

“But in my electorate, because it’s marginal, I may hear two different kinds of voices.”

Cheung said he can “bring the voices back to my caucus so we can slightly amend or adjust the policy to fit or benefit more people”.

The Herald asked for an example of where that had happened, but Cheung wouldn’t get into what is discussed in the National caucus room.

However, he did say one example of a policy on which he had heard from people with views different to National’s is KiwiSaver. National’s proposing to make KiwiSaver compulsory and increase the default contribution rate over time to 6% for both the employee and employer.

“I think a lot of people ask, ‘how about those people with low incomes or people struggling now’,” he said, picking up on criticism of that policy that people may struggle to put more money aside for savings.

Cheung said he goes to his National team with that type of feedback and asks what could be done to help.

“If they struggle, can they [pause contributing to] KiwiSaver for now?”

The Herald accompanied Cheung this week to an event he organised in the community for small business owners to mingle and meet their local MP.

After a speech from Cheung and guest National MP Cameron Brewer, the pair opened the floor for a Q+A. Immediately, there were questions over why National was hiking the employer KiwiSaver rate and whether the party recognised the impact on business.

The MPs’ responses boiled down to conveying the benefits of increased retirement savings for New Zealanders and creating an environment where the employee feels valued by their employer.

Cheung said it was an example of not being afraid to confront differing views.

The MP compliments National’s ministers for being open to feedback.

“They are very willing to hear different voices because I think all the ministers just want to set up the best policy to benefit more people.”

What about Christopher Luxon, National’s leader, who has faced persistent questions about his leadership and popularity? How does Cheung rate him?

The Mt Roskill MP says constituents want a Prime Minister who is “actually doing things rather than talking”.

“He may not be very good at a lot of media. You guys say he’s not good at talking, but he’s good at delivering,” the MP told the Herald.

Cheung said National’s ministers are well-regarded, but it is Luxon who has the final say on the policies they are implementing.

“I think this is why I believe that people need to give him back a little bit of credit. He is very different to the previous Prime Minister. He’s not going to give you a beautiful speech, or he’s not the one who tried to seek spotlight or try to get the credit.”

He said that’s demonstrated by Luxon giving time to his ministers during press conferences.

“I think that in a way is hurting him a bit, so people forget ... he is the leader. He is the one who [makes] the final decision.

“Credit should be given to him a little bit.”

Jamie Ensor is the NZ Herald’s chief political reporter, based in the press gallery at Parliament. He was previously a TV reporter and digital producer in the Newshub press gallery office. He was a finalist in 2025 for Political Journalist of the Year at the Voyager Media Awards.

A magnitude 7.7 earthquake has struck near Panama in Central America.

The earthquake was initially recorded at magnitude 8 before being adjusted.

The shaking set off panic in the high-rise capital Panama City, AFP reported.

USGS said the epicentre was 10km from the small town of Pitaloza Arriba in the south-centre of Panama.

It triggered a tsunami warning for Panama and warnings of smaller but dangerous waves along the coasts of other countries in Latin America and the south Pacific.

The National Emergency Management Agency said there was no tsunami threat for New Zealand.

The Pacific Tsunami Warning Centre said tsunami waves of up to 3m above tide levels were possible along the coast of Panama and up to 1m for some coasts of Ecuador.

Tremors were felt in Panama City, where buildings shook and people evacuated into the streets

AP reported: “Visibly shaken residents gathered outside as they waited for news of the quake’s impact.”

The quake, registered at a shallow depth of 12 kilometres, was felt across the country of around 4.5 million people, according to the National Civil Protection System, and lasted for around a minute.

There were no reports yet of casualties but extensive damage was expected, particularly in the centre of the Central American nation.

Luis Poveda, a factory worker in the central city of Santiago de Veraguas, told AFP: “I’m in shock right now and haven’t been able to contact my family.”

Arnulfo Santos, a worker at a flour mill in the same city, said: “We all ran out of the building, the power lines were swaying, and everyone was outside.”

AFP reported that part of a hotel had collapsed in the town of Penonome, 150km southwest of Panama City.

A church in Penonome was also seriously damaged and other buildings showed cracks, according to local reports.

More than a dozen large aftershocks, one a magnitude-6 tremor, were recorded by the local geosciences institute.

Writing on X, Panamanian President Jose Raul Mulino called for calm, saying: “What happened should not be used to generate alarms and disorder.”

Earthquakes are rare in Panama and when they do occur they usually strike in western Chiriqui province, bordering Costa Rica.

The Panamanian quake is at least the fourth quake this year in Latin America surpassing 7.0 in magnitude, after devastating earthquakes in Venezuela in June and a powerful earthquake in western Colombia in August.

Dansey Rd crash that killed Sakura Hall: Rotorua court summary details cannabis and sunstrike

A man who says he smokes cannabis daily was struck by bright sunshine when he crashed his van into a parked rubbish truck near Rotorua, killing a 2-year-old girl.

The man, who has interim name suppression, has admitted a charge of drugged driving causing the death of Sakura Hall on May 22 last year.

He pleaded guilty in April, but Rotorua District Court this week released details about what happened.

A police summary, provided to the Rotorua Daily Post, said the driver was found to have four times the high-risk level for tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) in his blood.

The man was driving a van on Dansey Rd at 8am when the crash happened. Sakura was in a car seat on the front passenger side.

The summary said the man did not wait for his vehicle to warm up before driving, and his windscreen was clouded or condensing.

Dansey Rd is a rural two-lane road, separated by a single centre line. The speed limit is 100km/h and the roadside has a solid white line leading into a grass verge. There is no cycle lane or footpath.

The man drove up an incline bordered by mature trees. Near the top of the hill, the landscape on both sides of the road was flat farm paddocks.

The summary said the man drove out of dissipating fog and was confronted by bright sunlight within his field of vision.

He did not stop to address the lack of visibility or slow down enough to stop or evade potential hazards.

A Hino rubbish truck was parked on the left-hand side of the live lane of Dansey Rd. The truck’s amber warning beacons were activated.

The rubbish truck had been parked there for one minute and 34 seconds before the crash. No pilot vehicle or other traffic management was in place, and there was no legal requirement for it.

The summary said the rubbish truck operator was complying with the road rules.

The operator was out of his vehicle, standing near the bins he was about to empty.

The sun’s low angle on the section of road immediately before the crash washed out all contrast, and the man did not see the truck, its flashing lights or warning signs.

The van travelled at least 205m between the defendant being exposed to sunstrike and the collision.

His van collided with the truck’s rear, causing severe damage. The impact speed was between 62km/h and 86km/h.

The summary said the man slowed as a result of the sunstrike, but he did not slow sufficiently or pull over.

“The combination of his failure to safely navigate the sunstrike and the position of the rubbish truck in the live lane are the primary causes of the crash,” the summary said.

The man made an evasive swerve to the right about 0.3 to 0.4 seconds before impact. The impact caused the front left-hand side of the defendant’s vehicle to cave in and down on top of Sakura. She died at the scene.

Police took a blood sample from the man, and he was found to have 12 (+/-4) nanograms of tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) per millilitre of blood. The high-risk level is three.

The man told police he smoked cannabis daily. He said his windscreen had fogged over; he slowed down, and within 10-15 seconds the rubbish truck was suddenly there without warning.

He stated that when he felt the sunstrike, he took his foot off the accelerator but didn’t think he had time to brake.

He will be sentenced on January 22.

Kelly Makiha is a senior journalist who has reported for the Rotorua Daily Post for more than 25 years, covering mainly police, court, human interest and social issues.

Letters: The billion-dollar question over morality; drug-testing beneficiaries; airfare refunds

New Zealand Herald October 09, 2026

First panel during the New Zealand Herald, The Future of New Zealand Debate. Photo: Dean Purcell

Letter of the week: John Key and the billion-dollar question

On the Herald/TV3 debate, former PM John Key spoke in defence of billionaires, saying “it’s nuts to think billionaires are morally offensive”.

Key has admitted he would’ve voted for Donald Trump in 2016.

By doing so he would’ve also voted for Peter Theil, Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos, Mark Zuckerberg. He would’ve voted for an administration directed by billionaires, and subservient to billionaires. This is morally offensive, and indefensible.

Billionaires tend not to enhance or encourage democracy. They distort, control and direct democracy, to retain and enhance their wealth.

Celebrating successful, risk-taking entrepreneurs who pay taxes is to be encouraged. Supporting political influencing billionaires, however, is not.

To quote Louis Brandeis (American Supreme Court Justice): “We may have democracy, or we may have wealth concentrated in the hands of a few, but we can’t have both”.

Ian Findlay, Napier

Success and morals

With all respect to Sir John Key and many others who find calling billionaires morally offensive “nuts”, I agree with them.

Hard-grafting and clever individuals become wealthy and good on them.

But that does not apply to all.

I can think of one internationally famous person, a leader, and many others who gained their wealth through being absolutely “morally indefensible”.

Paul Blakeney, Waihi

Pentagon’s climate predictions

It would seem that Linda McGrogan (Oct 9) is unaware of the more than 30 climate predictions that have failed to come true. Just one example is a 2004 Pentagon analysis that warned major European cities would be underwater by 2020, at which point Britain would suffer from a “Siberian” climate.

The reality is that the world is warming at a slow and steady rate as it comes out of the Little Ice Age. It is also true that we cannot affect the climate as long as China and India are building lots of coal-fired stations. Therefore, we are better off building resilience against whatever an ever-changing climate visits upon us rather than squandering billions of dollars on a futile attempt to change the world’s climate.

Bryan Leyland, Pt Chevalier

Drug testing? Check the data

Louise Upston and Christopher Luxton announced this week, as part of their election push, they want to drug test beneficiaries. The message I hear is, “We’re not succeeding. Blame beneficiaries. They must be stealing from us.” In my opinion there is nothing more pathetic than that.

They might want to check the data, which shows in New Zealand “cocaine users are likely to be employed and high earners” and are now using 7kg a week.

Drug testing CEOs may reveal a serious loss of productivity there.

Keith Burgess, Sumner

Opportunity ‘deafeningly silent’

Opportunity is receding as a gamechanger.

National wants to drug-test beneficiaries, to slash the benefit for drug-users, and introduce a raft of restrictions on all who seek or are receiving a social welfare benefit.

“Draconian” is the word that springs to mind.

It says much about who National (and Act, NZ First and Labour) expect to vote that so much energy is spent on trimming the social welfare benefit paid to people under 65, but that none of these parties will address the far, far greater cost of paying a universal social welfare benefit to millionaires over 65 who already have handsome incomes from other sources as well.

There’s an answer, of course: replace all social welfare benefits with the Universal Basic Income that Opportunity has advocated. Whether that would be paid for by the land tax Opportunity proposes, or by wealth taxes and inheritance and gift taxes, or by setting a higher minimum income-tax rate, or some combination of those, would be for Parliament to decide.

Yet Opportunity, instead of loudly advocating its Citizens’ Income in response to National’s intended cuts, is deafeningly silent. Why?

It seemed bad politics for Opportunity to announce election bottom lines that skipped its flagship land-tax-for-UBI for five policies so bland that no other party could take offence.

But worse, Opportunity now seems to have buried its UBI. And if it fails to speak up now for all the beneficiaries that National intends to harm, what is the point of Opportunity and the citizens’ income it seems not really to believe in?

John Trezise, Birkenhead

Airfare refunds

Well done Chris Hipkins (Oct 9). If elected he wants a law to provide automatic refunds if flights are cancelled. But he should extend it: if big events are cancelled before the flight, you get a full refund immediately.

I read in the Herald that demand for tickets on Air New Zealand to fly Warriors fans from Auckland to Sydney on the Friday, the day before the NRL Grand Final, was so enormous that they put on another plane to get them there.

I wondered at the time that when they surprisingly did not make the Grand Final if the hundreds of fans got a full refund? They absolutely deserve it for sure.

National looks after big companies and friendly billionaires. Labour looks after the ordinary people trying to survive who at times go to top entertainment and sporting events.

Murray Hunter, Titirangi

Gender on spectrum

Winston Peters appears to describe gender as “two variants — male and female”.

On the contrary, gender is best seen as on a spectrum or in some cases a zigzag.

I’d be willing to bet that almost all — if not all — of Peters’ coalition crew and wider party have some whanau or acquaintance connection who is or has been engaged in the hugely stressful transition from one “variant” to one they more closely feel.

Driven by his MAGA-influenced cruelty and Trump’s contempt for courts of law he has lost touch with the young of this country and certainly with those of us who are older and who desire to see people move from repression, fear and pain to gender self-realisation.

Peter Beyer, Sandringham

Execution hypocrisy

For a country that does a hell of a lot of hallelujah Bible-quoting, including by people like Secretary of War and Bible-retailing by its President, those southern US zealots sure love a good ol’ long-awaited execution.

No worry to those fine “people of God and eye-for-eye justice” that the crime was committed 30 years ago ... which in most countries is deemed a life sentence if on good behaviour.

Throw in two botched lethal doses non-fatally administered while the doomed woman is still kept cuffed to her hospital bed.

Now they talk of another crack at killing her.

Oddly 1500 warriors/patriots got complete pardons since Trump re-judged those who ransacked the Capitol with “get out of jail” cards.

That infamous day on January 6 led to several deaths including maiming of police officers yet no one was executed or held accountable.

The US is a weird wild west mob where I, thankfully, no longer dwell.

Rob Buchanan (US citizen), Kerikeri

A quick word

Ryan Bridge’s hosting of the Herald/TV3 Future of NZ debate was indeed a breath of fresh air. Thank you. .

Steve Clerk, Meadowbank

The massive US Air Force jets thundering over our countrywould send people in other parts of the world scrambling to bomb shelters and panic. In Aotearoa, we grab our sunnies, head outside, and admire the show. We’re pretty fortunate in this part of the pacific.

Chris Mann, Mt Albert

It would be a very good idea if time was set aside for members of the audience who are present at the election presentation to ask questions as so far, the presentations give the impression that politicians have not been attending to the concerns that are foremost in the minds of the public.

Ross Harvey, Remuera

Those billionaires who accrue their money from labour they pay less than a living wage for, are at best morally suspect. And John Key is not a businessman, he’s a professional gambler who made money on the stock exchange, without producing any goods.

Gordon Bowers, Auckland

Like many other citizens, I am disturbed by the appeal attempt being made by Malcolm Rewa - he has had his day in court already. Who is paying for the lawyers involved in this appeal?

El Niño 2026: What growers need to know this season - Chris Brandolino

New Zealand Herald October 09, 2026

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

This is a modal window.

Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window.

End of dialog window.

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

Severe heat and drought overseas have understandably raised questions about what New Zealand’s spring and summer may bring.

At the same time, El Niño is tracking alongside, or ahead of, the strongest modern events.

For growers, the sensible response is neither complacency nor alarm, but early preparation for a wider range of plausible conditions.

New Zealand differs from Europe and Australia.

Our maritime setting generally moderates temperature extremes, although short periods of exceptional heat remain possible, especially in eastern districts when hot air crosses the Tasman and descends on the lee side of mountain ranges.

Growers should identify risks specific to each crop, block, region and growth stage.

El Niño is a naturally occurring shift in winds and warm water along the equatorial Pacific.

When the usual easterly winds weaken or reverse, warm water moves eastwards.

This redistribution of ocean heat changes tropical rainfall and influences the jet stream and weather patterns far from the equator, including around New Zealand.

It is not possible to provide a single deterministic forecast.

Current conditions strengthen confidence in the broad seasonal signal, but not in precise rainfall or temperatures months ahead.

Every El Niño has its own “personality”, so the following patterns are broad zones rather than property-level forecasts, and significant local variation should be expected.

In northern and eastern parts of both islands, the odds are tilted towards drier-than-usual conditions, particularly as spring progresses into November and summer.

In the western North Island, dryness may occur at either end of the six-month period, with a potentially more normal rainfall window around December and early January.

Wetter-than-usual conditions are more likely in the western and southern South Island, increasing the risk of waterlogging, access disruption, disease pressure and localised flooding.

In the South Island and lower North Island, southwesterly outbreaks may keep the risk of late frosts or cold snaps elevated deeper into spring.

Eastern districts may experience brief spikes of very hot weather when west-northwest winds develop.

These warm, blustery periods can be followed within days by a front and a sharp southwesterly temperature change.

Growers therefore need to prepare for volatility, not just seasonal averages.

Drought risk is more than a lack of rain.

The most serious dryness is likely where below-normal rainfall, persistent wind and high temperatures coincide, accelerating evaporation and plant water loss.

Even within a broadly dry season, isolated heavy-rain events remain possible and may damage crops or disrupt individual businesses.

There is no single horticultural impact.

A dry summer may support flavour and sugar development in some fruit crops if adequate spring water has supported bud break and fruit set, while severely constraining shallow-rooted vegetables.

Year-round vegetable production in areas more accustomed to flooding may be exposed if systems and crop plans are not designed for prolonged dryness.

Practical preparation starts with mapping exposure by crop, block and growth stage rather than relying on one seasonal assumption.

Growers can set operational triggers for changing irrigation frequency, protecting young plants, delaying planting, adjusting harvest timing or activating frost protection.

Crop, place and timing will determine which actions matter most.

Growers should confirm water availability, including bore and well reliability, and check irrigation infrastructure before demand peaks.

This will help identify constraints and address failures while parts and contractors are still available.

Growers can also review soil-moisture monitoring, mulching, groundcover, cultivation and drainage so soils can retain useful rain while safely shedding excess water.

It’s important to review insurance, business-continuity arrangements, labour plans and alternative supply options where weather disruption could affect harvest or market commitments.

Listen to Jamie Mackay interview Chris Brandolino on The Country

Plans should cover water shortage and sudden excess, including drainage, erosion control, access, crop protection and recovery arrangements.

El Niño typically rises, peaks and weakens over many months.

Current expectations are for the event to peak around November or December and then weaken, with effects potentially persisting through at least the following autumn.

Even as equatorial ocean temperatures return towards neutral, the atmosphere can retain momentum.

El Niño changes the odds – it does not guarantee an outcome.

It explains only part of New Zealand’s weather variability, with ocean temperatures, pressure systems and individual events also important.

A season may be drier than normal overall yet still contain a damaging downpour, frost, cold change or heat spike.

Growers should match their forecast tool to particular decisions. Long-range outlooks support seasonal planning, while shorter-range forecasts guide spraying, irrigation, frost protection and harvest.

Use trusted meteorological advice and revisit forecasts frequently as a decision date approaches.

Where possible, consider an ensemble of model outcomes: agreement increases confidence, while a wide spread signals uncertainty that should be built into decisions.

The best-prepared growers will plan beyond the first hot or dry spell.

Water, crop, labour and financial decisions may need to cover a prolonged period of elevated variability.

Early preparation, clear triggers and regularly updated forecasts will provide the strongest basis for protecting production and responding quickly as conditions develop.

I’m looking forward to hosting a Horticulture New Zealand webinar for growers on October 13, where I’ll discuss the outlook and what it could mean for the season ahead.

Chris Brandolino is the principal scientist, forecasting, for Earth Sciences New Zealand.

Mount Maunganui-based kiwifruit marketer Zespri says fruit quality remains a key focus as the industry responds to increasing competition in export markets.

Chief executive Jason Te Brake said that while sales remained strong, lower harvest pressure this season meant the industry was managing slightly elevated levels of softer fruit and remained focused on quality management at the back end of the season.

“Our priority is keeping our sales rates up and moving fruit steadily through to customers to avoid a build-up of aged inventory,” he said.

“We’ve also increased checking onshore before fruit is shipped, while the industry has embraced targeted quality interventions and tighter inventory management to help protect customer confidence and grower value.”

Te Brake said recent conversations with the kiwifruit industry had also focused on strengthening Zespri’s position in a changing China market.

“We are confident in the future of our China market, but it is becoming more challenging.

“We are facing increased competition from locally grown G3, which is increasingly competing with more variable New Zealand G3 at the back end of our season.

“The emergence of Chinese G3, supported by strong quality, brands and routes to market, is something we need to respond to strongly.

“Our focus is on having high-quality fruit on shelves all year round to protect and build our brand, retain shelf space, strengthen relationships with our partners and maintain our category leadership.”

Te Brake said the focus was on delivering a solution that protected Zespri’s premium brand and grower returns in China, now and into the future.

“Our priority will always be maximising New Zealand grower returns and, as part of that, we need to give ourselves the ability to compete as strongly as possible, securing our retail, distribution and supply-chain relationships with the highest-quality fruit year-round.

“That fruit quality is critical. We can only command a premium when our quality consistently justifies it, and the clear feedback from our customers is that, at the moment, it does not, particularly at the back end of the season where quality is variable and where fruit is competing directly with Chinese G3.

“That means higher quality costs, slower sales and a risk to our brand premium over time if we don’t respond.

“Any solution also needs to be practical and sustainable.”

Zespri has been discussing two options with the industry.

The first is to continue competing from New Zealand, focusing on improving late-season quality, investing in post-harvest innovation and developing long-storing varieties.

The second is a tightly controlled China Supply procurement model.

“If we pursue China Supply, the model must create and protect value for New Zealand growers while giving Chinese partners a clear incentive to meet Zespri standards and support the brand long term,” Te Brake said.

“There are risks and opportunities with both options, and we will keep working through these openly with growers over the coming months.”

He said no decisions had been made and any proposal would proceed only with grower support through a producer vote.

With Zespri entering the latter stages of the 2026 season, its latest forecast expects strong returns for growers from a record crop of 225 million trays.

The August forecast shows average per-hectare returns are expected to exceed last year’s record returns for all categories except Green and Organic Green.

Te Brake said the forecast per-hectare returns reflect this season’s increased yields and the value secured across global markets despite a more challenging market environment.

Mike Murphy, head of communications and strategic projects at New Zealand Kiwifruit Growers Incorporated (NZKGI), said the higher yields resulted from good pollination, an increase in orchard hectares and favourable weather.

He also noted growers should prepare for the upcoming El Niño weather pattern, which was forecast to bring dry conditions interspersed with heavy rainfall.

“Preparedness for both irrigation and drainage systems will be front of mind.”

Te Brake said forecast per-tray returns remained within the indicative ranges provided by Zespri in June.

“Green and Organic per-tray returns reflect strong demand, lower Green volumes and the expectation of a shorter selling window this season,” he said.

“SunGold forecast returns reflect a more challenging market environment, with increased competition from summer fruit, pricing pressure across parts of Asia and a larger-than-expected crop.”

Te Brake said with more fruit to sell, the focus had been on managing the allocation of this year’s crop to help maximise grower returns.

“Quality remains our major focus as we move through the second half of the sales season, with our teams managing this through careful market allocation and inventory management, and by working closely with suppliers and customers to maximise value for growers.”

A dementia diagnosis has long been a death sentence. But are things about to change?

Sydney Morning Herald October 10, 2026

It’s been called our greatest health fear. But revolutionary new drugs, diagnostic tests and encouraging research into prevention and rehabilitation are improving the outlook.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.
