Flydubai co-pilot planned suicide attack on Israeli airport, UAE prosecutors say

The Guardian Fri, 09 Oct 2026 20:38:11 GMT

Hammam al-Hammami is believed to have been targeting the passenger terminal at Ben Gurion airport near Tel Aviv

The co-pilot who tried to seize control of a passenger jet flying from Dubai to Tel Aviv last week was planning to launch a suicide attack targeting the passenger terminal at Israel’s international airport, prosecutors in the United Arab Emirates said on Friday.

Hammam al-Hammami attacked the plane’s Indian pilot with an emergency axe, but failed to prevent his badly injured colleague from opening the cockpit’s security door to allow passengers to overpower his assailant.

Passengers then tried to control the aircraft, which was safely landed in Saudi Arabia by an off-duty relief pilot who was among about 180 passengers.

Dr Hamad Saif al-Shamsi, attorney-general of the UAE, said on Friday that al-Hammami, who is in Emirate custody, had admitted he had tried to execute a “premeditated terrorist plot to … launch a suicide attack targeting the passenger terminal at Ben Gurion airport near Tel Aviv, with the aim of causing the greatest possible loss of life”.

The 29-year-old, who was hired by flydubai, a government-owned low-cost airline, began a process of radicalisation while studying in Australia when he was influenced by the hardline takfiri ideology through reading extremist literature and online content glorifying terrorist organisations and suicide attacks, al-Shamsi said in a statement.

“[Al-Hammami] subsequently developed … ideas advocating violence and terrorism. He also drew inspiration from the 11 September 2001 attacks, and the idea of carrying out a similar operation using an aircraft became firmly established in his thinking. According to his confession, this was linked to his decision to pursue a career in aviation.”

Over the weekend, Australian security agencies launched an investigation after it emerged al-Hammami spent about two years in the country as a student until 2017. He left the country without completing his engineering degree.

New Zealand authorities have launched their own investigation after police confirmed al-Hammami underwent flight training there about a year after he abandoned a degree in Australia.

There has been widespread concern about how al-Hammami was able to pass vetting and join a crew flying to Israel. An Omani national, he earned a distance-learning aviation management degree from Buckinghamshire New University in 2023 and was employed by Oman Air from 2020-24, joined Royal Air Maroc in early 2025 and worked there for several months before moving to flydubai in January 2026.

Security officials have been keen to understand if al-Hammami was acting alone or had become involved with a group such as al-Qaida or Islamic State, which could suggest further such attacks might be planned. Emirate authorities believe this is not the case.

“In the presence of his lawyer and with all legally prescribed safeguards ensured, the suspect provided a detailed confession outlining his motives and the stages of planning and execution. He admitted that he had acted alone, without the involvement of others, although investigations are continuing to verify this claim,” al-Shamsi said.

Investigators have found al-Hammami had used two previous flights to Tel Aviv to “familiarise himself with the flight route ‌and the airport”, the Emirati state news agency WAM reported.

The passengers on board the aircraft were overwhelmingly Israeli, with prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu hailing them and the pilot for their bravery after the foiled attack.

Powerful 7.6-magnitude earthquake hits Panama and triggers tsunami warnings

The Guardian Fri, 09 Oct 2026 19:52:48 GMT

Hazardous waves are possible as far south as Ecuador and as far north as Mexico, as 13 aftershocks reported

A powerful 7.6 magnitude earthquake has struck Panama and triggered tsunami warnings along the west coast of Central and South America, according to the US Geological Survey (USGS).

The quake hit along the southern coast of the country, the USGS said. It was centered near the southern tip of the Central American country, about 14km (9 miles) south-west of the remote community of Pitaloza Arriba, the USGS said.

The Institute of Geosciences of the University of Panama said the quake struck at just before 1pm local time near the southern town of Tonosí. The Panamanian institute said that a second 6.0 magnitude earthquake struck soon after, at 1.22pm.

By 1.3opm there had reportedly been 13 aftershocks.

The president, José Raúl Mulino, said he had asked a key minister to call for calm. “What happened should not be used to generate alarm and disorder,” Mulino wrote on X.

Local newspaper La Prensa said that across the Central American country, buildings, schools and homes were evacuated as a result of the “powerful movement of the earth”.

Footage published by La Prensa showed severe damage to several buildings in the city of Penonomé, including the St John Baptist Cathedral. Other photos showed a highway to the west of the capital that had been completely sheared in half by the earthquake.

Tremors were felt strongly ​in the ⁠capital of ⁠Panama ​City, ‌according ‌to ‌witnesses who spoke to Reuters. The Associated Press reported that buildings shook and visibly shaken residents gathered outside as they waited for news of the quake’s impact.

The USGS said hazardous waves were possible along the coasts of Costa Rica, Ecuador, Peru, Nicaragua, Guatemala, El Salvador and Mexico, although the tsunami warning for Chile was cancelled at 4.18pm local time.

The Premier League is back: welcome to the new era of post-verdict unreality

The Guardian Fri, 09 Oct 2026 19:00:35 GMT

As the top flight returns, armed with the knowledge its serial champions have been the authors of a 10-year sham supremacy, the first question is simple: how is it going to feel?

The internet: an apology. It turns out you were right. It was actually a simulation all along. Now, talk to me about chemtrails again. And yes, maybe Vinícius Júnior has been replaced by a handsome, baffled-looking waxwork.

Welcome to the weirdest weekend of them all. We are now post-judgment, post-statement, postlapsarian. As the Premier League prepares to snap back into what must be described, out of habit, as reality, armed with the knowledge its serial champions have been the authors of a 10-year sham supremacy, the first question is fairly simple. How is it going to feel?

There is no precedent for this. Even the state of total confusion feels brittle given City maintain their complete state of innocence and deny all charges. We await the release of Irrefutable Body of Evidence, the great lost Madonna erotic thriller sequel, presumably recast around a steamy three-year regulatory tribunal scenario.

City’s appeal defence appears to be based around the government giving them money. This may or may not be related to how you control what the high court considers admissible. But it is also implied confirmation that the club is the propaganda tool of an overseas state, that Kyle Walker, for example, has basically been a civil servant all these years. Maybe the United Arab Emirates should have six stars on the national team jersey, one for each title. They even look like asterisks.

Beyond this there is the more basic issue of how to present this spectacle as entertainment. How do you structure a Match of the Day now? What’s the balance in the edit of bus-rage, taunting banner clips, managerial evasiveness content, versus the trivial stuff on the pitch with the balls and goals and men in shorts?

Mainly the Manchester City affair has created an existential problem. The key questions in English football are no longer things such as who will win the league, or will Tottenham get relegated (although this is still an excellent question). They are instead: what is real now? What was real then? What will be real in the future? Will something that seems real now become unreal later?

The whole experience brings to mind visiting the Yas Marina Formula One track in Abu Dhabi a few years back, a pristine place, all sweeping curves, perfect surfaces, dreamy floral boulevards. At that stage exploring its far reaches, following the curve around the final corner, led to: nothing. Out of sight the hanging baskets stopped dead. The sprinklers cut out. The pavement ended. The next step took you straight into sand and dead space.

Beyond the main stage the Yas track was a set, an imitation of life. And it turns out this is basically what Abu Dhabi was doing to the Premier League in the years 2009 to 2018: creating a product, a simulacrum, a pop-up.

At the end of which we have a blurring of edges, different versions of what could be real eliding into one another, a place where an AI video of Uncle Phil from the Fresh Prince scoring the Özil goal against Ludogorets seems just as real, just as plausible as City’s 6-0 thrashing of Watford in the FA Cup final. Seen through that lens this can feel like an extinction-level problem. Being real is, in the end, all sport actually has.

It feels fitting City’s first date in the new unreality is Liverpool at Anfield on Sunday, one of the great Premier League fixtures recast as a kind of ceremonial shame-event, a requiem for a dream. Liverpool have a clearer sense of grievance than most, having been deprived of league titles three times on the final day by a club that was colouring outside the lines.

In many ways the game at Anfield is a perfect snapshot of what we have lost. This should be an entirely pure and gripping sporting contest. Instead the biggest story in top-tier English football is the meaninglessness of top-tier English football. The headline product is gossip, side-eye, legal backstory.

In their next 14 league games City will play three teams who have reserved the right to sue them. How can these occasions be seen as credible acts of sport? Even the banter-culture is out of date. For the past 12 years City at Anfield has been soundtracked by the Steve Gerrard/He slipped on his arse incident, a source of public pain that has defined the late-stage career of Liverpool’s most beloved modern captain. Except, we now know the actual story is the club that finished above them were cheating.

It turns out this is the first stage of football grief. Poring over the endless counterfactuals. Some are pretty stark. The five league titles won on the last day of the season. The 1-0 FA Cup final victory against Stoke, coached by a man with two contracts, the winning goal scored by a player linked, by close association, with the book-cooking regime.

There is a butterfly effect here of endless interference. What do Inter make of all this? Imagine losing a Champions League final that could have transformed your modern history, by the narrowest margin, to a club that appear to have built their own era out of cheating on their income. Two years later Inter were thrashed by another nation-state team and Simone Inzaghi was shunted off the set. He’s in Saudi now. Just get on the train.

Then there’s the wider structural stuff. City spent nine years flooding the zone with government-backed transfer funds (€1.2bn in those nine years: miles out in front), skewing the money supply in every league in Europe. The extra £20m disbursed at the last moment to drag Kevin De Bruyne out of the Bundesliga. What happens if that doesn’t happen?

At home, Spurs missed the Champions League by one spot four times, always in City’s slipstream. Would Manchester United have signed Rasmus Højlund without that steamrollering model of Erling Haaland-era success?

How to reprocess the deep cultural influence of Pep Guardiola? This was based on Guardiola’s genius as a coach, which is still real, irrespective of the gradient of the playing field. But nothing succeeds like success. Winners get to rewrite history. How does it feel now that Guardiola’s style affected so profoundly the way kids play park football, the way young coaches work, all of it based on sustained blockbusting example?

Even the Football Association’s England DNA pathway was basically a Pep document, predicated on the undeniable evidence of his winning way. The method is still good, the detail unarguable, the tactical blueprint pure. But that 10-year spell in England was also supercharged by cheating.

Sign up to Football Daily

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

after newsletter promotion

We mourn too the legend of the Catalan brain trust, the hours spent studying this pure and monk-like dynamic. Yeah, fine. But also chuck vast amounts of hidden cash at it. Not to mention the hundreds of articles, podcasts, academic studies, fan tributes and personal tomes about purity, legacy, style, the glory that sailed above all other questions.

City’s fans are entitled to some space here, a chance to effect their own reckoning up. Elements of that support may have responded over the years with bizarre levels of aggression to any questioning of the process. But it is also normal to believe what you’re told, not least when it includes the profound transformation of the thing you love. How to process a total narrative U-turn?

The City documentary series A Beautiful Obsession is a far more interesting watch now, like The Sixth Sense when you know the ending. The project is cast by its editors as a pure passion play, Pep portrayed as a tunnel-vision obsessive, pictured most often staring at a whiteboard covered in magnets while the world turns beyond his line of vision.

It is impossible now not to see some kind of willed seclusion, Prospero on his island, rough magic starting to fray as reality crashes on to the shores. Episodes one to four are portrayed as a Viking funeral for the age of Pep. But they are now an unwitting farewell to something else too. In his final appearance Pep is shown quoting Kipling, saying triumph and disaster are both impostors. And he’s right. It turns out they were. Most notably the triumph bits.

Just before the end credits we see one of City’s club channel celebrations, with boards plastered in the usual phrases the club seems to feel drawn to. This is how it felt. We see things they’ll never see. Looking back this was always part of the dynamic, the insistence, which is usually just taken as read, that this is all real, that the feelings were feelings, that nobody can fake this away.

It is still the mantra for some. And maybe that’s true. But if so, what did it add up to in the first place? An episode of a TV show? An induced high, a snort of disposable pleasure?

But then, this is also not the end. There is always disasterism in football, the sense the thing happening now is the thing that will always happen. But football’s enduring strength, the one thing that marks it out as indestructible, is its relentlessness. We are in the period of rupture and parallax error. But how long will it last?

Plenty of good can still come from this. The idea that English football is profoundly damaged by this may prove wide of the mark. What is happening here, and this includes the outcome of the appeal, is that rules are being enforced. Andy Burnham may have confused the process with his tone-deaf and weirdly partial comments. But for all the delay and indecision this is still the rule of law in action.

And maybe English football gets to learn something. Maybe the unregulated nature of the league can reset a little. At the very least it seems axiomatic the new regulatory powers should ensure no nation state, or state fund, however you want to semanticise it, gets to own a club again.

There are still 33 rounds of Premier League games to run in the age of whiplash. The current interlude may feel like a football version of those bits in the Terminator films where Sarah Connor drives around in a Jeep looking glazed and distant, prepping for the time of skulls and robot death-rays, disengaged from the meaningless lives of blind and foolish humans.

Football always moves on. Throw flares at a bus, taunt the deceived souls in the away end. But the future is still wide open. Perhaps we can even face it with a little hope in the time of conflict.

Lionesses take control of World Cup playoff tie but unfancied Greece still in fight

The Guardian Fri, 09 Oct 2026 18:46:37 GMT

World Cup qualifying playoff: Greece 1-3 England

Stanway, Le Tissier and Russo on target

Sarina Wiegman said she wanted to see a bit more from her side after their fairly underwhelming performance against a hugely unfancied Greek side, despite securing a valuable first-leg victory in their Women’s World Cup playoff tie.

Georgia Stanway’s neat finish, Maya Le Tissier’s first England goal and Alessia Russo’s low strike were enough to give England control but a Kallisti Brouksair goal for Greece means that the tie is not definitively over, going into Tuesday’s second leg, and Wiegman acknowledged that England had been “a bit sloppy” at times.

“I think we made it a bit harder [for ourselves],” Wiegman said, while also giving credit to Greece for being “very well-prepared, very well-organised and very disciplined”, before adding: “Of course, I’m happy with the 3-1. I’m not happy with the 1.

“We were – in moments – really good on the ball, and we were, in moments, not so good on the ball and we could have made better decisions, too.

“We want to play really well. Of course, we go out to win, but we want to show more than winning, we want to play really well too.”

Facing a Greek side ranked 59th in the world, who have never qualified for a major tournament, England began as overwhelming favourites and dominated the ball but often appeared to be going through the motions, making hard work of breaking down Greece’s deep defensive shape. It would be too much of a stretch to describe it as a bad performance but, at the same time, England did lack their usual zip, charisma and urgency and their body language suggested they were focused on the job at hand, rather than enjoying themselves.

Perhaps the flat atmosphere was to blame for that. The Hellenic Football Federation had made the tickets free for this fixture but – despite that – only a few thousand turned up and there was scarcely any cheers from the home supporters. Instead, around 500 travelling England fans were generating the majority of the noise.

It meant that the first 45 minutes were largely forgettable and lacking in real quality, aside from a few isolated moments such as a delicious chip from 25 yards out from Lauren James, which drew a gasp of appreciation from the away fans as it hit the net and they thought England had taken the lead. A VAR check showed that James was offside.

England were playing with a back three when in possession, pushing Le Tissier very high up the pitch as a right wing-back, and with a back four when out of possession. They were untroubled defensively except for a huge let-off at 0-0 when the Greece striker Ionna Papatheodorou hit the woodwork. She eased past Esme Morgan and Leah Williamson with alarming ease and her shot from range looked to have beaten Hannah Hampton, but struck the bar.

England, who had gone close when Laura Blindkilde Brown shot straight at the goalkeeper, James curled a free-kick wide and Lauren Hemp drilled a low shot narrowly wide across the face of goal, eventually found their breakthrough when Blindkilde Brown played a quick ball to Russo, whose good touch to lay the ball off for Stanway allowed the midfielder to slot in low.

After the break, Le Tissier powered in a strong finish after clever work from Keira Walsh to open up space, and when Russo tucked a low finish into the bottom corner to make it 3-0 four minutes later, England might have been hoping the floodgates were open. However, some limp defending allowed Rangers’ Brouksair to pull a goal back, firing in a low finish after a hopeful, bouncing, high long ball was not initially dealt with by Morgan.

The Republic of Ireland cruised to an 8-0 victory in the first leg of their Women’s World Cup qualifying play-off against Kazakhstan in Astana. Kyra Carusa scored twice while further goals from Chloe Mustaki, Emily Murphy, Abbie Larkin, Jamie Finn, Shanade Hopcroft and Jessie Stapleton made Tuesday’s second leg in Cork a formality. Carusa had already grabbed her brace – and Mustaki also hit the target – before the Kazakhstan captain, Yulia Myasnikova, was sent off just beyond the half-hour mark for a foul on Larkin. The decision allowed the visitors to shrug off the absence of Katie McCabe due to injury and stroll to victory, with the outstanding Mustaki providing the assists for both Carusa’s goals as well as the fifth for Larkin shortly before half-time. Scotland defeated Czechia 2-0 in Pardubice, with Caroline Weir and Claire Emslie on target in the second half. Tereza Krejciríkova was sent off for the hosts three minutes from time. A 21st-minute Ezmiralda Franja own goal secured Wales a 1-0 win in Albania. Northern Ireland's World Cup hopes are all but over, however, after a 4-0 first leg home loss by Portugal. Telma Encarnação, Jéssica Silva, a Rebecca Holloway own goal and Fátima Pinto the scorers.

England went close to adding to their tally, as James curled narrowly wide and the substitute Jess Park’s effort hit the bar, on a night when Erica Meg Parkinson and Grace Fisk were handed senior international debuts, late on.

Assuming they finish the job off on Tuesday in the second leg in Leicester, England would face Slovakia or Ukraine in the second round of the playoffs in the November-December international window. That tie would also be staged over two legs and England would need to win that to secure their spot at next summer’s tournament in Brazil. To be competitive there, though, they know they will need to markedly improve on their cohesion and fluidity with the ball.

Wiegman said: “I have seen some fluid moments too. You just want more. And you want the final balls and the positions in front of the goal [to be] better, and of course we’re working on that, with the amount of time we have. Some things, we’d really want to do better and we’re working really hard to do so. We have an opportunity now to fix that, for Tuesday.”

‘Abolish ICE’: Mamdani, AOC and other Democrats urge action after New York shooting

The Guardian Fri, 09 Oct 2026 18:29:56 GMT

Immigration officer shot man in car where five-year-old child was sitting, sparking fierce protests

Leading New York Democrats expressed anger and demanded curbs on Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) violence after a federal officer shot a man driving a car in which his five-year-old son was sitting, sparking fierce protests.

At least seven shots were reportedly fired and the man was hit in the neck late on Thursday afternoon as children were coming home from school in the busy Marble Hill neighborhood of New York City. Marble Hill is considered part of Manhattan, but is physically located in the Bronx.

Federal authorities on Friday morning identified Oscar Belgal as the man shot, saying he was undocumented, from the Dominican Republic and had a felony record and gang affiliations.

Belgal was later booked into the Metropolitan Detention Center, Brooklyn, federal lockup, which is newly being used to detain immigrants, according to his attorneys and a US prosecutor who spoke during a hearing on Friday afternoon.

He still has a “bullet in his body” and has not been able to communicate with his family, his attorneys said during the hearing.

ICE took Belgal on Thursday from a New York hospital into New Jersey. He reportedly spent the night inside the Elizabeth Contract Detention Facility, a privately run ICE facility, before being brought back into New York and being booked into MDC Brooklyn.

Meanwhile, Belgal was able to have only one phone call with lawyers on Friday, his attorney Paige Austin with Make the Road New York said.

A New York federal judge on early Friday morning ordered ICE to keep Belgal in the area, after his attorneys filed emergency motions requesting his release.

The justice department is likely to argue that Belgal’s transfer into New Jersey took place before the judge’s order, making the order requiring ICE to keep him in the area moot. And Belgal’s attorneys have indicated that they will continue challenging his detention.

The Justice Department will likely argue that Bergal’s transfer into New Jersey took place before the New York judge’s order, which would make the judge’s order requiring ICE to keep him in the area moot. Bergal’s attorneys will continue to challenge his detention.

Marcos Charles, a senior ‌ICE official, said Belgal refused ​to exit his car when approached by ‌federal officers who were trying to arrest him, and then accelerated, ‌struck two ICE vehicles and drove towards other officers. An ICE officer then shot Belgal and Charles said the wound was “superficial”.

Footage showed a man in a high-visibility construction vest, possibly with a badge on a lanyard, carrying an assault-style rifle and standing close to Belgal, who is sat on the street, while another officer appears to hold a hand to his neck and shoulder area.

New York police officers in uniform shortly afterwards carry the man to an unmarked car and lay him in the back seat, handcuffed behind his back.

But Kathy Hochul, New York’s governor, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a New York congresswoman, and Zohran Mamdani, the city’s mayor – all of whom are Democrats – led strong condemnation of ICE’s conduct.

Darializa Avila Chevalier, the Democratic New York candidate, rushed to the protests and was knocked over in the chaos as local police and demonstrators clashed.

The wounded man was conscious and hospitalized, authorities said.

A joint statement from Bronx and Manhattan borough presidents Vanessa L Gibson and Brad Hoylman-Sigal, respectively, said their constituents “stand united in outrage” over Belgal’s shooting.

“The frustration, pain, anger and trauma stoked by this incident extends far beyond an individual,” the statement said.

Mamdani called the incident “unconscionable” and said on Thursday night that ICE, part of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), had “whisked him away” from the New York-Presbyterian Allen hospital in upper Manhattan.

A similar incident occurred in Texas last month after a man was shot by an ICE officer in Austin and despite a bullet lodged in his back was taken by the federal authorities from a local hospital to ICE detention about 140 miles away.

Ocasio-Cortez and Mamdani demanded ICE be abolished.

Both Hochul and Mamdani spoke to Donald Trump and Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, by phone on Thursday night.

“I have been on ​the phone with President Trump and Secretary Mullin negotiating ‌the release of the man ICE agents ‌shot. Those negotiations were unsuccessful,” Mamdani told a press conference. He demanded from the Trump ‌administration that ICE stop its enforcement actions in New York City. “ICE is rotten to its core,” he said.

ICE has been stepping up arrests all year despite withdrawing massed militarized ranks from Minneapolis in January and adopting a more covert approach to enforcement.

Both Hochul and Mamdani demanded that ICE cease enforcement operations in New York and the governor said she expressed outrage to the Trump administration on behalf of all New Yorkers. Hochul added that the incident could easily have ended in tragedy.

“No child should ever have to experience the terror of gunfire,” she said. The child was being looked after by his family on Friday.

The streets where the shooting and protests took place were calm on Friday morning but many residents remained shocked and angry.

“Here’s an innocent child that was caught in the crossfire,” said Calvin Hayden, a south Bronx native. “That child could have been killed.” Hayden heard about the shooting the night before and said he was immediately disturbed. He came to Marble Hill, the northernmost part of Manhattan, to see the aftermath.

“I don’t believe ICE has any reason or right to be in New York City,” he said, adding he thought New York was already equipped on its own to handle immigration disputes without ICE presence.

“There’s a lot of individuals who are not committing crimes and they just want to make a better life for themselves,” he said.

Some drivers on 225th Street yelled anti-ICE sentiments as they drove past the scene.

Mullin said on Friday morning that the ICE officers involved in the shooting did not know there was a child in the vehicle and defended the agency’s actions. But he pointed out that Belgal would have obviously known the child was in his car when he drove it at officers. The exact sequence of events leading up to the shooting have not yet become clear.

Mullin said that Hochul had asked the DHS for a pause on enforcement in New York.

“No, we are not putting a pause on enforcement,” he said.

Mullin criticized New York’s “sanctuary” policies, ​which restrict how much city agencies and police cooperate with immigration authoritie.

Belgal, 28, has prior convictions, was serving five years of probation for felony grand larceny and was also arrested on drug charges in 2025, a case that is still pending, according to the New York police department.

“What happened today was an outrage,” Mamdani said late on Thursday, adding: “When ICE agents opened fire, a five-year-old child – a five-year-old child! – was in the back seat of that car. Thank God that child is physically unharmed.”

Witnesses told local media they heard the child yelling at the officers after the shooting. At least 20 people have been shot by federal immigration agents under the second Trump administration, as well as a rise in deaths in detention.

“ICE is a rogue, lawless and paramilitary surveillance agency. It does not belong in New York City and it should not exist in the United States of America. Abolish ICE,” Ocasio-Cortez said in a statement.

The representative also condemned the retail company Target for allowing federal enforcement teams to use its parking lots as staging areas from which to launch arrest operations.

Protesters held signs saying:“Jail all killer ICE agents” and “Leave our neighbors alone.”

“ICE, get the fuck out of our neighborhood,” shouted Gibson, the Bronx borough president. “I’m angry that we have to be here … We are a working-class community. We don’t deserve this type of treatment from the White House.” She encouraged the crowd to get involved in opposing ICE, saying: “There are more of us than there are of them. I want this to be a moment that we turn into a movement.”

Protesters gathered at the hospital where Belgal was taken. The police set up barricades and protesters quickly clashed with officers in a chaotic scene.

Demonstrators banged drums and shouted: “Shut it down,” and “ICE out!” as cars driving by honked in support.

Standing outside the hospital, Murad Awawdeh, the president of the New York Immigration Coalition, said he wanted to see an independent investigation into the shooting led by New York officials.

“The pain that you’re witnessing is people who are witnessing their neighbors, their family members, their friends being ripped away,” he said.

ICE has arrested more than 19,500 people in New York and nearly 18,000 in New Jersey during the second Trump administration, mostly Latin American immigrant men without criminal histories, Gothamist reported earlier this week using government data, adding that those totals were more than double the number of such arrests in the last 18 months of the Biden administration.

The Premier League so far: draws, underperforming xG and other data pointers

The Guardian Fri, 09 Oct 2026 18:00:34 GMT

Goal averages are crumbling as players take fewer touches in the box and forwards underperform against xG

Goals are on the up in the Premier League. The average of 2.70 non-penalty goals per game in 2026-27 is higher than last season and two of the four previous campaigns. Yet we should have been even more royally entertained. Matches have averaged 2.88 non-penalty expected goals, the second most in the past six seasons. Chances have been going to waste.

If the 20 teams converted at the par rate, there would have been almost two extra goals per week. As few as that sounds, the proportion of games drawn is higher than in any past Premier League season. Some tied matches might have been settled had the finishing been up to the mark.

This is an issue across the Premier League. Fourteen clubs have scored fewer goals than expected, whether penalties are included or not, up from 10 last season. While there are eight teams that are within a goal of their underlying numbers and may see an immediate change of fortunes this weekend, the remaining 12 are split 8-4 towards the underachievers.

It is not just season-wide averages that are crumbling but week-by-week performances, too. There were 24 instances of a team scoring at least one goal fewer than their xG implied they should have across the first five match weeks, twice as many as occurred in the opening 50 games last season.

There are numerous possible explanations. Chance quality does not appear to be one of them, as the expected goals per non-penalty shot average only drops once more decimal places are applied than feels healthy.

At first glance, volume of touches in the penalty area has barely shifted either. A Premier League team is averaging 24.8 touches in the opposition box per game, down just 0.6 on last season.

The breakdown by team is more revealing. Four of last season’s top five are having fewer box touches per match, with Aston Villa and Liverpool having seen around a third disappear from their averages.

The one team from the quintet to increase is Manchester United, but they have only played one club that finished in the top 10 last season and five of their eight goals occurred against Championship runners-up Ipswich. A finely tuned attacking machine they are not. United top the Premier League for non-penalty shots, and are joint-second bottom for the average expected goal value.

They have not been helped by their top player for non-penalty xG: Bryan Mbeumo is one of 10 players who have scored at least one goal fewer than underlying numbers imply he should have. As he underachieved by 1.19 last season, this is not especially odd. The issue is how reliant United are upon the 27-year-old. This problem is not exclusive to this combination of club and player either.

The top player for expected goals at almost every Premier League club is having a bigger share of the xG pie than they enjoyed last season. This need not necessarily be a concern, as the figures will drop once playing time and chances are more equally shared within squads.

The most involved players themselves may help explain why goals are down, though. The top players from each club have collectively scored 6.8 non-penalty goals fewer than expected, almost 40% of the shortfall across the division from just 20 players.

Thierno Barry has been the player taking the chance for 49.4% of Everton’s non-penalty expected goals this season, up from 17.7% last term. It’s a massive increase in responsibility for a relatively young player – he has scored twice from chances valued at 3.5 xG.

Alexander Isak has seen a greater leap in share of team expected goals, though injuries meant he did not feature that often last season. There are seeds of growth for him at Liverpool, but he remains relatively new in terms of minutes played for the club. As with more than half of Premier League clubs, Isak is playing under a new man in the dugout.

Isak’s replacement at Newcastle, Yoanne Wissa, underperformed against xG by more than two goals last season, as did Marcus Tavernier at Bournemouth. They may not be the best players for their clubs to funnel their chances through. At least they are preferable to the situation at Tottenham, where centre-back Jan Paul van Hecke is their leading player for non-penalty expected goals.

Elsewhere, the players with the most xG for Fulham (Gonzalo García) and Ipswich (Emersonn) are 22 years old and new to English football. Hull’s Oli McBurnie, meanwhile, has never scored more than six goals in a Premier League campaign. Erling Haaland remains a reliable presence in the xG-heavy frontman stakes, but the situation at Manchester City may affect his form.

Excessive reliance on players who can be forgiven for underperforming could prove to be a small-sample statistical quirk that is quickly remedied. Until it is, do not bank on the goal rate reaching the expected goal level in the Premier League.

The Spurs of Prem Rugby: how Harlequins lost their swagger

The Guardian Fri, 09 Oct 2026 18:00:34 GMT

Marcus Smith’s return from injury offers hope but Quins appear a fragile side beset by entrenched problems

Speak to anyone who holds Harlequins close to their heart and a word that often comes up is “fragility”. Fragile in defence against Gloucester last weekend but mentally fragile too. The scars of recent seasons are deep and the problems entrenched. A club that is famed for its swagger has, in short, lost its mojo and the more you pull back the curtain, the longer it appears it will take to return.

A caveat. It would be oh so very typical of Harlequins to swashbuckle their way past Sale Sharks on Sunday but in many ways, that feels like part of the problem. During pre-season Harlequins set themselves the target of following in the footsteps of Exeter, who finished ninth two seasons ago before reaching the final last June. As Marcus Smith pointed out, it was not so long ago that Quins were seventh in January with only two wins and champions five months later. But in the eyes of supporters, these former glories, these roadmaps out of their current malaise are doing little but masking the extent of the problems, offering but false hope.

One former player drew a comparison with Tottenham this week. A club with an identity cemented in derring-do who have bottomed out of late. A club that’s spent big in an attempt to solve the problems – on George Furbank in Harlequins’ case – after years of wayward recruitment but largely overlooked areas that most needed strengthening.

There’s a sense that they will turn the corner but a sense too that they are just waiting for it to happen. A club with an eye on commercial exploits – for Spurs’ shiny stadium, see Harlequins’ Big Game pursuits. Even the comments this week by Harlequins’ head coach, Jason Gilmore, that he expected a difficult start to the campaign echoed those by Thomas Frank last season that, “I promise you one thing … we will lose football matches”, which incensed Tottenham supporters. Put it all together and the round-ball comparison rings true.

Shaun Edwards has agreed to join Argentina’s coaching staff through to the 2027 World Cup, ending any chance of the defence guru joining Steve Borthwick’s England set-up for next year’s tournament.

The 59-year-old, who is the most decorated coach in rugby history, joined the England women’s coaching staff on a short-term consultancy basis last month, raising the prospect he may potentially transfer to Borthwick’s staff for next year’s tournament. The Rugby Football Union has, however, allowed Edwards to slip through its fingers and Argentina will benefit in Australia.

Wigan-born Edwards has repeatedly expressed his desire to coach the England men’s team but while the RFU chief executive, Bill Sweeney, has admitted to a meeting in the past, a move has never materialised. Earlier this week, the RFU announced that Joe El-Abd will be leaving the men's coaching set-up after the World Cup. In theory, Edwards will also be available again then should England come calling. For now he is headed to Argentina with whom he will coach at his fifth World Cup and with his third different nation after three with Wales and his most recent, in 2023, with France.

The former rugby league great left his role with France earlier this year after seven years with Les Bleus and having helped them to the Six Nations title in March with a thrilling victory over England. It was his third with France, having won four with Wales during his 11-year stint.

Edwards joined John Mitchell’s England women’s set-up before they began their WXV campaign with a victory over New Zealand. He is to join Argentina in time for their November Nations Championship matches against Ireland, Italy and France while Mario Ledesma has also joined Felipe Contepomi’s Pumas’ staff as forwards coach.

“I’m thrilled to be joining Felipe Contepomi, his coaching staff, and the Argentinian team at the end of this month and through to next year’s World Cup in Australia,” said Edwards. “I’ve always admired the skill and quality of Argentinian players, and I look forward to contributing my international experience to the team over the next year.” Gerard Meagher

Gilmore, in fairness, finds himself in a difficult position. It is not his fault that after Danny Wilson’s abrupt exit, Harlequins promised “an exhaustive global coaching search” and then alighted on an in-house appointment. Gilmore is a popular figure with the squad but he has little previous head coaching experience. Robbie Deans has been appointed as performance director. The 67-year-old former Wallabies coach is vastly experienced but not in the English game and is spending “extended periods in the UK at critical points throughout the season” at the club while otherwise based overseas.

Gilmore’s first season in charge ended with a ninth-placed finish, Harlequins’ worst for eight years. Since the long-serving John Kingston left in 2018, Paul Gustard has occupied the position of head of rugby, then came the collective of Nick Evans, Adam Jones, Jerry Flannery and Charlie Mulchrone, who guided Harlequins to the 2021 title. Tabai Matson followed as senior coach, but he spent the last of his three seasons as performance director. Wilson was head coach between 2023 and 2025 until joining Wales and all the while there was Billy Millard, general manager from 2018 to 2021, director of performance from 2021 to 2023 then director of rugby until his exit in the summer of 2025. To put it kindly, it is a confusing roll call of appointments and job titles.

Evans left as attack coach over the summer after 18 years at the club and his replacement, Brad Cooper, is highly rated after joining from the Hurricanes. But Evans’s exit leaves Harlequins short on coaches with long-term associations with the club beyond Adam Jones. Indeed, it feels odd that club legends such as Joe Marler, Mike Brown, Danny Care and Ugo Monye have such little involvement. Freddie Burns may well prove himself to be a kicking coach of repute but there is little doubt he was appointed at Welford Road in part because he knows how it feels to pull on the Leicester Tigers jersey. It is a matter of time before Owen Farrell occupies the Saracens coaching box, George Ford will not be far behind at Sale but Harlequins seem to be missing a trick.

On the field, Harlequins’ front five is underpowered and they are light on quality at centre. The South Africans Wilco Louw and André Esterhuizen left in 2023 and 2024 respectively and have not been replaced by players of the same quality. That Nathan Jibulu and Will Joseph are thriving elsewhere indicates issues with developing young players.

It is true to say that the coaching changes this summer have led to an overhaul in playing systems, hence the point Gilmore was making. “We’ve been learning a brand new attack system and we’ve got a brand new lineout system that we’re putting in place that’s going to take four to six weeks just to bed down,” he said. “We’ve got the international players that have just come back into the building as well that are learning it on the run.” As Smith said before the season started: “It almost felt like we were playing catch-up coming back in from international duty.” But a 48-0 defeat by Gloucester, which leaves Harlequins bottom of the table, points to more grave problems.

For some, as long as Smith remains at the Stoop there is hope. He missed the first two defeats of the season but returns at Sale. He is contracted until 2028 but it remains to be seen if he will stay beyond that. It is said Smith was mightily close to joining Racing 92 a few years ago but was convinced to remain eligible for England’s 2023 World Cup campaign. If a similar offer comes again it may prove too hard to turn down. It says much about Harlequins’ current plight that few supporters would blame him.

Parties prepare for byelection in Farage seat amid speculation over £5m gift inquiry

The Guardian Fri, 09 Oct 2026 17:52:17 GMT

Tories said to be ready to fight in Clacton, with standards investigation rumoured to be nearing its end

Nigel Farage’s rivals are gearing up for a byelection in Clacton in the months ahead, amid speculation that the standards inquiry into his £5m gift is nearing a conclusion.

Conservative sources said the party was ready to fight in Farage’s seat, although senior figures in the shadow cabinet are divided about whether it would be winnable, given Farage’s victory in a byelection over the summer.

Other parties, including the hard-right Restore Britain, are also expected to put up candidates in the seat this time, after boycotting the August poll.

Westminster is poised for a battle over the future of Reform if the sanction from the standards inquiry is a heavy one.

The process could theoretically take place before Christmas if a decision is imminent, but the timelines of previous cases suggest it is more likely to be next year – if a serious sanction is imposed.

In the cases of Margaret Ferrier, the SNP MP who broke lockdown rules, and Peter Bone, the Tory MP found to have bullied staff, it took well over six months from the conclusion of the commissioner’s report for a byelection to take place.

The investigation into Farage’s gift began after the Guardian revealed in May that the crypto-billionaire Christopher Harborne had given him £5m just before the last election in 2024.

The Reform leader has said it was a personal matter, not political, and the money did not need to be declared. The rules state that financial support related to an MP’s job needs to be registered if given in the 12 months before they enter parliament.

Under the process, if a serious breach is found, the commissioner will pass a memorandum to the standards committee of MPs and lay members.

They would then have further discussions and call a further hearing or invite evidence from the MP before deciding on a penalty. That process can take weeks. The MP also has a right of appeal to the independent expert panel, which can take a further month or more.

If parliament agrees with a penalty of more than 10 days of suspension from the House of Commons, a recall petition could be held, requiring signatures from 10% of voters in the MP’s constituency over a period of six weeks.

In the cases of Bone and Ferrier, neither contested their seats, and Conservatives are hopeful that Farage could decide not to fight. “There’s a question of whether he will stand again,” said one shadow cabinet minister.

But Reform sources insisted Farage would fight for his seat again, having won the byelection against independent candidates including Count Binface by more than 11,000 votes.

He has also recently embarked on a tour of the country, in an attempt to shore up his core support, and a reorganisation of his party HQ. This includes launching a new Reform TV channel to pump out the party’s message direct to voters, hiring a team of 12 “journalists” headed by the former GB News producer Aaron Lobo, who had been director of operations.

Farage won a majority of 8,000 at the last general election, when he beat the sitting Tory MP, Giles Watling. The Conservative had previously won the seat with a majority of more than 25,000 in 2019, when there was no Brexit party candidate in the seat.

Two Latvians arrested at RAF base in Cambridgeshire released on bail

The Guardian Fri, 09 Oct 2026 17:46:16 GMT

Men found inside RAF Molesworth, used by US and Nato for intelligence, freed on strict conditions as police continue investigation

Two Latvian men have been released on bail after being arrested at an RAF base in Cambridgeshire used by the US military and Nato.

The two men, aged 32 and 26, were arrested at 2am on Thursday after they were discovered inside RAF Molesworth in Cambridgeshire, which is used by the US military and Nato for intelligence operations.

An investigation had begun four hours earlier, when military police found an abandoned vehicle near the facility at around 10pm on Wednesday.

Military police, joined by officers from Cambridgeshire police, discovered a small hole in the perimeter fence, before finding and arresting the two men inside the base.

The suspects, both Latvian nationals currently resident in the UK, were initially arrested on suspicion of trespass on a prohibited site and causing criminal damage. They were then further arrested on suspicion of an offence under section 4 of the National Security Act 2023, namely entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK.

They have since been released on bail, with strict conditions, as the police continue their investigation.

Commander Helen Flanagan, the head of Counter Terrorism Policing London, said they were “very aware of the recent heightened interest and concern around military sites”, but that there was nothing from their investigation so far to suggest a connection to an incident near RAF Fairford in September.

“Our investigation continues and we are working closely with colleagues from the Ministry of Defence police and Cambridgeshire constabulary on this. A key line of inquiry remains to identify any potential motivation behind why the men were at that location, and this includes whether it may be connected to any criminal activity,” she added.

Officers have since carried out two searches at addresses in the Peterborough area in connection with the investigation. The abandoned vehicle was also taken to a nearby police location.

Located west of Huntingdon, RAF Molesworth is home to Nato’s Intelligence Fusion Centre and the US Joint Intelligence Operations Center, Europe.

NHS faces exodus of ADHD and autism services staff to private clinics

The Guardian Fri, 09 Oct 2026 17:24:16 GMT

Brain drain of psychologists, psychiatrists and nurses leaves NHS ‘weaker’, driving patients to seek care elsewhere

Full report | NHS at risk of ‘system failures’ as demand for ADHD and autism care soars, inquiry finds

The NHS is facing an exodus of staff quitting its ADHD and autism services to join private clinics amid huge demand from children and adults to get a diagnosis.

The loss of specialist personnel to the private sector has already forced one NHS trust in England to limit access to its neurodevelopmental service to only the most urgent cases.

The brain drain of psychologists, psychiatrists, nurses and other staff are leaving the NHS “weaker” and making it more likely that people will be forced to seek private healthcare.

The NHS care watchdog announced on Friday it will start inspecting private clinics that offer diagnostic assessments for ADHD and autism, which are unregulated. The Care Quality Commission’s move follows the publication of the government-commissioned review of mental health and neurodiversity urging ministers to ensure all service providers are properly regulated amid claims of a “wild west” of private firms offering diagnostic tests.

Scores of private clinics have been set up in recent years offering assessments and treatment for ADHD and autism. They have capitalised on the large number of people who have been unable to access NHS care because services have been overwhelmed by an explosion in demand for diagnoses of neurodiversity, creating long waits for help and large backlogs.

Adrian James, the CQC’s interim inspector of mental health care, said: “This new responsibility will … close a significant gap in our oversight, meaning that people receiving these diagnoses can have far greater confidence in the service they are receiving.”

Prof Peter Fonagy’s report – thought to be the biggest inquiry of its kind in the world to date – voiced concern that private firms face the temptation of “financial incentives” to wrongly diagnose and treat patients whose symptoms mean they should not qualify for either.

The CQC already regulates services offering diagnosis and treatment. But the change means non-NHS clinics offering only diagnostic assessments will in future have to register with them.

Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, said the tighter regulation means “people can be confident that assessments are high quality and that the NHS is not being overcharged by independent or private providers”. About 810,000 children and adults in England are waiting for an assessment for ADHD or autism.

The risks to the NHS of losing staff to the private sector was highlighted last week when the Health Service Journal revealed that the Herefordshire and Worcestershire health and care NHS trust had been forced to restrict children and young people’s access to its neurodevelopmental service for that reason.

A paper presented to the trust’s board reported: “Neurodevelopmental staffing is reduced significantly, with the majority of leavers choosing to take up employment with ISP [independent sector providers] and RtC [Right to Choose] providers for ND [neurodiversity].”

Right to Choose gives NHS patients the right to have an NHS-funded ADHD or autism assessment with a private provider to help them receive care more quickly.

The trust responded to the exodus last month by limiting access by under-18s to only those with the most serious symptoms. It will revert to a normal service on Monday. A total of 1,298 people have already waited at least two years for an ADHD or autism assessment with the trust.

Thea Stein, the chief executive of the Nuffield Trust and a member of the government’s ADHD taskforce, said NHS services suffered when staff joined private operators, as also happens in physiotherapy and child and adolescent mental health services.

She said: “Some staff stay with the NHS part-time when they get a private-sector job, but many will walk away entirely, leaving the health service in a weaker position and under greater pressure.

“Concerning inequalities will widen further if the NHS can’t keep fully staffed teams or expand them to meet increasing demand for ADHD support. If these services continue to haemorrhage staff, some people will get much quicker support if they can afford to pay for private care,” Stein added.

The NHS Alliance, which represents trusts, confirmed the continuing exodus of staff. “We’re increasingly dealing with one ADHD workforce spread across different providers, both in the NHS and private sector,” Rebecca Gray, the director of the alliance’s mental health network, said.

“The significant growth in the private sector market, where people accessing services can often be seen more quickly than in stretched NHS services, will make working in the independent sector attractive to some staff.”

The Independent Healthcare Providers Network (IHPN), a trade body that represents many non-NHS firms, welcomed the CQC’s enhanced new role.

Sean Phillips, the IHPN’s head of policy, said: “While all of IHPN members who deliver ADHD and autism assessments are CQC registered – with 83% rated good or outstanding – we have long called for greater ‘end-to-end’ oversight of neurodevelopmental provision and it’s welcome to see that the CQC have confirmed they will now be regulating all providers of ADHD and autism assessments.”

Labour is starting to win back voters on the left who became disillusioned under Keir Starmer’s leadership, the party’s deputy leader has claimed after it saw off Zack Polanski and the Greens to win the Holborn and St Pancras byelection.

Labour’s Sagal Abdi-Wali took 45% of a relatively low turnout to keep Starmer’s old north London seat for the party, pushing Polanski, who had stood for the party he leads, into second place on 33%.

While the result was broadly as predicted, Labour strategists were buoyed up by the party’s relatively straightforward route to victory in a diverse inner-city area of the sort the Greens have been targeting with recent success.

The result “sends a clear message to those voters who lost faith in Labour in recent years”, said Lucy Powell, who called last month for the party to unite progressive voters under Andy Burnham if it wants to win the next election.

After the byelection win, she told the Guardian: “We hear you, we’ve listened and we know we needed to be clearer about what we stand for and what type of country we want to see, proudly putting our values centre stage. We’re delighted so many of you are backing us once again.”

The byelection came after the Green party voted at their conference last weekend to adopt a hugely controversial policy equating Zionism with racism, and saying Israel should be replaced with a single Palestinian state.

Polanski has been criticised for showing minimal leadership on the most toxic internal debate the Greens have faced in living memory, with the chair of Jewish Greens saying he should resign.

The byelection, called after Starmer resigned his Commons seat shortly after he was ousted by Burnham, saw a low turnout of 38.7%, possibly due to the widespread predictions that Labour was set to win, despite a major campaigning effort from the Greens.

The turnout also suggests Burnham could still face a battle to engage some voters in urban areas, particularly London, where the Greens took control of three councils in May’s local elections.

In an emotional victory speech, Abdi-Wali, a former child refugee who came to the UK from Somalia in the 1990s, hit out at “those who seek to divide us”, in what appeared to be a response to Reform UK’s Zia Yusuf, who suggested she was not British shortly after the byelection was called.

“I hope this moment says something about who gets to belong,” she said. “For people who look like me, I hope they see themselves reflected in this place and know that their path too belongs here. This is Camden, and this is Britain.”

Responding to the defeat, Polanski, who leads the Greens in England and Wales, said that while the result showed his party remained a major threat to Labour, many voters had told him they wanted to “give Andy Burnham a chance”.

It was the Greens’ second best-ever byelection result, more evidence of the party’s increased prominence and campaigning power since Polanski became leader 13 months ago.

The best came in February, when the Greens took an equally safe Labour seat, Gorton and Denton in Greater Manchester, in a major upset that weakened Starmer’s position. Around the same time, the Greens peaked at 21% in national polling, above Labour. They are now about 11%, more than 15 points behind Burnham’s party.

Polanski’s position has come under scrutiny since the Zionism motion was passed, with critics accusing him of abdicating leadership after he missed the debate to campaign in the byelection, giving no clear message about whether or not he backed it.

Andy Burnham is lucky – Polanski, Farage and Badenoch all seem determined to help him

The Guardian Fri, 09 Oct 2026 17:05:50 GMT

Everywhere the PM turns, he finds generous adversaries. They have made his early days in No 10 so much easier

I don’t know where Andy Burnham found his magic lamp, but I hope he’s taking good care of it. In the early hours of Friday morning, the genie that’s looked so kindly on him these past few months granted him yet another wish, with a byelection win in Holborn and St Pancras. It was just the latest gift for a prime minister for whom things keep going right – and who is especially blessed in his choice of opponents.

Let’s start with that win in London, where Labour’s Sagal Abdi-Wali defeated the Green party leader, Zack Polanski. It’s easy to miss how rare such a victory is. As the veteran psephologist Peter Kellner pointed out, this was a win that “defied history”. If the past half-century were any guide, Labour should have lost, thanks to a “truly dreadful record” defending its own seats when in government and facing a byelection challenge from the left or centre-left, the likes of the Greens or the Lib Dems. The average swing against Labour in such contests had been 24%. “On those figures,” wrote Kellner, “Polanski should have won at a canter.” But he lost.

That reinforces the case Burnham made for why he should replace the previous Holborn and St Pancras MP, one Keir Starmer, as Labour leader: namely, that he was uniquely placed to defeat challenges from both left and right. This latest win over the Greens, coupled with his own success in Makerfield in June, is early vindication of that argument.

Burnham can claim much credit for the London result: it’s his leftward shift that has persuaded many progressive voters that they don’t need to vote Green to get what they want and that they should give Labour another chance. But Burnham really ought to share the credit with Polanski himself, who has proved a most generous adversary.

Yes, Polanski brought an initial surge in energy, enthusiasm and membership to the Greens. But under him the party has steadily dismantled the moral halo it once enjoyed as the UK’s foremost advocate for the planet, reshaping itself into something darker. Thanks to Sunday’s conference vote branding Zionism as racism, which Polanski ducked, the party now demands the destruction of a state founded, and still regarded by most Jews, as an essential refuge, one whose creation was approved by a UN vote. “Destruction” is not metaphorical, by the way. The motion passed says that the change it seeks – a Palestinian state replacing, rather than existing alongside, Israel – must be secured “by all available means”, a phrase clarified in an accompanying booklet produced by the motion’s proposers to include “armed struggle”. Meaning, violence.

Thus have the Greens allowed themselves to become toxified by the kind of cranks and bigots whose manias crowd out anyone who dares hold a moderate or nuanced view, including many longtime, dedicated local activists. A moment like this calls for leadership, but all the Greens have is a quack hypnotherapist who once earned a living promising to make women’s breasts larger and who, when faced with a difficult decision, ran away. (Now, after the event, Polanski says he would not have voted for the Zionism resolution.) Instead of a leader, the Greens are stuck with a charlatan and a coward.

No wonder former leader Caroline Lucas could not say yes, when asked by Newsnight, whether Polanski should stay in his post. Burnham himself would have no such hesitation: the PM might even be quietly pleased that Polanski performed just well enough in Thursday’s byelection to fend off an immediate challenge. The longer Polanski leads the Greens, the better for Labour.

Meanwhile, Burnham’s other opponents seem similarly determined to do him a favour. Of course, there will be stormier times ahead, but the party conference season now concluded was like a warm, extended summer for the prime minister.

Reform UK, for so long Labour’s strongest challenger in the polls, saw its moment in the sun clouded by eve-of-conference revelations that two senior aides to Nigel Farage had been caught on film apparently discussing how they might get around UK electoral law to take a £500,000 donation from a US benefactor. In politics, the scandals that bite hardest are those that confirm suspicions the voters already harbour. In this case, three in four Britons told YouGov back in July that they regarded Farage as sleazy, with 56% describing him as “very sleazy”.

The party’s leading lights tried to make assorted policy announcements, but the only debate that really cut through was the one started by Suella Braverman, with her eccentric and exclusivist insistence that certain minorities, even those born in England into families rooted in the country for several generations, are not truly English – a definition that would exclude Rishi Sunak and a good portion of the England football team. Farage’s army of would-be mavericks and rebels looks increasingly like a rabble of crooks and spivs and – as if to prove the Greens have no monopoly on the demographic – cranks and bigots.

All this has created an opening for the Conservatives to reclaim their place as the dominant party of the right – but here, too, the genie has smiled on Burnham. True, Kemi Badenoch continues to enjoy higher ratings than her party, but that isn’t saying much. True, too, that she has, belatedly, woken up to the fact that victory will not come solely from trying to out-Reform Reform – people will always vote for the real thing – and that she has to appeal to that vast swathe of Middle England seats lost in 2024 to the Lib Dems.

Her conference pitch – promising to abolish inheritance tax on even the most expensive homes, and to extend free childcare to those earning over £100,000 – might conceivably appeal to some of those high earners. But it draws a dividing line with Labour that Burnham could only have dreamed of. Now the Tories have made plain that, in an age of stretched resources, their priority is to help some of the richest people in the land. That is a battle Burnham will be itching to fight.

As for the Lib Dems, the PM will be only too happy to see them muddling along, an inoffensive receptacle for Tory-sceptic voters in parts of the country that would never go to Labour. Though Burnham wants to eat into their vote too, promising that he will, in the next term, deliver on two of their signature issues: Europe and electoral reform.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

He did that in a speech that was the highlight of the conference season, one that showed a politician who understands the importance of making arguments – and is comfortable making them. After Starmer, who was the opposite in both respects, listening to Burnham was like “gulping down oxygen”, one cabinet minister told me.

And yet, everyone at Labour’s top table knows that the weather will change soon enough. The government, and everyone else, is paying too much to borrow money. At some point, the welfare budget will have to be cut: Labour MPs may be applauding now, but they will be less cheerful when asked to vote for reduced benefits, especially as they face re-selection contests in their local parties, a process that gets under way as soon as January.

There’s a hole in defence spending to fill, the full sweep of public services crying out for cash, a US president apparently bent on driving up global oil prices and therefore inflation, and a civil service machine that ministers privately curse as bloated and ineffective. What’s more, the period we’re in right now – the middle of the parliament – is when governments should be focused entirely on delivery, driving through their agenda. Instead, vital time has been spent on the transition from one PM to another – time Labour will not get back.

For now, Burnham is lucky in his opponents, whose choices hurt them and help him. But the skies will eventually darken and, when they do, the prime minister will reach once again for that magic lamp – hoping against hope that it still works.

Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnist

The Guardian view on Labour and the Greens: winning trust takes more than words

The Guardian Fri, 09 Oct 2026 16:52:10 GMT

A byelection win is a fillip for Andy Burnham and shows Zack Polanski must confront the failures damaging his party’s credibility and appeal

By holding Holborn and St Pancras, Andy Burnham’s Labour has shown it can attract liberal and left-leaning voters. The seat has substantial numbers of young adults, students, professionals and Muslims – offering fertile ground for the Greens’ ecopopulism. However, Labour prevailed. Having won leave-voting Makerfield in June, Mr Burnham can now claim an appeal that bridges Labour’s divided electorate. It’s worth noting that turnout in London was low and Labour’s vote share fell 3.7 points. But that compares with an average 19.3-point fall in four byelections under Mr Burnham’s predecessor. The new leader clearly has bought Labour breathing space and checked the Green advance.

The Greens more than tripled their vote share in the constituency to 33%. But they were beaten. Labour’s Sagal Abdi-Wali took 45% in Sir Keir Starmer’s former seat, leaving Zack Polanski’s ambition of entering parliament unfulfilled. For a party that began the year promising to turn voters’ hunger for change into a serious challenge to Labour, this was a sobering moment. The passing of a motion declaring “Zionism is racism” at its conference probably cost the party support – though the result in central London alone cannot definitively say that. There is a separate question of leadership. Mr Polanski now says he would have voted against the motion. Why, then, did he not make his opposition clear when it mattered last weekend?

He intends to remain leader – and the expanded, radical membership has given Mr Polanski a base in the party that likely insulates him from an instant coup. But with calls for his resignation growing, he has to try to stay in the job while restoring confidence in the Greens’ electoral chances. Clouds had emerged on the horizon long before the party’s conference. Its spring polling surge has faded. In March, YouGov put the party second nationally to Reform, on 21%. Mr Burnham has since stolen much of the Greens’ rhetorical thunder by consciously evoking a more leftwing agenda. The party is now in fourth place, polling 10% nationally.

As Mr Polanski’s profile has grown, it seems the public have become less convinced by his political talents. Since the beginning of the year his net favourability rating has fallen from -6 to -29. The Greens are not to be discounted. Mr Burnham has yet to turn hope into lasting support. That will depend on what his government delivers, especially as prices rise, rather than whom it defeats.

In an interview with the BBC, Jonathan Bartley, the Greens’ former party co-leader, warned that the influx of members has changed the party and that some newcomers are unaware of its traditions of consensus and opposition to political “purity tests”. Significantly, Mr Polanski’s deputy, Rachel Millward, said that the party structures needed to become “fully democratic and strategic”. This may not be enough for the Green MP Siân Berry, who said she wanted to “fix the serious flaws” in the controversial Zionism motion.

Leadership is missing, and responsibility for that falls squarely on Mr Polanski. He has shown that he can communicate persuasively. Now, if he remains in post, he must show that he can acknowledge what went wrong and build support for changing the controversial Zionism policy. Mr Polanski claims credit for Labour’s leftward turn. But the Green leader now needs to put his own party’s house in order.

The Guardian view on the 90s revival: the end of the analogue age

The Guardian Fri, 09 Oct 2026 16:50:48 GMT

The new exhibition at Tate Britain is part of a wider cultural resurgence from 30 years ago. This is nostalgia for a pre-digital era

Each generation imagines itself to be cooler than the one that went before it, and weirder than the one that comes after it, to update George Orwell. Gen X is no exception. “It felt like something was happening,” Pulp’s Jarvis Cocker writes in the catalogue for The 90s: Art and Fashion, which opened at Tate Britain this week. “Something good. It felt like the weirdos were taking over.”

The exhibition, curated by the former editor of British Vogue, Edward Enninful, is part of a wider 90s cultural revival. Oasis’s Wonderwall was the UK’s unofficial World Cup anthem this summer, after last year’s sellout reunion tour. Pulp have also just completed a world tour. The 1993 novel Trainspotting has become a musical; less surprisingly, so has 90s-set romance One Day, which found a new audience with 2024’s Netflix series. Love Story, which fictionalises the doomed relationship between John F Kennedy Jr and Carolyn Bessette, broke streaming records. Cult drama This Life is now on iPlayer. Vogue has described the era as “fashion’s most revisited decade”.

And there’s more in the pipeline. The National Theatre’s 2027 season will include two new plays celebrating the “optimism” of the 1990s: James Graham’s dramatisation of John Major’s rise to No 10 and Moira Buffini’s imagining of the lead-up to the 1998 Good Friday agreement.

This sense of optimism is surely behind the resurgence. Between the fall of the Berlin Wall and of the twin towers in New York, democracy, economics and creativity thrived, at least for some. The Young British Artists and Britpop put the UK on the contemporary cultural map. The common people could become pop stars, fashion designers and prize-winning artists. Magazine photoshoots were elevated to art. Kate Moss was the face of the era. Daring, youthful and “real” – this was Cool Britannia. No wonder the New Labour government was quick to get in on the act after its 1997 victory.

Nineties grunge is seen as a reaction against the excesses of the Thatcherite 80s. Yet, as last year’s exhibitions showcasing Leigh Bowery and The Face magazine showed, a youth counter-culture had emerged. In the 90s it became mainstream.

In hindsight Cool Britannia looks more than a little London-centric and elitist. And life wasn’t glossy for everyone. Racism, Aids and sexism form the backdrop to the Tate exhibition. Many of the images explore what it meant to be a young woman at a time when “girl power” was an empty slogan in the creative industries. One of the era’s greatest cultural legacies is that these female artists now command solo exhibitions, such as Tracey Emin’s blockbuster retrospective at Tate Modern this spring.

This 30-year renaissance cannot just be put down to the “nostalgia pendulum”, whereby influential figures like Enninful are able to curate their own past. The 1990s was the last decade of the analogue age. This nostalgia speaks to a longing for a time without smartphones, social media, selfies and streaming. People watched TV, listened to music and danced together. It was a period of freedom, possibility and fun for young people. It’s not hard to see why it appeals to Gen Z. Like the magazines set up to capture the zeitgeist, that world has gone for ever. We don’t look back in anger, but in sorrow.

Ed Davey faces growing revolt against leadership as senior Lib Dem MP quits

Treasury spokesperson Charlie Maynard reportedly resigned in attempt to unseat leader as party slips in polls

Ed Davey is facing a growing revolt against his leadership of the Liberal Democrats, after the resignation of a senior frontbench figure on Friday.

Charlie Maynard, the Liberal Democrat Treasury spokesperson, has resigned in an attempt to unseat Davey after months of frustration over concerns that the party is failing to cut through with voters, the Guardian understands.

Daisy Cooper, the party’s deputy leader, immediately backed Davey, saying he enjoyed the support of the “vast majority of MPs”, who wanted him to lead them into the next election and were “furious at this distraction”.

“We Liberal Democrats are the last line of defence against a Reform UK government, and Ed is determined to lead a strong and united party into the next general election whenever it comes,” Cooper said.

“As Ed said at conference, we are in the fight of our lives against the right who want to turn our country into their version of Trump’s America.”

Maynard’s resignation, first reported by the Financial Times, came four days after Alison Bennett, the Lib Dem care and carers spokesperson, stood down from the frontbench.

Davey has led the party since 2019, first as acting leader and then officially from August 2020. At the 2024 general election, he steered the party to its most successful result in more than 100 years. The party now has 71 MPs, and is the third largest party in the House of Commons.

But the Lib Dems have slipped to fourth or fifth in national opinion polls, behind the Greens and Reform UK, and frustration has mounted over the party’s failure to attract voters in a fragmented political landscape.

At the party’s conference in Brighton in September, Davey played down criticism from a Liberal Democrat council leader who questioned whether he was the right person to lead the party. Julian Brazil, the leader of Devon county council, said the party was “sleepwalking into irrelevance” and “lacking ambition”.

Davey announced a plan for a £17bn income tax cut in a speech aimed at shoring up the party’s support among former Conservative voters. He said the cut would be paid for entirely by increased growth generated by rejoining the EU’s single market and customs union.

However, Davey faced opposition by Andy Burnham at the Labour party conference to change the pension triple lock to help fund a national care service. One said his defence of the current policy “gaslights an entire generation into believing it’s for our benefit”.
