Verstappen takes pole in sprint qualifying in Singapore

Toto Wolff has condemned accusations of bias in how he has managed his drivers George Russell and Kimi Antonelli, with the Mercedes team principal describing those positing such theories as better off watching “Teletubbies or Mickey Mouse” rather than Formula One.

With Antonelli leading Russell by 84 points in the world championship as they go into this weekend’s Singapore Grand Prix, the Italian’s first title is within his reach. The 20-year-old has driven superbly in only his second season in F1 but Russell has struggled with poor fortune and reliability issues that have stymied his championship challenge.

At the last round, in Malaysia, an engine failure cost Russell a potential podium spot and led to a host of accusations online of bias towards Antonelli. Speaking in Singapore, Wolff’s exasperation was clear.

“They’re brainless, whoever thinks that, it’s completely nonsensical,” he said. “I don’t know what’s going on. Do they think I have a button that says: ‘George, engine failure now’? Or disadvantaging one driver against the other when we are fighting for a constructors’ championship when we have always had the mindset of providing everybody equal material?

“There’s a lot of polarisation and sometimes I read what people write. I find it hilarious. These people really contribute to my own entertainment when they are abusing the team or myself. I’m Satan, I’ve heard. So, overall funny. But really, zero understanding and respect for people who come up with these things. Rather than watching Formula One, they should do Teletubbies or some Mickey Mouse.”

Russell goes into Sunday’s night race on the Marina Bay circuit clinging on in the title fight. Not only did the engine failure cost him in Malaysia but it meant he has had to take a new engine for this race and with the attendant penalties will have to start from the back of the grid on a track where overtaking is enormously tricky.

Mercedes have further complications in Singapore. The upgrades they brought to Malaysia did not prove effective and have left the team somewhat perplexed as to why they had not delivered. They opted, with Russell’s approval, to split their options this weekend with the British driver reverting to the spec with which he had won in Baku and Antonelli running the new version in order to provide an insight into where the developments were wanting.

In qualifying for Saturday’s sprint race, Russell was clearly enjoying his pre-upgrade ride more than his teammate. He took second on the grid with Antonelli only in seventh, while Max Verstappen took an excellent pole to back up his win at Sepang. Antonelli certainly felt he was somewhat under the cosh in Singapore with a car far removed from what he is used to. “There is still a lot to understand about this package, the car is very difficult, very unpredictable,” he said. “I was coming in with high hopes but so far it has been very difficult. It’s going to be a difficult weekend, it’s going to be very tricky. I don’t see where we can find seven-tenths.”

Mercedes are clear they will continue to allow their drivers to race one another. Wolff, who managed three seasons of increasingly intense and rancorous rivalry between Lewis Hamilton and Nico Rosberg between 2014 and 2016, has always been insistent that he has practised even-handed management since he joined F1. He cited a conversation he had with Alain Prost about his bitter rivalry with Ayrton Senna while at McLaren in the 1980s.

‘Medieval’ and ‘disturbing’: US plan to livestream execution elicits global condemnation

The Guardian Fri, 09 Oct 2026 16:32:38 GMT

Pentagon said execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, who killed 13 people at Fort Hood in 2009, would be broadcast live

US politics live – latest updates

The US is facing worldwide condemnation over a “barbaric” plan to execute a disabled man by firing squad and livestream it to the public, with critics comparing the Trump administration to dictatorships in Iran and Afghanistan.

The Pentagon confirmed on Thursday that the execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, convicted of killing 13 people at a military base at Fort Hood in Texas in 2009, would be livestreamed on 3 December.

The United Nations’ office of the high commissioner for human rights warned on Friday that broadcasting the killing would amount to a public execution and “breach the absolute prohibition of torture”.

The plan also drew opprobrium from politicians, religious leaders and human rights advocates in the US and abroad. Hillary Clinton, the former US secretary of state, wrote on social media: “A barbaric idea, beneath our dignity as a country. Push back on this.”

Yassamin Ansari, the first Iranian American Democrat elected to the US Congress, posted: “In Trump’s America, we’re doing public executions now. WTF. This is what happens under brutal dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan. It’s all part of Trump’s authoritarian takeover of the United States.”

Britain, which abolished the death penalty in the 1960s, moved to distance itself from the execution. Bridget Phillipson, the UK’s equalities minister and Labour party chair, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme that she found the concept “rather disturbing”.

Phillipson stressed that the decision was a matter for the US government, adding: “They are a close ally. Does that mean that we support everything the US government does? No.”

Under US military law, a president must approve an execution by firing squad. Trump did so on the recommendation of his defence secretary, Pete Hegseth, according to the Pentagon.

JD Vance – a practicing Catholic – told reporters on Friday he wouldn’t watch the livestreamed execution of Hasan, but stopped short of criticizing the administration’s decision.

When asked how his Christian beliefs influence his view of the public execution, Vance dismissed controversy about the manner of execution and appeared to question whether the livestream will happen.

“Whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope the people don’t forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people,” the US vice-president told reporters. “That said, if it’s ultimately livestreamed, I’m not going to be watching it.”

Hegseth gleefully confirmed the livestream plan after previously saying that the execution would be public. Speaking to the conservative broadcaster Real America’s Voice, he said people should be able to watch because they need to understand that there were “serious consequences” for such crimes.

Asked whether Hasan had made any final requests, Hegseth replied: “Don’t care. We’ll see him on December 3.”

Now 56, Hasan was sentenced to death by a military jury in 2013 after being convicted of 13 counts of premeditated murder and 32 counts of attempted premeditated murder. Twelve of those killed and 30 of the wounded were soldiers.

The former army psychiatrist opened fire with a handgun at a medical facility at Fort Hood on 5 November 2009 as soldiers waited for medical checks before deployment. He was shot by a police officer during his arrest and left partly paralysed, and now uses a wheelchair.

The execution is expected to be the first by firing squad carried out by the US military since 1945, when army private Eddie Slovik was executed for desertion during the second world war. The last US military execution of any kind took place in 1961, when John Bennett was hanged.

Hasan’s case comes amid renewed scrutiny of capital punishment in the US following the botched lethal injection of Tennessee death-row prisoner Christa Pike last week. Her lawyers said she awoke in hospital “angry and confused” and remained seriously ill and shackled to her hospital bed.

Media have sought to televise US executions ⁠in the past, but have been blocked by the courts. No other country is known to televise or livestream legal executions, experts said.

Indeed, public executions have largely disappeared around the world. Amnesty International recorded at least 17 in 2025, including 11 in Iran and six in Taliban-run Afghanistan.

In the US, executions have been conducted privately for about nine decades. The hanging of Rainey Bethea in Kentucky in 1936, witnessed by thousands, is generally regarded as the country’s last public execution, although another hanging took place in Missouri the following year.

after newsletter promotion

Experts said there was no known precedent for livestreaming a legal execution. The execution of the Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh in 2001 was made available to victims’ relatives through closed-circuit television, but was not broadcast publicly.

The proposed live stream has prompted criticism from religious leaders. Archbishop Paul Coakley, president of the US Conference of Catholic Bishops, said it was a “barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered”.

Politicians from both sides of the aisle also spoke out. Adam Smith, the top Democrat on the House of Representatives armed services committee, said the plan was “disturbing and makes a mockery of our legal system”. The Democratic senator Chris Murphy described public executions as “medieval”.

The Republican senator Thom Tillis said Hasan should face the death penalty but that broadcasting his execution was “beyond disgusting”, arguing that public executions were associated with oppressive regimes.

Others warned that the spectacle would be counterproductive and act as a recruiting sergeant for US enemies seeking fresh propaganda.

Ned Price, a former deputy to the US representative to the United Nations, posted on X: “You can take it from those of us who’ve spent years working on terrorism: the surest way to spawn more radicalized zealots is to glorify violence, embrace a cult of death, and create a martyr for the cause.

“Or take it from [al-Qaida] and ISIS, whose tactics offer the closest modern-day approximation of Hegseth’s proposal. Either way, it’s hard to conjure a more vivid example of his trademark performative bravado, which routinely damages America’s image and, in this case, so ghoulishly leaves us more vulnerable.”

Some experts have raised questions about whether the live stream could be challenged in court. Eugene Fidell, a military law specialist at Yale Law School, said Hasan could seek legal action to block the public display of his death.

Elisabeth Semel, co-director of the Death Penalty Clinic at the University of California, Berkeley, said the announcement raised serious questions about the dignity of the condemned prisoner and the government’s motivation for staging such an unusual spectacle.

“This is a president who’s about spectacle and that’s, I think, precisely the message that he intends to deliver,” she told the Associated Press.

Justin Mazzola, deputy director of research at Amnesty International USA, said: “Livestreaming the taking of a life by firing squad would only compound the cruelty of the death penalty and perpetuate the cycle of violence that the authorities purportedly seek to end.

“This announcement adds to the display of cruelty that we have just witnessed in the senseless pursuit of the execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee. The US death penalty is irredeemably broken. It is high time that the US authorities, at all levels, use their power to show human rights leadership and end this ultimate cruel, inhuman and degrading punishment once and for all.”

Other experts argued that public access could increase transparency around capital punishment. Deborah Denno, a death penalty specialist at Fordham University, told the AP that a live stream could make the process more transparent at a time when the botched execution in Tennessee had renewed questions about how the state puts prisoners to death.

It remains unclear whether Hasan will seek to challenge his execution in civilian court, a move that could significantly delay the proceedings.

Does Polanski have to go? Greens at the crossroads after Holborn and St Pancras

The Guardian Fri, 09 Oct 2026 16:32:30 GMT

Pressure is building on the party leader after byelection defeat, a damaging row over Zionism and polls that show him less popular than Nigel Farage

When Zack Polanski addressed his campaigners flush with victory after the Gorton and Denton byelection in February, he declared: “Labour’s electoral stranglehold is over.” The election of Hannah Spencer as the new Green MP for the Greater Manchester seat was a seismic victory, he continued: “I said we were here to replace Labour and this is what replacing looks like.”

But in the wake of Polanski’s defeat in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection on Thursday, and a calamitous row over the party’s stance on Zionism, the debate around what, or who, could be replaced has shifted to Polanski himself.

On Friday the leader of the Green party in England and Wales was defiant after losing to Labour’s Sagal Abdi-Wali, who took 45% of the vote, to Polanski’s 33%. Asked what was going wrong in his party, which has fallen from highs of 21% in some polls after the victory in Gorton and Denton to around 10-11%, Polanski, responded: “If things are going wrong by the fact that we just tripled our vote share and had our second best byelection result in Green party history, you know what? I’ll take that.” While emphasising that Green members would ultimately decide who they wanted as leader, he said: “Of course I can carry on.”.

That the last few months have been difficult for the Greens – and Polanski in particular – is beyond doubt. Polanski himself is, according to new polling from More in Common, now less popular with voters than Nigel Farage, and is the least popular major UK party leader, falling by four points to a -28 net approval.

His standing, bruised by a series of controversies over a failure to pay council tax and the sharing of a post criticising police, has been further damaged by a controversial motion that was adopted at the Green party conference in Brighton last weekend, equating Zionism, the movement for a Jewish state, with racism. Polanski’s decision to abstain from the debate and the vote to instead campaign in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, was condemned by his detractors, but also, more significantly, criticised by senior figures in his own party.

The former Green leader Caroline Lucas told BBC Newsnight on Thursday that Polanski “should have been there and he should have voted”. Asked if he should stand down, she said: “I think let’s just see what happens in the coming days and weeks. Obviously he has been completely taken up with this byelection.” Following his defeat she appeared to temper her position, saying Polanski had “transformed the party” and she hoped he would now “help resolve huge issues we face and transform our internal structures”.

On Friday, pressure mounted, as the leader of the Jewish Greens, Vivien Lichtenstein, called for Polanski to step down, saying it was a “big mistake” for him not to have spoken and voted for amendments stating that any future structure of a Palestinian state should be decided by Palestinians, rather than impose a one-state system.

But there was bullishness among the Polanski faithful, with Greens Organise, the leftwing faction that backed his leadership bid, saying he should stay on. A statement from the group said that “not all growth and success is linear, there will be ups and downs; the real test for a political organisation is how we deal with failure”. It added: “We have reshaped the British political landscape. The Green party can still become the ecosocialist party we need. Zack is still the leader who can get us there.”

Green party supporters pointed out that the party achieved a 13-point swing from Labour in Holborn and St Pancras, traditionally a safe Labour seat. The Camden councillor Hamza Chowdhury – who was overlooked as the candidate in the constituency in favour of Polanski – went as far as saying the result was “a huge win for the Green party and the wider movement”.

Polanski supporters point out that since he was elected leader in September 2025, the party has quadrupled its membership to more than 230,000. As well as the winning of its first ever seat in the north of England, he presided over the Greens’ best-ever performance in May’s local and mayoral elections, including gaining their first-ever directly elected mayoralty, in Hackney, east London.

Nonetheless, the result in north London exposed the dual challenge Polanski now faced, said Luke Tryl, the director of More in Common. At the same time as the replacement of Keir Starmer with Andy Burnham had brought disillusioned progressives back to Labour, Polanski had become a more polarising figure.

A series of missteps, starting when he shared a social media post critical of police after the Golders Green stabbings, had damaged his popularity with the wider UK public, added Tryl. “It was just one of those moments which gave soft Green supporters pause for thought. Similarly, many people don’t vote directly on something like the Zionism is racism motion, but it adds to that sense of ‘oh, I thought these were nice guys who were focused on the environment’.”

The result in north London was a “good one” for Labour, he added, despite the drop in its majority. While governing parties usually get hit hard in byelections, the drop in Holborn was below the average for defending a seat at byelections in any postwar parliament, he noted.

But Labour hopes of the death of the Green party were likely to have been exaggerated. “I think writing off the Greens is premature,” he said. “Burnham has managed, for now, to unite the left, but a lot of big decisions, including on North Sea oil drilling and, more importantly, the budget, are coming down the line.”

As for Polanski, the path towards rebuilding the popularity that saw him win the support of young voters desperate for hope and change would lie in a return to his original economic messaging around “rip-off Britain” and generational fairness, rather than divisive internal battles, said James Baggaley from UCL’s Policy Lab. “The question for the Greens and Polanski now is: do they want to reassure voters on questions of antisemitism and also get back to what they were actually winning on, which was the economy?”

Balding was still around £700,000 adrift of O’Brien, the defending champion, at the end of August but has made steady progress since and moved into the lead for the first time when Blue Bolt won the Group One Sun Chariot Stakes at Newmarket last weekend.

Never So Brave’s defeat of his stable companion, Flora Of Bermuda, in the Challenge Stakes was worth a total of £129,000, less than half an hour after Balding’s juvenile Nakila Sun had made all in the British EBF Final at York, which was worth £51,000 to the winner.

O’Brien then had to settle for second place in the Group One Fillies’ Mile here, as his runner Haven was overhauled inside the final furlong by the odds-on favourite, Musical Times, with Balding’s runners, Forbidden Fire and Scommessa Sicura, picking up minor place money in third and fifth.

“I’ve been at the sales all week, but I’d imagine the team at home are pretty pumped for it,” Balding said after his Challenge Stakes success. “If we’re still the same after Champions Day then I’ll start to get excited, but I wouldn’t dare say it will be.”

O’Brien has more than a dozen entries on Champions Day at Ascot next weekend, although Jan Brueghel, at 6-4 for the Long Distance Cup, is currently his only favourite on the afternoon. Constitution River, the winner of the French Derby and Eclipse earlier in the season, is a 4-1 chance for the Queen Elizabeth II Stakes and around 10-1 for the Champion Stakes, while Gstaad, the Irish 2,000 Guineas winner, is also quoted for both of the card’s most valuable events.

Paddy Power quotes O’Brien at 2-7 (from 1-4) to win the title race after Friday’s action, while Balding is a 5-2 chance (from 11-4).

Musical Times, meanwhile, is around 5-2 for next year’s 1,000 Guineas after overcoming significant traffic problems in the Fillies’ Mile. Charlie Appleby’s filly remains unbeaten after three starts and showed a high-class turn of foot to run down Haven after William Buick finally found some daylight a furlong out.

“After two furlongs, we just had to hold our breath a little bit, but William was on the class filly in the race and he knew it himself,” Appleby said. “He was just trying to find those gaps and when he did she quickened up smartly.”

James Owen has established himself as a top-15 trainer on the Flat and over jumps in recent seasons, thanks not least to his habit of coaxing major improvement from other trainers’ castoffs, and his dual-purpose gelding High Fibre (3.40) is a fascinating contender for the Cesarewitch Handicap at Newmarket on Saturday.

The seven-year-old has already picked up decent handicap prizes both over hurdles and on the Flat in his four starts since joining Owen from Harry Fry. A recent close second at York suggests he remains on a fair mark and Silvestre de Sousa, already a three-times winner of this race, is drawn in stall one for a race in which – despite the extreme distance – low numbers often enjoy a slight edge.

Stark warning – does new footage in Avengers: Endgame reveal the truth about Doctor Doom?

The Guardian Fri, 09 Oct 2026 16:25:44 GMT

Warning: contains spoilersThe four short scenes added to the new version has made the film the highest-grossing of all time – but the only people really enjoying this are the Disney accountants

Does it really matter which film is the highest-grossing of all time at the global box office? Will James Cameron be lying awake at night staring into the darkness and pondering whether to withdraw humanity’s access to giant, blue-skinned space elves out of sheer spite, just because Avatar has been dethroned once again by Avengers: Endgame? It seems unlikely. Are the Russo brothers at this very moment leaping and capering with wild abandon because adding a few new scenes and releasing their film for the umpteenth time has led to this momentous changing of the guard? Probably not. Is a Disney accountant somewhere holding a tiny awards ceremony in which every nominee is himself? Well yes, absolutely, because the mouse house ultimately owns both films.

And yet the most interesting thing about Avengers: Endgame’s return to cinemas is not how much money it has made – for the record, the rerelease, titled Avengers Endgame: Encore, had brought in another $126m worldwide by last weekend, taking its lifetime total to approximately $2.925bn (just ahead of Avatar’s $2.923bn) – but what Marvel added to the picture while we were all busy counting.

Premium-format presentations of the new version feature a new scene at the end of the film and another three during and after its credits, with some also appearing in standard screenings. The idea is presumably that these tantalising snippets will segue viewers smoothly into the upcoming Avengers: Doomsday with the sort of spring in the step that can only come from being convinced that they are now three tiny clues away from understanding the mind of Kevin Feige.

The original Endgame featured a closing shot of Chris Evans’ Steve Rogers, who has apparently used Tony Stark’s discovery of time travel to return to the 1940s, dancing contentedly with Hayley Atwell’s Peggy Carter. In the new version, the couple are interrupted by a knock at the door, only to find Tom Hiddleston’s Loki standing outside offering to help them. Given that the Norse trickster ended Loki season two holding the branching timelines of the multiverse together, this is unlikely to be just a neighbour popping round to complain about the hedge. We are presumably meant to infer that whatever is about to go wrong with reality is serious enough to reach Steve even in his carefully arranged retirement, and that his happy ending may now have to be put on hold. The man has defeated the Nazis and helped reverse the extinction of half of all life, but apparently still hasn’t accrued enough annual leave to finish a dance.

Scene two turns up during the credits, and finds Bruce Banner holed up in an underground facility following the events of Spider-Man: Brand New Day, trying to keep his inner Hulk under control. As if matters couldn’t get any worse, the voice of Robert Downey Jr’s Doctor Doom is heard announcing that he has come to “collect” the troubled scientist. Whether he wants Banner’s genius, the Hulk’s muscle or something considerably less agreeable remains unclear, but it seems safe to assume he is not putting together a pub quiz team.

A second mid-credits scene sees the Time Variance Authority’s Mobius (Owen Wilson), OB (Ke Huy Quan) and Casey (Eugene Cordero) – whose organisation is tasked, following the events of Loki season two, with protecting the branching timelines it once ruthlessly pruned – watching in horror as universes collide and vanish in their thousands. Crucially, the reality inhabited by the X-Men during the 20th Century Fox era is among those that are threatened. In the comics, similar incursions unfold through Jonathan Hickman’s Avengers and New Avengers, culminating in the Time Runs Out storyline and leading into the 2015 event Secret Wars. The main Marvel and Ultimate universes are the last to be destroyed, after which Doctor Doom assembles remnants of ruined realities into the patchwork planet Battleworld. Might Doomsday see the Fox universe, the retro-futuristic reality occupied by the Fantastic Four and the main Marvel Cinematic Universe similarly stitched together, with Doom appointing himself ruler of whatever survives?

Encore’s final scene arrives after the credits, and reworks Endgame’s original audio farewell: Tony Stark building his first Iron Man armour in an Afghan cave. The new version pairs the blows of the hammer with flashing images, culminating in a final, ominous shot of Doctor Doom’s mask. Is Marvel trying to tell us that the Latverian sorcerer really is a Stark variant after all? Or is the studio just exploiting the unsettling associations of a familiar din coming from the wrong metal visage? Either way, the film-makers clearly want us to carry the memory of Tony Stark into Doomsday, and perhaps ponder how much of the man who saved the universe might lurk inside the one now threatening it.

This is, admittedly, a more intriguing setup than we might expect from a common-or-garden Marvel mashup. If Doom has the face of a lost friend and the power to offer ravaged worlds the merest glimpse of a future beyond torture and oblivion, resisting him could require more than Thor locating a larger hammer than usual.

What is clear is that Marvel has somehow persuaded audiences to pay again for a film they already know, then rewarded them with the news that retirement is cancelled, the Hulk’s attempts to retreat from public life have failed and existence itself is falling apart. Somewhere, that Disney accountant is probably giving himself a lifetime achievement award.

Zionism, racism and the Green party in turmoil

The Guardian Fri, 09 Oct 2026 16:22:50 GMT

Readers respond to articles on the Green party’s motion

As ever, Jonathan Freedland is on the money in his article (The Green party’s anti-Zionism motion is yet another attempt to tell Jews how we should think, 3 October). As a non-religious Jew-ish Londoner, I am appalled at the passing of the motion to declare Zionism as a form of racism, and I am seriously considering leaving the Green party as a result.

While I condemn the Israeli government’s actions against the Palestinian people, and I am not a Zionist myself, Zionism as defined by the motion is only one political interpretation and completely ignores ancient religious and cultural definitions held by many Jews who also condemn the current Israeli government.

I have worked with Palestinians and Israelis on the West Bank and in Jerusalem in the cause of peace and reconciliation, and firmly believe in equal rights for everyone in Israel and the occupied territories. That cause will be set back by this decision, which will give fuel to antisemites who hide their racism under an anti-Zionist guise.

This decision is a shot in the foot for the Green party, risking the alienation of British Jews and others who, like me, support peace and reconciliation, believe in equal rights for Israelis and Palestinians, and strongly oppose the actions of the current Israeli government. Simon LawsonLondon

Jonathan Freedland is right that Zionism means different things to different people, and that Jewish historical attachment to Israel cannot simply be dismissed. But that complexity can also become a way of avoiding the more important question: what has Zionism produced in practice?

“Fire is destructive” does not mean every use of fire is destructive. It means fire has destructive potential, which is why we recognise boundaries around its use. The same applies to Zionism. Jewish self-determination is not inherently racist; but when a political project pursued in its name produces permanent occupation, settlement, displacement, unequal rights and Palestinian subordination, it is legitimate to ask whether the project has crossed those boundaries. Therefore, “Zionism is racist” can be a true description of the manifestation of Zionism embodied in the current Israeli state.

The issue, therefore, isn’t whether a benign definition of Zionism can be imagined. It plainly can. The issue is whether the political reality created in its name conforms to that definition. We should be able to examine Zionism as we examine any other political ideology: by its effects, its institutions, and the boundaries it recognises. Criticising a political ideology or the actions of a state is not the same thing as attacking Jews or Judaism. Raymond O’BrienLondon

Those who do not learn from history are doomed to repeat it. Green party success in the EU elections in 1989 saw a huge increase in membership and a wave of entryism. By 1991 it was fragmented and irrelevant. Zack Polanski’s election as leader of the Green party also saw a wave of entryism.

It was never tenable to allow a gathering composed of those who can afford, or choose, to turn up to be the party’s policymaking body. But for many Greens it is an article of faith; proof of the party’s commitment to “democracy”. They were called “fundis” (fundamentalists) in my day. A group of us (“realos”) tried to change things in 1990 with a motion arguing that a “leadership” structure was necessary in a world where we were under the media microscope. The motion passed, but the party split.

It is tragic to see a party that has pulled itself up by its bootstraps since the early 1990s, that has worked hard to win representation locally, and that has won seats in Westminster under a voting system that disadvantages newcomers, being stopped in its tracks by its lack of internal democracy.

Here’s a suggestion from an oldie. Organise an internal referendum on the motion and let the whole membership decide. And put an end to the travesty of democracy that saw it adopted in the first place. Lyn DadeTwickenham, London

As a member of the Green party, I was dismayed by the profoundly counterproductive “Zionism is racism” motion passed at conference on Sunday. Since his election as leader and his success in broadening the party’s appeal, opponents of Zack Polanski and the Greens have repeatedly sought to portray the party as antisemitic. This motion hands them the ammunition they have been looking for.

Until now, the Greens have stood out among UK political parties in their willingness to describe Israel as an apartheid state and to condemn its actions in Gaza as genocidal. That argument risks being obscured by an entirely avoidable debate over accusations of antisemitism.

The motion is also historically and politically flawed. While the form of Zionism represented by the Israeli state today is exclusionary and discriminatory, it does not follow that all forms of Zionism are racist.

Zionism emerged, in large part, as a response to the persecution of Jews in Europe. To erase that history from our understanding of Zionism is to overlook the reality of anti-Jewish racism that helped give rise to the movement.

I hope the Green party leadership can find a way to distance itself from this damaging motion and refocus attention on holding the Israeli government accountable for its treatment of the Palestinians. Prof Benjamin SelwynUniversity of Sussex

Be more Jagger? How BBC’s Matt Brittin could follow up Elvis appeal to staff

The Guardian Fri, 09 Oct 2026 15:57:13 GMT

Director general called for ‘a little less conversation, a little more action’ – but from what other songs could he draw inspiration?

The BBC director general, Matt Brittin, has started the job at a time of huge crisis. Money is short, jobs are being cut and it’s likely entire channels will be culled to stem the tide. This is a moment that requires great motivational charisma, which is why, in a recent all-staff call, he urged BBC employees to be “a bit more Elvis – a little less conversation, a little more action”.

Clearly, this isn’t great. But maybe this is how things are now. Perhaps, if you really want to unite a flagging workforce against a vast and inevitable decline, you need to start quoting song lyrics at them. With that in mind, here are some more that Brittin could use in his next call.

This may be a better tactic, given the sour mood at the BBC right now. Sure, employees may wish for lots of things – like a bigger commissioning budget, more exclusive coverage of big sporting events, and a functioning BBC Three. But Mick Jagger was right. You can’t always get what you want, but if you try sometimes, you just might find you get what you need. Note: this only really works if what you need is having Romesh Ranganathan present everything.

It doesn’t matter how many cuts the BBC faces. It doesn’t matter how many staff it has to lose. The corporation’s ethos is to inform, educate and entertain, and that’s what it will do, no matter what. If that means Sophie Raworth has to do the news over Zoom from inside a wardrobe, so be it. If it means the Olympics have to be replaced by footage of raindrops racing each other down a window for several hours at a time, bring it on.

The media landscape is going through a stage of permanent transformation. Maybe the idea of an elderly institution such as the BBC thriving in this new environment is too much to ask. Perhaps the real motivating war cry should be about clinging on to life at any cost. What do we want? Survival, if only in a heavily diminished capacity. When do we want it? Now!

The BBC finds itself in a moment of extreme belt-tightening, and every penny must be utilised to its best advantage. As such, turning on the office bathroom lights is too expensive and therefore banned. Your phone has a torch, doesn’t it?

This one speaks for itself. An enormous part of running the BBC involves figuring out what to do with Nigel Farage. If Brittin wants to maintain any form of continuity with the previous administration, this will mean putting him on television at every possible opportunity. Does it hurt the corporation to give so much airtime to someone who wants to abolish the licence fee? Absolutely. But also, could he guest host The One Show for a couple of weeks? Couldn’t hurt to ask.

Mike Ditka, legendary Chicago Bears head coach, dies aged 86

The Guardian Fri, 09 Oct 2026 15:33:16 GMT

Hall of Famer led 1985 Bears to Super Bowl title

Coach was known for tough, gruff demeanor

The Super Bowl Shuffle to SNL: a life in pictures

Mike Ditka, who won NFL titles as a player and coach with the Chicago Bears, has died at 86, his family announced Friday.

“It is with profound sadness that we announce the passing of our beloved husband, father, grandfather, and friend, Mike Ditka,” the family said. “While the world knew Mike as a Hall of Fame football player, legendary coach, and leader of the Chicago Bears’ Super Bowl XX championship team, we knew him as the heart of our family. Mike will be missed beyond measure and remembered forever.”

Nicknamed “Iron Mike” as a player, Ditka helped revolutionize the tight end position, then moved to the sidelines and took over as Chicago’s coach. His 1985 Bears team featured one of football’s most dominant defenses ever. It also had enough outsized personalities to record a rap video, The Super Bowl Shuffle, and back up their boasting in the championship game three months later.

After retiring as a coach, Ditka became a restaurateur, pitchman and TV personality, as well as an advocate for improved medical and retirement benefits for former players.

Ditka was tough and gruff, the quintessential Chicago Bear nicknamed “Da Coach”. He did everything from order off the menu to knock defensive backs on their butts with a growl, and his adopted home town reveled in every minute. He was enshrined in the College and Pro Football Halls of Fame, and the Bears said during a ceremony in 2013 that his “No 89” jersey will be the last one retired by the team.

He was born in Carnegie, Pennsylvania, the son of a welder who changed the family name from Dyczko. He grew up in nearby Aliquippa, close to the coal-mining and steel-manufacturing plants that dotted the western part of the state, a big, talented, three-sport athlete and All-American at Pitt whose bruising style made his first nickname, “Iron Mike” a good fit.

Selected fifth overall by flinty Chicago owner George Halas in the 1961 draft, Ditka went on to Rookie of the Year honors, multiple Pro Bowl trips and the 1963 NFL championship. He left Chicago in 1966, playing briefly for Philadelphia and Dallas. He moved to the sideline in 1973 as an assistant to the revered Tom Landry and stayed with the Cowboys for eight seasons, before returning to a hero’s welcome in Chicago as head coach in 1982.

Ditka’s return to the Bears lasted 10 tumultuous years, including five straight NFC Central titles, the Super Bowl win, a DUI conviction, a heart attack, a long-running feud with defensive coordinator Buddy Ryan and a new nickname – “Da Coach.”

The public beefs with Ryan mirrored the behind-the-scenes battles Ditka waged trying to contain a team bristling with outsized personalities.

“It was more than a team,” Ditka once said. “It was a team of characters that had character that played for a crazy man, who let him be crazy and had fun doing it and don’t apologize for it ever. I wouldn’t want to be one of these suits walking around on the sideline today. I have no desire to be that. I was what I was and they were what they were and, damn, it was fun.”

It wasn’t until two dozen players recorded The Super Bowl Shuffle – an audacious rap-styled video released three months ahead of the 1986 title game – that the rest of the football world wondered whether Ditka was losing his grip. His players never did.

“We call him ‘Sybil’ after that girl in the movie,” quarterback Jim McMahon once explained. “You know, the one that had all those personalities. Mike will be calm one minute, then throw a clipboard the next. People don’t understand that, but we do.”

The Bears demolished the New England Patriots 46-10 in the Super Bowl, but Ditka often said he regretted having McMahon and defensive tackle William “The Refrigerator” Perry run for touchdowns instead of Walter Payton, Chicago’s loyal and longsuffering running back.

Ryan departed for a head coaching job in Philadelphia soon after. While the Bears continued to be a contender for most of the next five years, a 5-11 season prompted Ditka’s departure in 1992.

After a five-year absence, he returned to coaching with the New Orleans Saints, but failed to revive the franchise. After a miserable 1999 season ended with a 3-13 record- his worst as either a player or coach – he left the sidelines for good.

His face and demeanor were so familiar by then that a second act became an easy segue. Ditka began building a stable of restaurants and appeared as himself in TV sitcoms from Cheers to Third Rock from the Sun, as well as shows such as LA Law and Saturday Night Live.

He also stayed close to the game as an NFL analyst and game-day show personality at ESPN. Ditka’s high-profile status also made him an effective advocate to secure improved health and retirement benefits for former players.

His name also circulated for years in Illinois political circles. Though he never ran for office, Ditka described himself as a staunch conservative and was mentioned several times as a possible Republican candidate, including a congressional race against then state representative Barack Obama for the US Senate.

Renshaw and Cummins keep hosts’ attack at bay

If we accept that sporting tenures are results-based, then the Australian selectors George Bailey and Tony Dodemaide should be conferring with the coach Andrew McDonald to submit a mass resignation. The opening moments of the first Test in Durban were enough to return the predictable harvest of one of the most bizarre selection decisions ever made for the national XI, with Nic Maddinson bowled for a torturous 33-ball duck, early impetus for Australia’s slide to 187 for 6 by the time bad light ended play.

Maddinson should not have lasted half that long, nailed on the pad by Wiaan Mulder after 15 balls but spared by umpire error and a timid South African non-review. Even that huge slice of luck never looked like becoming anything more. His innings went nowhere, shuffling, defensive, missing opportunities on his legs, dealing in extras. His only shots were a few cuts hurled at wild width, all air-swings until the bottom edge that took out his stumps.

Fault does not belong to Maddinson. It was the entirely predictable outcome of deciding that October 2026 was the time to catapult in a guy who hadn’t played first-class cricket since March 2025, and hadn’t played it well since March 2024.

If it was bizarre to bring him into squad, then into the XI, the finishing touch was sending him to the top of the order. The selectors’ defence a few days ago was that Maddinson is strong against spin, foreshadowing two South African slow bowlers against Australia’s middle order. But apparently words are meaningless, just a way to invent rationale after the fact. Because here was their spin specialist, given one of the toughest pace assignments in the world: opening the batting against bounce and movement in South Africa.

Australia have a nationally contracted opener sitting at home, in Jake Weatherald. They have his notional replacement, Matt Renshaw, who got one innings in the job. They have an entire Australia A squad running around in India and a Shield round full of openers with more recent game time. Apparently none of those were better options than a guy whose career record can be found in the British Museum inscribed into clay tablets.

Maddinson chopping on from Marco Jansen made the score 24 for 2, after Travis Head had already nicked Mulder down the leg-side. Yet again, an opening combo for Australia had made way for the throwback partnership of Steve Smith and Marnus Labuschagne.

The latter especially looked the sharpest he has in a long time. His early flick through midwicket from Mulder set the tone, and he followed Smith’s lead in being busy against the left-arm spin of Keshav Maharaj, with Smith thumping Maharaj for two straight sixes in an over, and Labuschagne driving four through cover.

The stand of 60 by lunch was promising, having come in good time, but the last ball of the session swung the calculation. With the ball nipping in from the accurate Mulder, Labuschagne will probably claim to be aggrieved that ball-tracking showed a marginal umpire’s call on impact in line with off-stump, but the ball was going on to take out middle. Three balls and 40 minutes later, Smith was caught at gully straight after the lunch break, a ball after Jansen had pulverised his glove. Australia’s twin engines had made 37 and 25.

That set the scene for a fierce Anrich Nortje spell, the moustachioed pace merchant getting short balls to leap uncomfortably at Alex Carey, around the wicket to the left-hander. As soon as the bowler moved over the wicket, with Carey hanging back for the bouncer, a fuller ball drew a drive to slip for 14. Beau Webster followed immediately, slight movement away drawing a nick that wasn’t given. Temba Bavuma had already burned two reviews by this stage, so it was a brave and correct call to risk his last.

At 124 for 6, disaster beckoned for Australia, but Renshaw got the bailing bucket in his unexpected new middle-order spot, and Pat Cummins joined his work. Renshaw batted time and used the occasional bad ball, while Cummins did not relish Nortje’s pace but used it effectively to pick off boundaries. Batting beyond the tea break, they took their partnership to 63 before the early close.

With only 65.2 overs faced, Australia have a vast amount of time left in this Test match. The challenge will be using it effectively. Renshaw will need the support of his bowlers to turn his 46 into something far more substantial on day two for the visitors to keep a foothold in the game. Their troubles do not hinge on a single selection decision, but that decision does reflect the specialist batting troubles that have become endemic in this side.

Without Manchester City’s woes, Michael Carrick may have faced a more difficult time, with plenty to review in regards to the first five games of the season.

United sit solemnly in 12th with only one league win, and misery needs company. The hosts will find just that at Old Trafford on Saturday evening. Tottenham, bottom of the Premier League, visit, with both sides hoping to kickstart their season. Spurs have secured a measly two points after a summer where £300m was spent on Roberto De Zerbi’s rebuild but the architect’s drawings are already at risk of being set alight. For Carrick and United, beating the worst team in the league is close to a necessity as they enter a very difficult run of fixtures.

October is theoretically and practically problematic for United, who have six fixtures this month, with away games against Leeds, Atlético Madrid, Como and Chelsea, who play a variety of styles that need preparing for, making a home game against Spurs a must-win. On paper, the second easiest game of the month is Bournemouth at home. Carrick has plenty of credit in the bank from his work in the second half of last season, and will be afforded as much time as possible to get things right because no one is eager for another mid-season change of manager. United need to be in a better position by the end of October than they started it, which will require significant improvement on the pitch.

For Carrick there are plenty of small margins he can point to. The opening-day defeat at Hull was a grisly performance and worthy of criticism; Ipswich were eventually dispatched, while the derby was a tight and controversial loss, coming between two draws. The truth of the matter is United know they need to be better in both boxes. United have conceded fewer opposition touches in their box than any other team in the league but, on the other hand, they are the only side yet to keep a clean sheet. They can also boast the most touches in opposition boxes but are largely incapable of killing matches off.

United, like Tottenham, are very good at dominating possession, averaging 60% per match, but cannot translate that to goals and points. Even in the victory against Ipswich, United were unable to put a full 90 minutes of composure together, relying on Bruno Fernandes to drag them through against a promoted side. The forwards are yet to synchronise, with Matheus Cunha, the man tasked with leading the line, having only one goal to his name, and even that took a heavy deflection.

No one has more than one assist so far, while only Fernandes and Bryan Mbeumo have scored twice or more, the Portuguese getting a hat-trick against Ipswich. Marcus Rashford has shown glimpses of promise on the left but has no goal involvements, giving the impression of a man who requires a confidence boost after returning to the club where he was not wanted for 18 months. Nor is there the option of Benjamin Sesko playing as a more traditional central striker given he is sidelined with injury, while Joshua Zirkzee cannot even class himself as a plan B. But United are prolific compared with Tottenham, whose only league goals came in a 3-2 defeat by Aston Villa just before the international break.

Losing to 10-man Manchester City was the most worrying of United’s defeats, showing how far off they look against a Champions League side. Phil Foden’s red card gave United plenty of space but they were unable to take advantage, instead plodding around, short of ideas, barely threatening. United are expert at dominating possession but not games, traits that create hope and frustration in equal measure.

The summer signings of a goalkeeper who cost nothing and three central midfielders is coming under as much scrutiny as Carrick’s tactics. At least Carlos Baleba is poised to finally make his debut after joining from Brighton for £65m in August and Carrick desperately needs him to provide the energy lacking in central areas thus far. Having recovered from an ankle injury, the Cameroonian has what it takes to snuff out the danger that has been leading to the concession of goals.

‘Sometimes she publishes notes she’s scribbled on her hand’: Édouard Louis on 10 reasons to love Anne Carson

The Guardian Fri, 09 Oct 2026 15:08:23 GMT

The French author discovered Carson on a bus while stranded in a snowstorm and has been enthralled by her fearless imagination ever since

Where to start with Anne Carson

‘Delights await!’: Margaret Atwood and other writers on Nobel winner Anne Carson

1. Anne Carson is one of the greatest writers of our time. I discovered her work on a Peter Pan bus from New York to New England. I’d bought Antigonick in a bookstore a few days earlier, almost randomly. From the very first lines, I was enthralled. While we were on the bus, a snowstorm suddenly blanketed the roads, and the other passengers and I found ourselves stuck for 10 hours in rural America, surrounded by an entirely white landscape. I took my computer out of my backpack and started to translate Antigonick into French. Spontaneously. I was so absorbed by the power of Carson’s text that I didn’t notice the hours pass.

2. One of Carson’s greatest strengths is that, unlike so many other contemporary writers, she doesn’t try to “make literature”. She writes. Sometimes clouds do the speaking, in her work, and sometimes monsters do; sometimes, in the middle of a collection of poems, she lets an imaginary Catherine Deneuve take over the narration. Sometimes she writes a letter to her own sleep and sometimes she publishes notes she’s scribbled on her hand. She writes about Homer, but also Rosalía; about Brecht, but also Marilyn Monroe.

3. In Carson’s work, time is upside down – out of joint, as Shakespeare writes in Hamlet. This is one of the strangest aspects of her work and it has fascinated me from my first reading. In her rewriting of Antigone, in the first scene, Antigone and her sister Ismene talk about Hegel. And yet, in Carson’s play, the conversation happens as if entirely normal, as if the ancient Greek Antigone and Ismene really had discussed Hegel together. One day, my friend Ivo van Hove decided to put on Sophocles’ Antigone and called Carson to ask her if she would do a new translation. Carson responded, “I already did a translation, titled Antigonick.” Ivo said, “Of course, but that’s not a literal translation of Sophocles – in the first scene, the two sisters talk about Hegel.” Carson responded, “That’s what’s written in Sophocles’ text. All I did was translate.”

4. One of Carson’s most wrenching texts is called Nox. In it, she tells the story of her brother, or rather, the story of her brother’s absence. When he was very young, her brother was convicted by a Canadian court. Rather than go to prison, he fled. He hid in Europe and Asia for decades under false identities. During the time of his disappearance, he would sometimes send his family a brief letter, or a postcard with quick phrases scribbled on the back. On a few occasions he called, just for a few minutes. One day, the Carson family received a call informing them of his death in Copenhagen. Carson gathered the photos she had of this brother who had just died and whom she hardly knew, and also theletters he had sent her, and she wrote fragments about her memories of him interspersed with an analysis of a poem by Catullus. She added in reflections on Herodotus and history, and very personal notes on pain and loss, reminiscent of Barthes’s Mourning Diary. Then she put all these notes into a box. And later Nox was published in the form of this box, with a single sheet of paper folded accordion-style inside bearing all the notes and images and fragments that she had accumulated. Never had a book looked like this – a shoebox with an enormous accordion foldout inside.

5. Carson thus spurns the limits of what a book is; her work Float is made up of several booklets on different subjects gathered together in a plastic envelope. Nox is indeed a box. H of H Playbook is a wide rectangular facsimile edition, impossible to put on a bookshelf. Lots of writers across history have tried to reinvent writing. Very few of them have also had the idea of reinventing what a book is, or transforming the book-object itself. Anne Carson did.

6. But Carson’s formal inventiveness should not lead us to forget the powerfully political dimension of her work. In Autobiography of Red, she takes inspiration from the ancient poet Stesichorus to tell the story of the monster killed by Hercules during his 12 labours. She chooses to tell the story of the monster, the victim, rather than repeat the tale of the hero, the executioner. She imagines a story in which a young Hercules and Geryon have a devastating homosexual affair. In her books, Carson often places herself in the position of the defeated.

7. For a long time she identified with Oscar Wilde, to the point of having a Wilde outfit that she regularly wore during her adolescence.

8. Women are also at the heart of her work, and always have been. In Norma Jeane Baker of Troy, one of her most beautiful texts, she makes Marilyn Monroe and Helen of Troy into one and the same character: two women who, despite the centuries between them, remain the object of the same masculine violence, the same dictates of obligatory beauty. Carson has also translated Sappho’s poems. And in her version of Euripides’s Bacchae, she gives an unheard-of psychological depth to the female characters.

9. On a more personal level, I can say that Carson has a distaste for the kind of social interaction that tends to come with a literary life. I sincerely believe that she likes nothing more than to be at home, writing. One day when we were signing copies of our books side by side, she said to me, “I really hate this!” Another time, after a performance we did together at the House of Literature in Oslo, she proposed that we quickly head for the restaurant in order to avoid the small talk.

10. Recently, we were talking about a trip I’m getting ready to take to Iceland, where she lives. I suggested to Anne that we do a performance together, with two voices, like we had done in the past. Then I felt bad about adding work to her life and so I sent her a follow-up message saying, “But we don’t have to do something public. We can just relax and enjoy ourselves.” Anne responded: “I prefer working. That way I don’t have to think about the world. Or myself.” How better to sum up the greatness of Anne Carson?

Lost generation: the AI threat to Britain’s next great directors

The Guardian Fri, 09 Oct 2026 15:00:31 GMT

Commercials once launched careers from Ridley Scott to Guy Ritchie, now automated production is cutting costs – and the chance to learn by doing

When Ridley Scott was awarded the UK’s highest accolade for a glittering career directing films from Alien and Blade Runner to Gladiator and The Martian, he reminded those attending the Bafta event eight years ago that making commercials had been his “film school”.

The advertising industry has long been a breeding ground for British film and TV talent who have gone on to make the jump to Hollywood productions, including Guy Ritchie, who started out making music videos and commercials, and Paddington in Peru director Dougal Wilson, whose credits include a number of John Lewis’s famous Christmas ads.

But the panicked race to introduce AI technology across the advertising industry, to cut client costs and avoid being pushed aside by big tech, has raised fears of a lost generation who may be denied the opportunity to develop into great British film and TV directors.

“100%, yes, I have fears,” says Luke Scott, who runs the group that includes Ridley Scott Associates, the media production company that was co-founded by his father in the 1960s.

“I’m grown up enough to recognise that change is inevitable. But what I’ve seen generally in terms of generative AI output is a very mixed bag. You can turn to it and do something and say ‘Look what I made and isn’t it edifying’. But that is very misleading and sort of introducing us to an ersatz creativity.

“The grave danger is the monoculturalisation of everything. The creative business is something you learn by doing. It is in the doing that is most valuable. Flying a drone isn’t like flying, there isn’t that visceral feeling to it, you are not actually flying. What do you do with that lost generation? Maybe in 20 or 30 years the whole notion of the ad industry as we work now will be an [anachronistic] joke.”

Last month, the global advertising group WPP officially opened its flagship production facility in a converted warehouse in east London. It was the first in an international rollout spearheading its £600m WPP Production business, as it aims to bring “world-class creativity and advanced AI capabilities under one roof”.

Cindy Rose, a former Microsoft executive appointed WPP’s CEO to turn around its fortunes, said that AI is ushering in a “golden age of marketing”.

“WPP and the industry as a whole is at a critical inflection point,” she said, against a backdrop of a Ford Capri being shot cruising the streets of an AI-generated Paris. “We have to better leverage the AI advantage we have. We no longer need to spend our clients’ budgets on expensive shoots abroad. We can do it in the studio [and] completely change the economics of our content supply chain. We can deliver content at the speed of culture.”

One industry source said that some ads can be made up to 60% cheaper, which has some clients embracing AI-led ads to “show finance directors they are making savings”, even though the output often looks “cookie cutter” and suffers a creative “erosion from the diminished role of a director”.

On the topic of the automotive sector the source questioned whether, in an increasingly AI-first ad industry, Top Gun would have become the quintessential 1980s blockbuster that it did. The film’s producers, Don Simpson and Jerry Bruckheimer, chose their director, Ridley Scott’s late brother Tony, after seeing a TV ad in which he depicted a Saab car racing a fighter jet in what could pass for a trailer for the cinematic style adopted throughout the film.

However, Richard Glasson, the chief executive of WPP Production, said that new technologies have always been embraced by the industry and the use of AI is no different.

“It is the future of where content is going, an AI production powerhouse for the future,” he said. “The underlying tech we use to create work is changing. It is being introduced in TV and film but not widely adopted in advertising to this point.”

He added that AI is being embraced by clients who need to be able to keep up with creating content across dozens more digital media platforms than ad agencies have ever had to keep pace with.

“All clients need a vastly greater amount of content,” he said. “There has been an explosion in the number of channels that they are talking to their consumers. To win against the algorithms you have to be producing new content, not just repurposing one ad campaign for six months, those days are gone. It is about speed to market, making the previous impossible possible. We can place a brand anywhere in the world in a single afternoon.”

Yet he does not believe that the days of the classic blockbuster ad campaign, and the need for the talent to create award-winning work, are numbered.

“We still make Super Bowl ads that take nine months, football World Cup campaigns and ads with celebrities in exotic locales,” he said. “They still exist and will continue to exist. The elephant in the room is whether AI is coming for jobs, in production we are seeing the opposite. I see AI as an enabler of abundance, and the people working in production as infinitely adaptable and curious about tech and what it will allow us to do.”

Privileged and proud: how nepo babies took fashion month by storm

The Guardian Fri, 09 Oct 2026 14:31:20 GMT

From commanding the catwalks to acting as plus-ones for their famous parents, celebrity kids are bang on trend

Knee-length skirts and bras worn as tops were two of the main takeaways from fashion month, which wrapped up this week. But the biggest trend had nothing to do with clothing. From New York and London to Milan and Paris, the shows were the ultimate proof of a nepo baby takeover.

John Travolta’s daughter, Ella Bleu, 26, made her Paris catwalk debut at Miu Miu. Apple Martin, 22, the daughter of Chris Martin and Gwyneth Paltrow, walked the Chloé show.

Meanwhile, the Vogue World event in Milan featured the Italian tenor Andrea Bocelli’s son Matteo, 29, Nick and Susie Cave’s son Earl, 26, Ava Phillippe, 27, the daughter of the actors Reese Witherspoon and Ryan Phillippe, and many more nepo babies in attendance.

Mark Borkowski, a PR consultant, described the nepo baby phenomenon as “a wonderful cocktail of youth, nostalgia and inherited glamour”.

Fran Hoepfner, the author of The Field Guide to Nepo Babies, said it was vital that a nepo had both a family connection and a direct or adjacent industry connection. “Simply having rich parents does not automatically make someone a nepo baby,” she said. “It just makes you lucky.”

Previously, the children of famous people tended to downplay their family connections or even change their surnames. Nicolas Cage was born Coppola – his uncle is the legendary US film-maker – while Angelina Jolie dropped the Voight from her surname in an attempt to distance herself from her actor father, Jon Voight.

According to Borkowski, we are now seeing play out “the industrialisation of inherited fame”. He described it as a cultural shift. “For years people tried to escape from the shadow of their parents because it actually hindered their career. Now they are no longer apologising for their privilege.”

Nicole Kidman brought her daughter Faith Urban, 15, to Chanel, while The Diplomat star Keri Russell’s plus one at the Louis Vuitton show was her 13-year-old daughter, Willa. Elsewhere, the supermodels Karen Elson and Kristen McMenamy danced with their daughters Scarlett Teresa White, 20, and Lily McMenamy, 32, on the H&M catwalk.

Four years after New York magazine declared 2022 the “year of the nepo baby”, the boom is showing no sign of slowing down. The appeal for brands is simple: the casting of a nepo instantly captures mass audience attention.

It is not limited only to fashion. The new Sense and Sensibility’s film credits read like a nepo roll-call. Samantha Morton’s daughter Esmé Creed-Miles plays Marianne Dashwood, while Sting’s non-binary child Eliot Sumner stars as Mr Palmer. Meanwhile, Cillian Murphy’s son Aran is currently on TV screens as Sharon Horgan’s son in Youth, and Kate Winslet’s son Joe Anders stars in Netflix’s adaptation of John Steinbeck’s 1952 novel East of Eden.

“It’s a marketing tool,” Borkowski said. “Casting an unknown model or actor is one thing, but casting the daughter of a Hollywood legend gives a brand all that inherited fame and decades of cultural recognition.”

The internet has been crucial to the nepo baby coup. In an age where anyone with a phone and internet access can become famous, why not lean into those existing famous family roots? “You don’t have to have any real talent to develop a fanbase,” Borkowski said.

In 2023 Romy Mars, the daughter of the film-maker Sofia Coppola and musician Thomas Mars, went viral after posting about being grounded because she had tried to charter a helicopter to have dinner with a friend using her father’s credit card.

In the now deleted video, she also revealed she wasn’t meant to have a social media account. “They don’t want me to be a nepotism kid but TikTok is not gonna make me famous, so it doesn’t really matter,” she said. Three years later she has amassed nearly 800,000 followers, starred in a film directed by her grandfather and released an album. Her debut music video was directed by her mum.

Hoepfner described Mars’s behaviour as “sheer nepo baby perfection”. She said today’s generation had “learned lessons from their older millennial peers, who either deflected or tried to play off their privilege with some degree of false humility.”

Elsewhere, Francesca Scorsese is a budding actor and film-maker, but it is her TikTok videos starring her Goodfellas director dad, Martin, that have led to millions of followers. In one, she asks him to identify “feminine items” including a menstrual cup, which Scorsese mistakes for a drinks container; in another, she tests him on gen Z slang.

Even if someone does try to move beyond their family name, they often continue to leverage their connections. In January, in a six-page Instagram statement, Brooklyn Beckham said he was cutting ties with his parents. That decision led to him becoming more famous than ever. Borkowski described the continuing attention that unfolded as a cross between “the Big Brother house and a soap opera”, with fans of each member of the family waiting to see what happened next.

Hoepfner said: “The fact of the matter is that there’s nothing they can really do about the fact that they’re a nepo baby, so they might as well own it. The best way to go about that at this point might as well be by doing it brazenly, with some degree of style or panache – especially if they aren’t really sorry about it.”

11 questions to ask yourself before going no contact with a family member

The Guardian Fri, 09 Oct 2026 14:00:31 GMT

In the UK, one in five families are affected by permanent estrangement – it’s not a decision to be taken lightly. These are the questions experts suggest you ask yourself before cutting a relative out of your life

It’s important to be certain you aren’t walking away because it feels more manageable than addressing challenging issues. “Sometimes estrangement is exactly what’s needed for safety and healing. Other times it functions as an attempt to avoid grief, conflict, disappointment or the painful acceptance that a parent cannot become the person one longs for,” says Joshua Coleman, a clinical psychologist and the author of Rules of Estrangement. “Distance alone doesn’t resolve those emotions.”

Fern Schumer Chapman, the author of Brothers, Sisters, Strangers, says people can become estranged due to poor communication skills, learned through family dynamics: “When parents are unable to express feelings and negotiate differences, they don’t model the necessary skills – listening, apologising, cooling off. As a result, small disagreements can explode into nasty rifts. Those with poor communication skills may handle stress by simply shutting down and cutting off.”

Ultimately, though, says Terri Apter, a psychologist and the author of Grandparenting, “people who decide to be estranged make the decision that the extent of discomfort from contact is unbearable”.

This is about double-checking your expectations. “One of the hardest psychological tasks is distinguishing between what someone should be and what they’re capable of being,” says Coleman. “Many adults understandably long for parents who can become emotionally attuned, validating or apologetic. The healthiest outcome isn’t always getting the relationship you wanted; sometimes it’s grieving the relationship you never had while deciding what level of contact is sustainable.”

Phil Lane, a clinical social worker and psychotherapist who has been estranged from his father for eight years, adds that it’s “important to consider if the other person is willing and/or able to provide what you need. This is not to suggest that we should cut someone off if they don’t meet our expectations, but rather it can help us determine if our expectations are reasonable and if we, not the other person, need to adjust.”

As Coleman says: “Most families are neither entirely loving nor entirely harmful.” Therefore, it’s useful to take a second look through adult eyes, which allows us to “understand pressures our parents were facing – mental illness, financial hardship, divorce, trauma, cultural expectations – that were invisible to us as children”. Crucially, though, Coleman adds: “Context doesn’t excuse harmful behaviour.”

Becca Bland, a researcher and counsellor in estrangement who has been estranged from her parents for 18 years, agrees: “It’s important to appreciate context, but not to explain away harm. Harm is harm. Seeing people in their context doesn’t take away the impact on you.”

Cutting ties can also mean losing other relationships. It’s something Schumer Chapman, who was estranged from her brother for decades, experienced. With the loss of her role as sister, she also lost that of her sister-in-law and aunt, and her children lost their cousins. “I felt like a whole branch of our small family had been sawed off, and all the responsibilities for our parents fell on me,” she says. She describes this estrangement as “a grief state that produces ongoing distress and deep insecurity and longing that can go on for decades”. For Apter, ultimately, “there are always trade-offs. In most cases you decide that you cannot take the pain, humiliation or chaos that comes with the relationship and have to accept the collateral.”

Lane echoes this: “While I stand by my decision, there is grief attached to the fact my son does not have a relationship with his grandfather. Factors like this should be considered deeply.”

Mismatched values are often a factor in estrangement – families not accepting someone’s religion, sexuality or life partner, for example – and the rigidity of those views matters. “Differences in morals, values and beliefs can be well dealt with in families if everyone is adaptable and respectful. It’s when family members need values reaffirmed rigidly that it all falls apart,” says Bland. Coleman agrees: “If both people can accept differences without constant attempts to convert, shame or control one another, many relationships can adapt. If every interaction becomes psychologically unsafe, greater distance may be healthier.”

Going no contact is a deeply personal decision, so it needs to be one that you make without outside influence. Pressure can come from romantic partners, online communities, friends, siblings, other relatives and therapists, says Coleman, who wants to distinguish between helpful and unhelpful interactions. “Support can be invaluable. Pressure is different,” he says. “The decision should ultimately reflect your own considered judgment.” Specifically, when it comes to social media and “therapy speak”, exercise caution. “Terms such as ‘toxic’, ‘narcissist’, ‘gaslighting’ and ‘boundaries’ can be useful when applied carefully, but social media often rewards certainty over complexity. Good therapy increases curiosity. Poor advice encourages premature certainty,” says Coleman.

Apter warns that “unreliable therapists make judgments about a family member’s personality when they have never met them, which can influence the client’s views”.

This is about feeling sure you have tried everything, so the decision can be as comfortable as possible. It took Lane five years “and much excruciating consideration” to arrive at his choice to estrange. “I felt I had exhausted all options. I was nearly 40, so it was certainly not a youthful or impulsive response. Sometimes it’s important to trust your instincts, even if they are telling you to do something that goes against the grain.”

Bland recommends involving a professional, who “can see a broader picture and help identify blind spots in a less confrontational way. In attempting to repair a relationship, we can get angry with people because they’ve hurt, neglected or harmed us. It helps to include a professional who understands when to say ‘stop’.”

You may be able to heal after some time away. Schumer Chapman finally managed to reconcile with her brother over the course of a year. “We met every week. Sometimes we went for a bike ride to become reacquainted with each other. Sometimes we discussed the estrangement, what had happened and why. Other times we recalled memories and laughed about our childhood, which was bonding.” She says the most important change was the way they communicated: “When we did have disagreements, which are inevitable, we talked our differences out.”

You won’t know if your relative hits hard times, becomes ill or even dies. You will need to consider whether you can live with that level of uncertainty. “Many people imagine estrangement will provide relief. What they’re less prepared for is ambiguous loss – the uncertainty of not knowing whether they will ever reconcile, whether they will hear about illness second-hand, or whether a death will occur before anything is resolved. Those are burdens worth considering,” says Coleman. Bland cautions: “It’s an unresolved attachment, and our brain wants to resolve it. It’s not a case of they’re out of my life, they’re out of my head – they will be in your head more. My research has found that people reconsider their decision almost every couple of days.” Lane, meanwhile, describes this uncertainty as something you ultimately have to “accept as part of the process, with the belief that the larger outcome will be positive and healthy for you”.

This is crucial for you to be able to cope with the emotional after-effects. “I don’t think people can do it without social support, because the sense of isolation is crippling,” says Bland. “It’s about having people around you who understand you’re breaking free of a heavily abusive pattern.” Bland’s other family members were instrumental in her decision and her ability to stick with it: “They gave me validation that my parents weren’t safe, which reinforced I had made the right choice.”

Lane describes the emotional fallout as producing “grief, very similar to that associated with the death of a family member. It’s psychologically unhealthy to go through grief and loss in isolation.” It may also be associated with stigma and shame. Bland describes how she often sees “the perpetrators of abuse getting sympathy from the rest of the family because they present themselves as the victim. People will potentially judge your decision because they don’t understand the relationship you’ve had from the inside.” In those instances, support is critical.

Bland recommends that you “consider what your window of tolerance is. Can you tolerate one meeting in a park every few months? Would that cost you more than having no relationship at all?” She describes it as cost/benefit analysis, but adds: “If people are in a very harmful situation where there’s abuse, I wouldn’t recommend going low contact because that doesn’t help them get out of the cycle.”

Lane has seen “many clients change the nature of a relationship, implement boundaries and recalibrate expectations to improve negative relationships”. Coleman says estrangement “exists on a spectrum”, and that many people could benefit from “limited contact, shorter visits, communicating primarily by text or email, avoiding volatile topics, seeing relatives only in group settings and having clear expectations about frequency and duration of contact. Sometimes these arrangements preserve enough connection while protecting emotional wellbeing.”

Apter adds: “Most people try going low contact before they decide to cut themselves off from a family member, but many discover it is not possible to set boundaries or avoid painful interactions”.

This is potentially the most salient question you can ask. Coleman says: “Estrangement is sometimes the healthiest option, particularly when there is ongoing abuse, coercion or repeated violation of boundaries.” Lane agrees, saying: “If a person consistently causes you to feel unsafe – physically or emotionally – you will live in a persistent state of feeling at risk. Over a long period of time, this can become unsustainable, and removing the abusive or harmful element may be necessary.”

Illiyoon ceramide ato concentrate cream, 75ml

Brick

I wrote about Brick, a device that helps reduce screen time, for my phone addiction piece. Micro bandana
