Execution TV? Pete Hegseth has taken the once ‘greatest democracy’ to a horrific new low

The Guardian Fri, 09 Oct 2026 01:19:07 GMT

A proposal to livestream the killing of Nidal Hasan by firing squad opens a window ever wider to the Trump administration’s complete moral vacuity

More fool me! Here I was thinking nothing that America’s Trump administration could do or say, no matter how politically and morally bankrupt, no matter how venal or violent, was capable of shocking me any longer.

Then I woke to today’s news that one of the Trump cabinet’s bigger boofheads – the uber Christian nationalist, crusader-fantasist and “secretary of war” Pete Hegseth had announced that America would have a public firing squad execution of murderer Nidal Hasan.

Reckless global militarisation including a threat at the UN to annihilate Iran, a litany of sexual misconduct allegations against the commander in chief, claims of blatant presidential corruption … they have all ceased to surprise and shock us, so inured has the world become to Donald Trump’s monstrous narcissism and maladministration.

But now we have execution TV. Tune in to the livestream on Thursday 3 December to watch a military firing squad shoot the life out of Hasan, the former army psychiatrist who killed 13 people at a US army base in 2009.

State-sanctioned killing as entertainment! Yes, the world’s supposedly greatest (or formerly greatest) democracy has arrived at an horrific new moral nadir.

The fact that America remains Australia and the west’s most relied-upon and trusted ally despite the global wrecking ball the second Trump administration has proved to be, was already cause for deep concern.

But being so closely allied to a country that now wants to turn the execution of a human being – no matter what their crimes – into a live entertainment event, promises to redefine depravity.

Given that American states continue to execute so many convicted criminals, where might the United States ultimately draw the line? No doubt the ilk of Hegseth in American society – and elsewhere – will count down the days until they can tune in to the live coverage of Hasan’s execution in droves. Might the audience cry out for more – for livestream cameras in the death chambers across the land of the free?

How would this populist administration respond? If you think it’s a fanciful question, consider how far American governance and presidential values have slid in the moral murk in the past two years alone.

Meanwhile, it’s hard to contemplate a more audacious appeal to American society’s darker angels than this looming entertainment event.

But there we are. We have arrived.

Pass the popcorn, Don and Pete!

It would be heartening today to hear political leaders the world over condemn Hegseth and Trump’s planned introduction of Ghoul TV.

But let’s please start in Australia, where federal governments have for a long time opposed capital punishment – let alone turning it into a public spectacle. Will the prime minister and his senior ministers stand up and condemn without qualification this depraved plan for America to livestream an execution? What about the leaders of other political parties here, some of whom have, after all, supported capital punishment?

We’re waiting.

Meanwhile, how much further into the moral quagmire must America wallow before Australia rethinks its craven military dependence on Washington – not least via the reckless shackling of our strategic reliance to the US via the $368bn (and counting) Aukus submarine deal?

Announcing America’s decision to turn killing into a form of entertainment, Hegseth said: “It was a radical Islamist attack in uniform inside the ranks, and so he’s going to get a firing squad of soldiers, as it should be, and we’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public, because people need to understand there’s serious consequences for these types of things.”

America’s defense department later confirmed the execution would be livestreamed.

This represents a significant lurch in the US from civilisation towards savagery.

You can’t choose your family. But you can choose your friends and allies. And you can also tell them firmly when they’ve careened off the ethical rails.

Actions speak louder than words.

And this planned livestreamed execution says it all about what is happening in America today, opening the window ever wider on the Trump administration’s moral vacuity and its paucity of human decency.

Paul Daley is a Guardian Australia columnist

He Left Behind Millions. Who Would Get It — His Family, or the D. S. A.?

The New York Times October 09, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

When a New York University professor died in 2024, it set off a legal dispute over a quietly accumulated fortune.

By Benjamin Weiser

David F. Greenberg was an academic who lived modestly in a small, rent-controlled apartment in the West Village that was, by one account, piled high with papers — the sort of man who leaves a legacy of ideas, not money.

He earned a Ph. D. in physics before joining New York University, which hired him to its sociology department in 1973 even though he did not hold a degree in that field. He worked there for half a century, building an expansive body of scholarship and a reputation as a caring teacher and mentor.

He was also building something else: a retirement fund. By the time Mr. Greenberg died two years ago, at the age of 82, its balance had grown enormously. Today, the fund is worth more than $6.6 million.

But there was a problem. It wasn’t clear who should get it.

The professor, who was not married, had no children and left no will, had listed his parents as his beneficiaries, but they were already dead. He also had selected a backup beneficiary, an obscure 1970s socialist group called the New American Movement, or N. A. M. — “or any successor thereof.”

N. A. M. had disappeared. But it didn’t take long for the fund’s managers to figure out what had happened to it. In 1982, N. A. M. merged with another group to form an organization that does exist: the Democratic Socialists of America.

The professor’s unexpected bequest could be an enormous financial boon to D. S. A., whose membership has more than doubled to about 126,000 in the past two years. Large donations are uncommon for the group, which brings in most of its money from dues. Its last publicly filed tax return, in 2024, showed net assets of $4.7 million.

Ashik Siddique, a D. S. A. national co-chair, said the group would have no qualms with accepting the professor’s funds.

“We don’t see any contradiction between being socialists and organizing to have money in a capitalist society,” Mr. Siddique said. “The more the better,” he added, “as long as it is meaningfully supporting the decisions that our members make together.”

But before any money was transferred to the organization, one of the professor’s nephews, Martin Hecht, as the administrator of his estate, filed suit, arguing that his uncle had not left his money to the D. S. A. but rather to N. A. M., which was “now defunct.” The lawsuit argued that Mr. Greenberg’s family, not the modern socialist group, would be the rightful recipient of his millions.

“Our Uncle David never missed an important family occasion, especially a birthday, because family meant more to him than anything,” Mr. Hecht said Wednesday in a statement. “Even in the months before he passed, he was working on our family lineage, reflecting the deep importance he placed on where we came from and the people we loved.”

The dispute over Mr. Greenberg’s wishes played out in Manhattan federal court over nearly a year and a half, pitting ideological bonds against familial ones, and seemed to near a conclusion on Friday.

The court filings illuminated the origins of the Democratic Socialists of America, which has become a force in Democratic politics in recent years. They also shed light on an unassuming but prolific man — a radical thinker, in his time — who stood to become, according to the group’s records, the D. S. A.’s largest donor ever. Whether he meant to or not.

In his 49 years with the sociology department, Mr. Greenberg was its institutional memory — “and he was also often its conscience,” according to David Garland, a fellow N. Y. U. professor.

“He spoke up clearly and forcefully, popular or not, whenever he felt we were going in the wrong direction, whenever he felt that there was departing from some past practice or some injustice was being perpetrated,” Mr. Garland said at a September 2024 memorial service for his colleague, before Mr. Greenberg’s sizable bequest became known. “He cared deeply about the department, about teaching, about students.”

He also cared about his family. Dayna Bender, a cousin of Mr. Greenberg’s from Chicago who spoke over Zoom at the service, said he was always the uncle who was free with his time and his smile. She related a story from one nephew who remembered being stumped on a physics problem. “He called Uncle David, who explained it in a way that made the problem simple,” Ms. Bender said. The nephew was working in renewable energy, she added.

Born in Evanston, Ill., in 1942, Mr. Greenberg became involved in the civil rights movement in the 1960s and 1970s. He took part in voter registration drives in rural South Carolina, where he was shot at — and, on one occasion, arrested, according to an obituary prepared by N. Y. U.’s sociology department. He also joined in anti-Vietnam War protests and in organized draft resistance, the obituary says. He argued for the abolition of prisons — a position he later dropped after an inmate wrote to him urging that he focus on more attainable goals. (He continued to believe that prisons required radical reform.)

Mr. Greenberg’s early writings on radical criminology caught the attention of the N. Y. U. sociology department, according to the obituary, and his body of work continued to expand. A 1981 collection of essays on Marxist criminology that he edited was widely used in the United States and elsewhere, the obituary says. His 1988 book, “The Construction of Homosexuality,” traced the history of same-sex relationships from ancient civilizations to modern times. The historian Nicholas B. Dirks, in a review for The New York Times, called the 635-page volume “careful, encyclopedic and important.”

“He was intensely curious about so many things,” said Mariana Veras, an N. Y. U. doctoral student with a math background. When they first met, she said, they talked about number theory.

Several of Mr. Greenberg’s former colleagues and students recall him as a shy and, at times, eccentric man whose office at the university was cluttered with papers he was unwilling to throw away. It was the same story at his Village apartment, on Bank Street, where he lived by himself.

At his 2024 memorial service, Mr. Greenberg’s cousin, Ms. Bender, read a message from an out-of-town relative who recalled staying with the professor once. “Every room was filled with corridors of paper stacked up to the ceiling,” the relative wrote. “We had to clear off a space to eat our Chinese food. And then I had to clear off space on the couch to sleep. I felt like I had walked right into a Charles Dickens novel.”

Former students said that, even years after they left school, Mr. Greenberg would send them carefully cut-out newspaper clippings on what their areas of study had been.

And he kept an open door for pupils who had questions or wanted feedback on their work, Valerie West, a former doctoral student and research assistant who counted Mr. Greenberg as a friend, said at the memorial service. Although the professor “did not give compliments lightly,” she said, he was “generous and kind in spirit.”

In a recent interview, Ms. West said she had two conversations with Mr. Greenberg, years ago, in which he made it clear he wanted to leave his estate to his family.

“It was to his sisters, and then later on he specifically said his nephews broadly,” Ms. West recalled.

She did not know how much money they were talking about, she said.

They spoke again after his sisters died. She said he reiterated his position.

“There was never a question in my mind that his relatives were going to get it,” she said.

Mr. Greenberg, who once described himself as living an “abstemious, spartan lifestyle,” also left behind stocks, bonds and cash worth a total of at least $1 million, New York probate court records show. Those assets were not involved in the dispute with the D. S. A.

In 1996, he enrolled in a second N. Y. U. plan, designating his two sisters as primary beneficiaries. He listed no backup recipients for that account. By the time he died in July 2024, his sisters were already dead, and the $1.3 million in the second plan went to his nephews. There was no disagreement over that money, either.

When he enrolled in the second N. Y. U. plan, Mr. Greenberg was in his 50s and “a loving uncle to four nephews,” who themselves were starting to have children, the lawsuit said. Motivated by his growing family responsibilities, the suit argued, the professor would have assumed his choice of his sisters as beneficiaries for the smaller fund would also apply to his earlier, more valuable account.

But Mr. Greenberg only ever made one change to that first account. In 1975, a year after enrolling, Mr. Greenberg changed the form to say that if his parents were no longer alive, the fund should go to N. A. M. “or any successor thereof.”

On the question of succession, the D. S. A.’s lawyers argued that the line was clear — that the merger of N. A. M. and the other leftist group, the Democratic Socialist Organizing Committee, had been seamless, intentional and immediate.

To bolster its case, the D. S. A. submitted to the judge, among other evidence, news coverage of the vote at the March 1982 convention in Detroit that drew hundreds of members from the two organizations.

N. A. M. and the Democratic Socialist Organizing Committee each met in separate rooms to consider the resolution, according to the socialist newspaper “In These Times,” which also described an emotional scene: “N. A. M.’s finale resembled the last moments of a ’60s commune, with tributes, tears and raised fists.”

Mr. Greenberg was not only aware of the new organization, he actively supported it, according to the D. S. A.’s records. Those records show he was a member of the organization since at least 1993, when the group began keeping electronic records, and that he paid dues to the group 29 times, totaling $1,815, over the next three decades until his death.

Tiffany Gong, the organization’s development director, said it was “incredibly meaningful” for Mr. Greenberg to have designated N. A. M. or its successor as a beneficiary — at such a young age, without seeking credit.

“You’re not getting a building named after you,” Ms. Gong said.

Jeff Manza, the former chairman of N. Y. U.’s sociology department, said he wasn’t certain how Mr. Greenberg would feel about his retirement fund ending up with the D. S. A. But the nature of his politics, at least, was clear.

“He was a principled radical throughout his life,” Mr. Manza said, adding, “I think he never deviated from a belief in the possibility of a just and socialist world.”

In July, Judge Paul A. Engelmayer ruled in the D. S. A.’s favor, saying it was “emphatically” clear that the organization was N. A. M.’s legal successor — and thereby entitled to the funds. The judge based the ruling not just on old newspaper clips but also on declarations from former N. A. M. leaders and other records. The professor’s estate appealed.

The judge ordered Mr. Greenberg’s retirement funds — which stood at $6,609,236.13 last month — to be deposited in a court account until the appeal was resolved. A recent legal filing suggested that a settlement was in the works, and on Friday afternoon, the parties indicated they had reached an agreement.

The Democratic Socialists of America would receive the full balance being held in the court’s account, a legal filing shows. As part of the agreement, the D. S. A. has dropped a request that Mr. Greenberg’s estate pay its legal fees. As of late Friday afternoon, the transfer of the roughly $6.6 million to D. S. A. still needed to be approved by the judge.

Benjamin Weiser is a Times reporter covering the federal courts and U. S. attorney’s office in Manhattan, and the justice system more broadly.

Attacker in FlyDubai Flight Meant to Crash Into Israeli Airport, Emiratis Say

The New York Times October 09, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The attorney general of the United Arab Emirates said that the co-pilot had been inspired by the Sept. 11 attacks after years of developing extreme Islamist views.

By Pranav Baskar

Emirati investigators said on Friday that the co-pilot who attacked the captain of a FlyDubai flight last week had intended to carry out a Sept-11-inspired suicide mission, crashing the airliner into Israel’s biggest airport.

The co-pilot, investigators said, had developed increasingly extreme Islamist views over several years.

The details, disclosed by the Emirati attorney general, offered the most comprehensive official account so far of the co-pilot’s motives and preparation. The report also deepened questions about how signs of his radicalization were missed before he was allowed to fly such a sensitive route.

More than 170 passengers, mostly Israelis, were on FlyDubai Flight 1073 last week when the co-pilot began attacking the pilot with the plane’s crash ax and then tried to crash the airliner. The pilot, Capt. Smit Machchhar, managed to unlock the cockpit door, and passengers were able to subdue the assailant, narrowly averting a catastrophe.

Backup pilots were on board and ultimately stabilized the plane, bringing it to an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.

The Emirati attorney general, Hamad Saif Al Shamsi, said the co-pilot, a 29-year-old Omani national, had planned to crash the plane into the passenger terminal at Ben Gurion Airport in Tel Aviv “with the aim of causing the greatest possible loss of life.”

The Emirati statement did not identify the co-pilot, but people familiar with the investigation have said that his name is Hamam al-Hammami, and that his embrace of radical Islamist views prompted the Omani authorities to scrutinize him earlier.

The Emirati investigation found that the co-pilot had begun a “drift towards extremism and terrorism” almost a decade ago, while he was a student in Melbourne, Australia. The Royal Melbourne Institute of Technology said in a statement that the co-pilot was enrolled at the university between 2015 and 2017 but did not complete his engineering degree.

While in Australia, Mr. al-Hammami developed a fascination with extremist literature and online content “glorifying terrorist organizations and suicide operations” the Emirati statement said. He also “received support” from groups related to the Muslim Brotherhood, an international Islamist movement, according to the statement, without elaborating further.

Taking inspiration from the attacks of Sept. 11, 2001, and takfir ideology — a view that effectively allows one Muslim to declare another an apostate — the co-pilot became increasingly interested in a similar attack, the Emirati statement said.

He confessed to the authorities that following through on that vision was “linked to his decision to pursue a career in aviation,” according to investigators. Before coming to FlyDubai in January 2026, he was employed by Oman Air for four years and spent a brief stint at Royal Maroc Air, a Moroccan airline, the investigation found.

The co-pilot told the authorities that he acted alone, investigators said, though they added that they were still looking into that question. To prepare for the operation, he had used two previous flights to Tel Aviv to familiarize himself with the route, consumed more “material promoting terrorism” and trained in boxing, the Emirati statement said.

But the disclosure left open questions about how Mr. al-Hammami was cleared to fly such a sensitive route. It is unclear whether Omani investigators had shared their concerns with security officials in Israel, the United Arab Emirates — where the flight originated — or with the airline.

Mr. Al Shamsi said the co-pilot “had met the professional and security requirements for employment” at FlyDubai, including completing required checks and providing a certificate of “good conduct.” He added that none of the steps revealed “any indications of his extremist views or his intention to carry out a terrorist plot.”

The plane’s passengers were mostly Israelis, some of whom said the crisis evoked the feelings of dread they had last felt on Oct. 7, 2023, during the Hamas-led attack on Israel, in which about 1,200 people were killed.

After the failed attack on the plane, two posts appeared on a LinkedIn profile bearing Mr. al-Hammami’s name. One depicted a photo of Ayman al-Zawahri, who led Al Qaeda after Osama bin Laden’s death and was killed by the United States in 2022. It was not clear who made the posts or whether they had been scheduled in advance to be published.

Victoria Kim contributed reporting.

Pranav Baskar is an international reporter at The Times, based in New York.

Trump Says He Will Import Russian Diesel Fuel Amid High Prices

The New York Times October 09, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

President Trump said Russia had agreed to ship potentially millions of tons of diesel fuel in the coming months. But Russia has an ongoing ban on exporting diesel.

By Chris Cameron

Reporting from Washington

President Trump said on Friday that he had reached an agreement with President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia to immediately import Russian diesel fuel to the U. S. market, despite a Russian ban on exporting fuel.

It was not immediately clear if Mr. Putin had signed off on that deal. But minutes after Mr. Trump’s announcement, the Treasury Department said it was lifting sanctions on Russian diesel exports “to allow the supply of Russian diesel to the global market.” The announcement gave Russian energy producers a general license to sell diesel fuel until April.

Russia, a crucial supplier of diesel to the rest of the world, said last week that it was extending its ban on diesel exports until the end of October, amid punishing Ukrainian strikes on oil refineries and other fuel infrastructure. Those attacks, and the export ban, have kept fuel prices high ahead of the midterm elections. Mr. Trump has recently criticized Ukraine for the strikes, saying they were driving up prices.

But Mr. Trump said in a social media post on Friday that Mr. Putin had approved shipping potentially millions of tons of diesel fuel in the coming months.

“It was agreed,” Mr. Trump said, “that Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace, another 500,000 Tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 Tons immediately thereafter. Additionally, based on the condition of their Diesel Refineries, Russia will then deliver, within a short period of time, 3,000,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel.”

The return of Russian diesel to international markets would be a win for Mr. Putin, who has sought for years to break the ice on U. S. sanctions against Moscow’s energy sector.

Despite suffering from the most acute gasoline crisis in decades, Moscow still has an excess supply of diesel. But Edward Fishman, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, said he doubted that Russia could supply as much diesel fuel as Mr. Trump said it had promised.

“The reason Russia imposed an export ban was that Ukrainian strikes had degraded its refining output, necessitating fuel rationing for domestic use,” Mr. Fishman said. “This strikes me as classic Putin — empty promises aimed at sowing further divisions in the trans-Atlantic alliance.”

It is the latest effort by the Trump administration to ease sanctions on Russia in a bid to lower energy prices. At the beginning of the war with Iran, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent lifted sanctions on Russian oil that was at sea, saying that it would add hundreds of millions of barrels of crude to global markets, and would curb prices.

Alan Rappeport and Ivan Nechepurenko contributed reporting.

Chris Cameron is a Times reporter covering Washington, focusing on breaking news and the Trump administration.

Want to Avoid Another Jan. 6? Defeat These Republicans.

The New York Times October 09, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Guest Essay

By Ben Wikler

Mr. Wikler was the chairman of the Democratic Party of Wisconsin from 2019 to 2025.

The stakes in November’s midterms aren’t merely about who will hold power over the next two years. Some of this year’s elections will also determine who oversees the presidential election in 2028.

The races with perhaps the greatest significance for election security two years from now are contests for governor — and in more than one battleground state, Republicans have nominated candidates who’ve expressed skepticism about, or who have outright denied, the results of the 2020 presidential election.

These states include Arizona, Pennsylvania, Michigan and my home state, Wisconsin.

It would be bad enough for an election-denying Republican to lead one of those states. What’s worse, a G. O. P. victory in one of those governor’s races could create a potential opening for President Trump’s party to subvert the 2028 election.

Democrats are right to feel bullish about their odds in a slew of this year’s congressional races, and to lean into those contests. But to avoid another Jan. 6 scenario, they should devote just as much attention to — and sufficient resources toward — electing Democratic governors.

Perhaps nowhere is this more important than in Wisconsin, where the 2026 Republican cash advantage is extremely worrisome.

In Wisconsin, the Republican nominee for governor is Representative Tom Tiffany. After the 2020 election, Mr. Tiffany was the only member of Wisconsin’s congressional delegation to sign onto a legal brief supporting a lawsuit to overturn the results in Wisconsin and other battleground states. Then he announced that he would vote in Congress against certifying Wisconsin’s Electoral College votes. On Jan. 7, 2021, Joe Biden’s election as president was certified, despite Mr. Tiffany’s votes against certifying the results from both Pennsylvania and Arizona. Perhaps to appeal to concerned voters, he now concedes that Mr. Biden won. But as recently as August, Mr. Tiffany said he didn’t regret those votes.

Mr. Tiffany’s Democratic opponent this year is David Crowley, the Milwaukee County executive. According to one analysis, Mr. Tiffany and his allies are outspending Mr. Crowley and his supporters $54.8 million to $21.6 million.

How? Much of the money being spent to elect Mr. Tiffany comes from one multibillionaire couple, Richard and Elizabeth Uihlein. Mr. Uihlein was reportedly among the largest funders of the rally that morphed into the Capitol riot. The Uihleins have given more than $30 million to the Republican Party of Wisconsin this year. By late last month, the party had transferred close to $35 million to Mr. Tiffany’s campaign. And Mr. Uihlein is the main contributor to the Restoration of America PAC, which has reported spending more than $12 million in support of Mr. Tiffany.

Wisconsin’s governor signs the certificate naming the state’s presidential electors, and transmits it to Washington. In theory, a governor could refuse to do so in 2028 — very likely triggering a court battle that could slow the process of determining who becomes our next president. In Wisconsin, the last three presidential elections came down to margins of less than one percentage point, making the state attractive to those fraudulently claiming that chicanery has affected election results.

The Wisconsin governor’s race isn’t the only one Democrats should keep their eyes on.

Arizona is another swing state with a race that features an election-denying Republican candidate for governor, Representative Andy Biggs, who backed the same lawsuit that Mr. Tiffany did. The Democratic governor, Katie Hobbs, is favored against Mr. Biggs, but Democrats should take nothing for granted.

The same is true in Michigan, where Representative John James has called the 2020 election “rigged and manipulated.” And in Pennsylvania, where the state treasurer, Stacy Garrity, has said “we know” that Mr. Trump won in 2020. Neither of them is favored against their Democratic opponents, Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson in Michigan, and Gov. Josh Shapiro in Pennsylvania.

Then there’s another category in Georgia, where the Republican running for governor and the billionaire funder of his campaign are the same person: Rick Jackson. He has conceded Mr. Biden’s 2020 win, but his stance on that election is more cryptic. In August, CNN reported that in one recording, Mr. Jackson said, “What happened in 2020 is just unconscionable.” In his successful primary campaign against Georgia Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger — who famously declined to “find” enough votes to hand Mr. Trump a victory in Georgia — one of Mr. Jackson’s campaign ads tags Mr. Raffensperger as “Brad ‘Judas’ Raffensperger,” presumably a reference to Judas Iscariot.

Mr. Jackson, the founder of Jackson Healthcare, has put more than $100 million of his own money into his race. In September, The Atlanta Journal-Constitution reported that “pro-Jackson groups have spent or reserved nearly $76 million in airtime ahead of the general election.” That is almost 10 times as much as his Democratic opponent, Keisha Lance Bottoms, a former mayor of Atlanta.

If any one of these Republican candidates wins, it’s not hard to imagine election subversion attempts taking place again in that state.

Understandably, Democrats across the country have their sights set on retaking one or both houses of Congress. But we can’t neglect these races for governor, particularly those with election-denying candidates, close polling or huge Republican cash advantages — or, in Wisconsin, all three.

The Constitution puts election administration in the hands of the states. In more than one race this year, voters aren’t just deciding between a Democrat and a Republican. They’re deciding whether their states should be run by people who don’t stand firmly for free and fair elections. For Americans concerned that Mr. Trump and his movement pose a danger to the security and legitimacy of future presidential elections — the sanctity of the vote — the time to stop them is now.

Ben Wikler is the host of “This Is Wisconsin” and the author of “This Is the Plan: How to End America’s Meltdown and Save Democracy.”

Millions Lose Private Medicare Plans and Face Rising Costs

The New York Times October 09, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

As enrollment for Medicare Advantage begins this month, older Americans are confronting fewer options because insurers are discontinuing coverage in many areas.

By Christopher Rowland and Reed Abelson

Millions of people with private Medicare coverage are being forced to change their insurance for 2027 and will pay higher prices for prescriptions and medical care, prompting some experts to warn that more older Americans will face greater financial hardship.

Major insurers, like UnitedHealth, Centene and state Blue Cross plans, have shuttered plans that they viewed as unprofitable in certain markets, leaving some people with fewer choices of policies, and even more limited choices of doctors in 2027. In some rural counties from Oregon to New Hampshire, older Americans shopping for private Medicare Advantage plans will find that options have vanished completely or are dwindling to just a few plans.

Overall, as open enrollment begins this month, roughly five million people will be forced to switch plans because their current policy has been canceled or is no longer offered in the county where they live, according to an estimate from Duos, a health technology firm. Other estimates are lower, but analysts who have been studying the issue said cancellations would probably surpass the number this year, which was the highest on record.

Dependent on Social Security and other fixed incomes, recipients also will be paying substantially more in out-of-pocket costs next year when they need a prescription drug or go to a doctor or hospital.

The upheaval and confusion in some areas of the country are in sharp contrast to the Trump administration’s claims that the Medicare Advantage program is “stable” and that average premiums will be lower next year. Now that about 35 million older Americans are covered by Medicare’s private plans, many will face an enrollment period that is likely to be volatile, according to insurance brokers, industry analysts and experts.

The disruptions risk angering older voters before the midterm elections. Many voters say they are unable to afford increases in health care, groceries and gas. A KFF poll released this week found that nearly twice as many likely voters trust Democrats more than Republicans to handle health care costs.

President Trump has announced that the administration was sending out pre-election payments of at least $90 to 20 million traditional Medicare beneficiaries — but not those covered by private plans. Democrats called it a “desperate” move in the face of voter disapproval.

The changes to Medicare Advantage will require members to carefully scrutinize the fine print of plan options, because costs are rising in multiple ways — from co-payments for doctors and prescriptions to deductibles, health analysts said.

In Pahoa, on the Big Island of Hawaii, Ann and Mick Kalber received a registered letter last week advising them their plan was being discontinued.

Mr. Kalber, 78, has a history of throat cancer and jaw surgeries, and he is now on a feeding tube. This year he was hospitalized twice in nearby Hilo. Together the couple are paying less than $300 in monthly premiums. Now they are bracing to pay hundreds more. A high priority for the couple is maintaining access to a Mayo Clinic surgeon in Florida who has operated on Mr. Kalber’s jaw.

Asked if they could afford any increase while living on a combination of Social Security income, an inheritance and savings from careers making videos of volcanic eruptions, Ms. Kalber said, “No — but we can’t afford not to.”

Republicans and many Democrats have long championed privatization of Medicare, but some supporters are concerned that Medicare Advantage is losing its luster. For years, the private market for Medicare plans seemed like a gold rush for insurers, which offered low-cost plans and policies that offered benefits like vision and dental care that were not available in the traditional program. By 2023, more than half of the people eligible to enroll had signed up for a private plan.

But the insurance companies soon came under sharp criticism for overbilling the program, prompting government officials to reduce reimbursements. Health care costs also began to climb more sharply, and some insurers say they struggled to make money.

In 187 counties, insurers are not offering any Medicare Advantage plans next year. Rural counties with low populations, fewer hospitals and higher costs are disproportionately losing plans.

Source: KFF.

Rebecca Robbins/The New York Times

Health Care Service Corporation, which operates nonprofit Blue Cross plans in several states, is sharply reducing the number of places where it offers plans and exiting some half-dozen states.

Like other insurers, the company points to numerous reasons for dropping out of various regions of the country, including changing government policies, medical costs in certain communities and the number of people enrolled in its plans.

The company said it remained committed to the market. “Medicare Advantage is very important to us,” said Stephen Harris, who oversees government programs for the insurer.

Cutbacks by UnitedHealth, the nation’s largest insurer, are causing some 390,000 people to switch policies.

The company emphasized that 94 percent of individuals eligible for the program would still have access to one of their plans. “The program is delivering real value today,” said Bobby Hunter, the president of UnitedHealthcare.

Some of the extra benefits, like dental care, that have made Medicare Advantage especially popular and have been used by insurers for years to woo new customers and build market share are being pared back.

In announcing what plans would be available for 2027, the Trump administration emphasized the program’s stability. It said people would pay lower premiums overall and pointed out that most parts of the country would have a robust number of plans competing for business.

Medicare “is fighting to keep high-quality care options affordable and accessible for the millions of beneficiaries who rely on Medicare Advantage and Part D prescription drug plans,” said Dr. Mehmet Oz, the administrator of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services. “By slashing handouts to big insurance companies,” he said, the government “is keeping premiums stable.”

“Individual plans make business decisions every year about where and how they participate, but those decisions should not be confused with M. A. instability,” Dr. Oz said in a statement, referring to Medicare Advantage.

But industry experts estimate that millions of people will no longer have access to the plans they had chosen, particularly those plans that did not charge a premium.

“In my decade of working in the industry, I have never seen the announcement so disconnected with what the market is experiencing as a whole,” said Jenn Kerfoot, the president of Duos, which helps people navigate Medicare. “We’re seeing the compounding forces of changes in this program.”

Many older Americans on fixed budgets will see monthly premiums rise — and what they must pay toward their medical and drug expenses will also go up. By one estimate, the average out-of-pocket limit on a typical plan will rise to $6,600, from about $5,000 in 2024.

Michele Harris-Padron, 74, who lives in Santa Barbara, Calif., can keep her plan but will have to pay $30 more a month in premiums next year. Her out-of-pocket costs could also go up. The amount she pays to see a specialist will go up from $45 to $60 a visit.

She and her husband switched plans two years ago from Blue Shield of California to UnitedHealthcare when her Blue Shield plan no longer covered her doctors.

“I’m really struggling to see if there are any other options for us, but I don’t really believe that there are,” Ms. Harris-Padron said.

Some states are getting hit harder than others. Insurers in Minnesota cut plans in 2026 and plan to again for 2027, with another 387,000 people caught in plans that are ending coverage either because companies closed the plan or left a county, according to Duos.

The number of counties with no plans available at all in 2027 rose to 187, from 118 this year, out of the nation’s 3,069 counties, according KFF, a nonprofit health policy organization. States with counties that have no plans in 2027 for the first time are New Hampshire, North Dakota and Oklahoma. Alaska’s vast rural area and tiny population have made it prohibitive for Medicare Advantage insurers for years.

One of those places where all plans have dried up is Minnesota’s Crow Wing County, a two-hour drive from Minneapolis in the center of the state. Nicole Converse, a broker at RG Insurance, said she was advising Medicare Advantage beneficiaries there that they would have to switch to traditional Medicare and purchase a supplemental Medigap plan, which she said would cost $330 a month in premiums. They also will have to purchase a separate Medicare Part D drug plan. She said the firm had about 1,000 Medicare Advantage clients in the county who would be affected.

“It’s been pretty rough so far having to explain that to people,” Ms. Converse said. “The biggest concern is they are going to have a hard time affording this.”

Rural states are experiencing more turmoil because paying for care in those places can be more expensive for insurers. The limited number of hospitals and doctors outside urban areas makes it difficult for insurers to negotiate favorable contracts, said Roshan Desai, vice president for product and strategy at Rebellis Group, which advises health plans.

“There’s a lot of volatility,” he said. “Before, plans would never reduce a service area. Now it’s common.”

For many people in traditional Medicare, their stand-alone prescription benefit insurance, called Part D, also will be changing. About four million people who received this drug insurance with no monthly premium will now be required to pay, because the Trump administration is ending temporary subsidies.

The number of stand-alone Part D plans has declined by two-thirds, to 316 from nearly 1,000 in 2021, according to Duos.

Whether erosion and higher costs in Medicare Advantage will continue after next year depends on a number of factors, including any government response.

“This doesn’t have to be the new normal, and it shouldn’t be,” said Rebecca Buck, senior vice president for public affairs for the Better Medicare Alliance, which represents the private insurers. “It all starts by fully funding Medicare Advantage and good stable policymaking.”

Reed Abelson covers the business of health care, focusing on how financial incentives are affecting the delivery of care, from the costs to consumers to the profits to providers.

Mike Ditka Has Died. Bears Coach Was Beloved for Winning and Shouting.

The New York Times October 09, 2026

Mike Ditka (1939-2026)

He and the Bears won the Super Bowl in 1986, and after coaching he became one of the sport’s most visible and enduring talking heads. He was 86.

He and the Bears won the Super Bowl in 1986, and after coaching he became one of the sport’s most visible and enduring talking heads. He was 86.

Mike Ditka being carried off the field by members of his Chicago Bears after they defeated the New England Patriots in Super Bowl XX in January 1986. Credit... Phil Sandlin/Associated Press

Supported by

By Barry Bearak

Mike Ditka, a tenacious tight end for the Chicago Bears who relished each collision and fought for every yard, then a Super Bowl-winning Bears coach so well-known for his sideline rants that he became a symbol of competitive fire, died on Friday. “Da Coach,” as he was commonly known, was 86.

The death was announced by his family through Jarrett Payton, the son of the former Bears running back Walter Payton. No further details were provided.

Ditka, who at times could be a bully, more often exuded a kind of crusty charm that fans found endearing. He was glib and amusing and opinionated. After leaving football, he became one of the sport’s most visible and enduring talking heads, working as an analyst for NBC, CBS and finally ESPN.

Nowhere was he more esteemed than in Chicago, his adopted home, where he was exalted as someone who epitomized the city’s grit. He was viewed as tough and authentic, a man who spoke his mind no matter the consequences.

To a large degree, the Windy City felt in his debt. He starred on the 1963 Chicago Bears, a team that won the N. F. L. title, and coached the 1985 Bears to the franchise’s only Super Bowl victory, a 46-10 win over the New England Patriots.

Ditka favored a basic style of play that he called “Bears football,” taking the game back to its primal roots: Hit the other guy harder than he hits you. With a protruding chin, combed-back hair and bushy mustache, he even resembled the fierce bear on the team’s emblem. He certainly could growl.

Chicago’s affection for its coach was the subject of several memorable sketches on “Saturday Night Live.” Devoted Bears fans, always shown seated in a restaurant and gorging themselves with meat and beer, extolled their hero, claiming “Da Coach” could win a game even without his players. They prayed, “We thank God and Ditka for all they have provided.”

Ditka portrayed himself and his team as the “Grabowskis,” blue-collar guys who carried a lunch pail to work and weren’t afraid of getting dirty. “We were the hard-hat guys,” he wrote in a 2005 memoir called “In Life, First You Kick Ass.” “The other guys ride in limos. We ride in trucks.”

But Ditka himself enjoyed vintage cars and exclusive golf club memberships. He opened a chain of pricey restaurants that featured 38-ounce pork chops. For three decades, he was one of America’s most prominent pitchmen, doing ads for Hanes underwear, Campbell’s chunky soups, American Express and, as he aged, Levitra, a medication for erectile dysfunction. He sold everything from antifreeze to frozen yogurt and started his own line of fine wines and cigars. He opened Mike Ditka Resorts in Florida. Despite being a “Grabowski,” he had his own limousine service.

How The Times decides who gets an obituary. There is no formula, scoring system or checklist in determining the news value of a life. We investigate, research and ask around before settling on our subjects. If you know of someone who might be a candidate for a Times obituary, please suggest it here.

As a coach, Ditka displayed wild mood swings, in a rage one day and penitent the next. He was notorious for screaming at his players and berating sportswriters. He chewed gum as if he was angry at it. His intensity could be both admirable and intimidating.

After a loss in 1983, his second year as a head coach, he punched a locker in front of the team and broke his hand. And yet he could also laugh at himself. A week later, he held up his cast and told his players, “Win one for Lefty.”

Ditka made profitable use of this gruff persona, playing a parody of himself on TV commercials and in the 2005 film comedy “Kicking & Screaming,” where he coached a kids’ soccer team with Will Ferrell. “I eat quitters for breakfast and spit out their bones,” he bellowed at the young players.

Armen Keteyian, who wrote the 1992 biography “Ditka: Monster of the Midway,” portrayed the coach as “a complex and contradictory man,” a hard drinker who “played more cards than Amarillo Slim and as much golf as Arnold Palmer.” Keteyian added, “His self-esteem and temperament are forever tied to that one constant in his life, the one elixir that cured any ill — winning.”

Keteyian quoted Megan Ditka, the coach’s only daughter: “I asked my mom once. I said, ‘Mom, was he the same person when you married him?’ She said honest to God, he was a very shy and unassuming person before he got into the Pro Bowl. Then it was women. Fame. This and that. She said the priorities in his head got a little crowded.”

Michael Keller Ditka was born on Oct. 18, 1939, in Carnegie, Pa., outside of Pittsburgh, and grew up in nearby Aliquippa. The family name had been Dyzcko in Ukraine, and the surname was changed by Ditka’s father, also named Mike. His mother was Charlotte (Keller) Ditka.

The elder Ditka, himself a forceful man, worked at a steel mill, coming home with burn marks on his arms and scorched clothing. He became president of the local union and held the job for 34 years. He was a strict father, “not afraid of taking the belt out to whip you,” his son said.

Young Mike, the eldest of four children, was a fierce competitor even as a boy. He’d chew out his teammates for making errors in Little League. He once chased his younger brother over a fence after he dropped a fly ball.

In high school, he was captain of the football, basketball and baseball teams. He had a chance to sign a professional baseball contract but decided instead to attend college. He was recruited heavily to play football by Pitt and Penn State. At the time, he thought he might one day become a dentist, and Pitt alumni convinced him that their dental school would be easier to get into.

Reflecting later on his career choices, Ditka said: “The dentistry thing wouldn’t have happened. I mean, think of Dr. Ditka. Me looking into people’s mouths? I think I’d rather knock teeth out than put them in.”

At Pitt, Ditka played tight end and split end on offense and on the defensive line. He also punted. The Bears drafted him with the fifth pick of the first round in 1961, signing him for a $12,000 salary (about $130,000 today) and a $6,000 bonus. That same year, he wed Margery Dougherty, whom he had known since high school. The marriage produced four children and lasted 12 years until their divorce.

Though just a rookie, Ditka redefined the notion of what a tight end could add to an offense. At 6-foot-3, 230 pounds, he was not just a blocker, but also a prolific pass catcher who bulled his way over tacklers downfield. He became rookie of the year and made the first of five Pro Bowl appearances.

The take-no-guff tight end inevitably feuded with his domineering coach, George Halas, who was also the team’s owner. Their biggest dispute was about money. Halas was a skinflint who, Ditka said, “tosses around nickels like manhole covers.” In 1966, in a secret deal, Ditka accepted $50,000 to sign with the Houston Oilers of the rival American Football League. The deal fell through when the N. F. L. and the A. F. L. merged.

Halas traded Ditka the following year to the then-lowly Philadelphia Eagles, where, slowed by injuries, he played two miserable seasons. Though he was never again an All-Pro, he enjoyed three better years after that with the Dallas Cowboys before retiring in 1972.

Tom Landry, the Cowboys’ coach, thought enough of Ditka to hire him as an assistant. The two were an odd couple, one a stone-faced man who taught Bible classes and the other a hot-tempered carouser. In a foreword to Ditka’s autobiography “Ditka,” Landry cautiously wrote, “Although I cannot condone the use of four-letter words in this book or elsewhere, I can endorse the book’s Christian intent.”

In 1977, Ditka married Diana Trantham. In addition to his wife, his survivors include his four children.

Ditka remained a Cowboys assistant for nine years. In late 1981, eager to become a head coach, he took a long shot, writing to the 86-year-old George Halas and asking to be considered if the Bears were ever looking to replace their coach.

Halas had given up the on-field reins in 1967; the Bears glory days were in mothballs. He was in the market for a new coach, someone as tough as himself, and by hiring Ditka he got what he wanted. The team’s new coach cursed and threatened. He said he told his players that “they were cowards for not hitting anybody. Then I threw chalk at the chalkboard.”

The Bears were coming off a 6-10 season and, in Ditka’s first year, a strike-shortened season, they went 3-6. But the new coach had inherited a strong core with running back Payton, middle linebacker Mike Singletary and defensive lineman Dan Hampton, all future Hall of Famers.

The team drafted well. In 1983, the Bears went 8-8; in 1984, they were 10-6.

In 1985, they finished 15-1 and won Super Bowl XX. The Bears were not only one of the most dominant teams ever, they were also a fun house of outlandish characters, including a player so massive he was called the Refrigerator and a defense that woofed like hounds before each play.

Ditka’s subsequent Bears teams, though abundant with talent, never again made it to football’s biggest game. Indeed, the fun house was only great fun the first time around. The Bears suffered from key injuries, salary disputes and internal bickering about endorsements. Ditka’s tirades no longer seemed master strokes of motivation, just displays of an uncontrollable temper. He was fired after the Bears went 5-11 in the 1992 season.

Five years later, Ditka, a man with such bad hips that he waddled more than walked, returned to the game as head coach of the New Orleans Saints. His teams were awful. In Ditka’s third and final year, he said, “God puts people in places for reasons, and he probably put me here to be humbled.”

This general was not one to fade away. His TV appearances continued. He maintained a business empire. In his later years, he became a leading advocate for former N. F. L. players suffering from injuries incurred during their careers. The hard-hitting Ditka criticized the sport for failing to effectively deal with the problem of concussions.

In 2004, Republican leaders asked him to run for the U. S. Senate from Illinois against a state senator named Barack Obama, a greenhorn candidate with far less name recognition than a Hall of Fame football legend. Ditka, a staunch conservative, decided he already had too many other commitments. He came to regret the decision.

“Biggest mistake I ever made,” he told a reporter in 2013. “Not that I would have won, but I probably would have and he wouldn’t be in the White House.”

Donor Says Kimberly Guilfoyle Sought Money From Him to Cover Debt

The New York Times October 09, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

Correspondence suggests that Ms. Guilfoyle, the U. S. ambassador to Greece and former fiancée of Donald Trump Jr., asked a G. O. P. donor to pay off her credit card.

By Sharon LaFraniere

Reporting from Washington

Kimberly Guilfoyle, the former fiancée of Donald Trump Jr., secretly begged a Republican donor to pay her credit card debt while she was waiting to be confirmed as ambassador to Greece, according to an interview with the donor.

The donor, Eric Deters, said that Ms. Guilfoyle had asked him to wire $100,000 to pay off her American Express card just before her Senate confirmation hearing in early July 2025, promising to serve as his “ride or die in Trump world” if he did.

“Honey please I need you to get this done for me today,” she wrote in what appeared to be a text message. Communications between Mr. Deters and Ms. Guilfoyle were reported earlier by The Wall Street Journal. Mr. Deters provided what appeared to be screenshots of their correspondence to The New York Times.

Mr. Deters sketched out a tawdry tale in which a member of the Trump family’s inner circle promised access to top administration officials as part of a financial arrangement she insisted be kept hidden. The donor wanted to connect with Pam Bondi, then attorney general, and Billy Long, then the Internal Revenue Service commissioner, for business and personal reasons.

“Every secretary you know defense, transportation, treasury commerce IRS commissioner everyone gets right back to me,” she appears to have written the donor in late June 2025, shortly before her Senate confirmation hearing.

The texts suggest that Ms. Guilfoyle warned him to call her on Signal and keep their interactions strictly private. “You’ll literally cost me my ambassadorship,” she wrote, according to one of the screenshots Mr. Deters shared with The Times.

“Eric, I really wish you would stop papering all these things,” another message said. “It’s really dangerous.”

Democrats immediately pounced on the allegations as evidence of a pay-to-play pattern during the second Trump administration. Representative Robert Garcia, a California Democrat and ranking member of the House Oversight Committee, said such influence-peddling “would be a brazen abuse of power.” Representative Madeleine Dean, a Pennsylvania Democrat who sits on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said Ms. Guilfoyle should be fired.

A lawyer for Ms. Guilfoyle declined to comment. Secretary of State Marco Rubio refused to answer questions on Thursday about the ambassador’s conduct as he wound up a visit to Athens.

“Just because some source told you something,” he said vehemently, does not mean “it’s gospel.”

Mr. Deters, who has hosted annual pro-Trump events in Kentucky, is a firebrand with his own controversies. In the interview, he said he retired as a lawyer in 2013 after facing disciplinary actions in Kentucky and Ohio. He is now battling an adversary’s motion to hold him in civil contempt in an Ohio case.

He said that he supported President Trump’s policies, but not his administration’s “open grifting and enrichment,” which he said Ms. Guilfoyle exemplified.

Mr. Deters said he met Ms. Guilfoyle after he began holding an annual “Patriots Day Freedom Fest” in Kentucky in 2020. He said he paid $300,000 to Ms. Guilfoyle, $200,000 to Donald Trump Jr. and $100,000 to Eric Trump to speak at the events between 2021 and 2024.

He also donated $125,000 to a pro-Trump super PAC in 2022, according to Federal Election Commission records.

His relationship with Ms. Guilfoyle seems to have intensified after she and Donald Trump Jr. ended their engagement in 2024 and the president nominated her to be an ambassador.

At that point, Mr. Deters asked Ms. Guilfoyle to help him resolve an issue with the I. R. S. involving his tax deductions. He also wanted her to influence the Justice Department to extradite from Pakistan a doctor who had been criminally charged in connection with botched spinal surgeries and to investigate the doctor’s medical insurance company. He said in the interview that he was representing patients in litigation over their operations.

He promised Ms. Guilfoyle a million dollars if he got a legal settlement, and if Tucker Carlson invited Mr. Deters on his podcast to talk about the case.

In the early summer of 2025, as Ms. Guilfoyle’s confirmation hearing neared, he grew increasingly frustrated with what he saw as a lack of results. He claimed that she never broke through with either Ms. Bondi or Mr. Long.

She insisted that she had pulled out all the stops. “I have never worked harder in my life than to promote and protect you,” the texts indicate that she wrote.

She shared with him a copy of a message she said she had sent to Mr. Long, asking him to look into Mr. Deters’s situation. “Don Jr. and I are very close with Eric Deters,” that message reads.

On June 25, 2025, the texts indicate she wrote Mr. Deters: “Please call IRS commissioner Billy Long wrote me back. BOOM.”

Two days later, the texts indicate that Ms. Guilfoyle said Ms. Bondi was the only cabinet member who did not respond immediately to her — even though she claimed that “we are tight.”

Earlier that month, the texts suggest that Ms. Guilfoyle had asked Mr. Deters for backdated invoices. He sent her a letter on June 11 proposing to pay her $50,000 on July 1 — an amount he wrote that he owed — followed by $50,000 on August 1.

“At the time, I’m her friend, I was considering doing it,” he said in the interview. He described the letter as “bs,” saying she wanted it to disguise their arrangement.

On July 3, six days before her confirmation hearing, Ms. Guilfoyle sent an urgent plea for money, a text indicates. “Banks are closed tomorrow,” she wrote with a praying emoji.

“You could just send it here. It won’t show up anywhere if you wire money to American Express that’s all that will show,” she said in the text exchange. She included a PDF with American Express instructions, adding that he would be her “special guest” at her confirmation hearing the following week.

He turned her down, saying his wife would divorce him if he paid.

“Your needing $100,000 urgent unfortunately is not going to work,” he wrote. “I wish you luck.”

Susan C. Beachy and Kitty Bennett contributed research.

Sharon LaFraniere is an investigative reporter focusing on the Trump administration.

The Midterm Senate Fight Spreads to a Surprising New Battleground

The New York Times October 09, 2026

Republicans are suddenly racing to defend a seat in Kansas, where Democrats are trying to win a Senate race for the first time in nearly a century.

Republicans are suddenly racing to defend a seat in Kansas, where Democrats are trying to win a Senate race for the first time in nearly a century.

Adam Hamilton, a Democrat and a megachurch pastor, is running for Senate in Kansas against Senator Roger Marshall, a Republican. Credit... David Robert Elliott for The New York Times

Supported by

By Jess Bidgood

Reporting from Hutchinson and Lindsborg, Kansas

Kansas has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1932. The Republican domination of the state’s two Senate seats, lasting nearly a century, is one of the longest partisan winning streaks in Senate history.

But suddenly, a megachurch pastor who became a Democrat this spring appears to have a shot at breaking it.

A race that once barely registered nationally has emerged as one of the most unexpected battlegrounds on a midterm map that has rapidly expanded into longtime Republican strongholds. The arrival of the pastor, Adam Hamilton, as a serious Senate contender in Kansas has come so fast, it appears to have caught the incumbent Republican, Senator Roger Marshall, by surprise.

Polls suggest that the race is neck and neck. This week, the Cook Political Report, a political forecaster, declared the contest a “tossup.” And national Republicans who once hoped that red-state incumbents would look after themselves have promised $14 million to save the seat.

National Democrats are now entering the fray, too. Senate Majority PAC, the top super PAC for Senate Democrats, on Friday revealed plans to spend $5 million in the race.

The pairing of an unconventional challenger — one who was a registered Republican until February — and an embattled incumbent has tantalized Democrats, who believe they just might be able to notch an upset in a state where economic headwinds are hitting particularly hard.

Republicans believe they can muscle through — as long as their base turns out.

“Money won’t be an issue,” said Rob Fillion, the executive director of the Kansas Republican Party. “It’s whether or not Republicans show up to the booths.”

In public, Republicans have worked to project confidence about Mr. Marshall, 66, an obstetrician-gynecologist and a former congressman who dashed Democratic hopes of a surprise flip when he first won his seat in 2020.

In private, though, some Republicans in Washington and Kansas are frustrated that he has not mounted a more robust or nimble response to his challenger in a souring political climate. He has raised just $2.5 million in individual campaign contributions, compared with more than $4 million for Mr. Hamilton.

Voters in Kansas enthusiastically backed President Trump all three times he was on the ballot here, but the deeply agricultural state has been buffeted this year by a series of problems exacerbated by his administration.

The Iran War pushed the cost of diesel fuel to a record high of $6.52 per gallon in September, driving up the costs of shipping and operating farm equipment. (In Kansas, the average price of a gallon of diesel now hovers at just under $6.)

Kansas cattle ranchers were incensed by a Trump administration plan to lower the price of beef by dropping import tariffs. And they pushed back last month when highly visible immigration enforcement raids disrupted the cattle harvest by keeping workers at home.

“Our members want to be left alone,” said Matt Teagarden, the chief executive of the Kansas Livestock Association. “We don’t look for the government to intervene in our markets.”

In a sign of flagging enthusiasm for Mr. Marshall, the trade group decided to sit out this election after endorsing him in 2020, although Mr. Teagarden declined to explain why.

“We had some concerns in terms of where Senator Marshall is,” Mr. Teagarden said.

The senator, who has attacked Mr. Hamilton as “too woke,” has faced persistent questions about how much time he spends at his Florida home, and how those trips were paid for. He sought to rebut those questions this week by inviting a reporter from The Washington Examiner to his hunting cabin in Kansas (he also told the news outlet that the Florida house had just been sold).

And attack ads against him have pointed to the findings of an investigation by The New York Times that found he had sued hundreds of his patients over unpaid medical bills, leading to the arrests of 81 of them for missing court dates.

“That’s just an absolute lie,” he told reporters this week. “I wouldn’t want anyone to be thrown in jail because of that.”

The chairwoman of the Kansas Democratic Party, Jeanna Repass, learned this year that Mr. Hamilton, who switched his party affiliation from Republican to unaffiliated in February, was considering an independent run for the Senate.

She got in touch with him over text. If he ran, she asked, would he please do it as a Democrat?

He did.

As a candidate, Mr. Hamilton, 62, has sought to pin the blame for Kansas’s economic trouble squarely on Mr. Marshall and his support for Mr. Trump. He has assailed the administration for its cuts to health care and — in a rarer message for a Democrat — its ballooning of the national debt.

“The senator that I’m trying to replace — that I’m hoping to help bless by letting him retire to Florida — is not being a champion for the people of Kansas,” Mr. Hamilton said on Thursday night.

Mr. Hamilton was speaking in front of several hundred people at an ornate theater in Hutchinson, a small city in south-central Kansas that boasts either the world’s longest or second-longest grain elevator, depending on whom you ask.

In a stump speech that unspooled his life story in painstaking detail, he spoke of founding the 24,000-member Church of the Resurrection, the largest United Methodist congregation in the country.

And he levied a particularly Kansan insult at the U. S. Senate, saying that like the characters in “The Wizard of Oz,” it’s missing a brain, a heart and courage.

He is more comfortable talking about scripture than policy. When a woman in the crowd asked how he would fix the health care system, he said he was reading as much as he could about it, rather than offering up “some bogus answer.” In interviews, he has struggled to clearly articulate his position on hot-button issues like artificial intelligence.

But his work in the church has lifted his name recognition. “Adam has a reach through the Methodist Church in corners of the state that I don’t even have county parties in,” said Ms. Repass, the state Democratic chair.

And his willingness to sound conciliatory in a moment when Democrats elsewhere are demanding bombastic fighters appears to be helping him build support, particularly among moderate Democrats and among Republicans disillusioned with Mr. Marshall and Mr. Trump. Two Republican former governors, Bill Graves and Mike Hayden, have endorsed Mr. Hamilton. (The other two living Republican former governors, Sam Brownback and Jeff Colyer, have stayed neutral.)

As she left a campaign event in Lindsborg, Kan., a Swedish American enclave where the local university is affiliated with the Evangelical Lutheran Church, Dianna Dawdy, 81, said she thought she would vote for Mr. Hamilton. A Republican, she said she had voted for Mr. Trump three times.

“A traditional Democrat wouldn’t be having this kind of effect,” said David Kerr, a Republican and a former president of the Kansas State Senate. Mr. Kerr helped organize the event on Thursday night in Hutchinson, where people in the crowd milled around in “Ag for Hamilton” and “Republicans for Hamilton” buttons. It is the first time Mr. Kerr has ever come out so publicly in support of a Democrat.

Democrats in Kansas haven’t won a Senate race in a while, but they have posted other victories in recent years.

The second-term governor, Laura Kelly, is a Democrat. And Democrats in the state celebrated when, after the fall of Roe v. Wade in 2022, Kansas voters handily defeated a referendum on a constitutional amendment that would have said there was no right to abortion in the state.

Last week, a poll by The New York Times and Siena University found the race to be evenly split between Mr. Hamilton and Mr. Marshall.

Republicans believe that their base will lock in as the race enters its final weeks — and that partisanship will ultimately win the day.

“The Democrats this cycle don’t have anything to run for,” said Mr. Fillion, the executive director of the state Republican Party. “They’re simply running against President Trump and using fear mongering.”

David Kensinger, a Republican strategist in Kansas, said the state’s Republican tilt was so strong, it could well outweigh any dip in voter enthusiasm caused by high prices or frustration with the president.

“You could both have the closest Senate race in 50 years,” he said, and Mr. Marshall “gets re-elected.”

I went to Kansas this week to try to understand how a state that hasn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1932 is becoming a surprisingly competitive battlegrounds this midterm election. In an era of tribalized politics and Democrats who want “fighters,” the Democrat in the race, Adam Hamilton, is an unusual candidate. He was a registered Republican until earlier this year, and he’s welcomed support from a parade of prominent and not-so-prominent Republicans across the state.

Jess Bidgood is a managing correspondent for The Times and writes the On Politics newsletter, a guide to this pivotal moment in American politics.

Democrats and Some Republicans Pan Hegseth’s Plan to Air Execution

The New York Times October 09, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

Some G. O. P. members of Congress said that broadcasting the execution of the Fort Hood shooter was inappropriate, though others gleefully applauded it.

By Robert Jimison

A handful of Republicans in Congress joined Democrats on Friday in criticizing Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s plan to livestream the execution of the man responsible for the 2009 mass shooting at Fort Hood, comparing it to the tactics of terrorist organizations, authoritarian governments and fallen empires.

”I absolutely support the sentence of death, but live-streaming executions is what jihadists do,” Representative Austin Scott, Republican of Georgia, wrote on social media on Friday morning. “America is better than that.”

Senator Thom Tillis of North Carolina, a Republican who is retiring and increasingly critical of President Trump and his administration, said the decision was “beyond disgusting.” He likened it to the actions of some of the United States’ most brutal adversaries.

“Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do. It should not be happening in America,” he wrote in a social media post.

The criticism came after an announcement by the Pentagon that it would broadcast the execution of Maj. Nidal Malik Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist who killed 13 people and wounded 32 others in a shooting rampage at Fort Hood, Texas, in 2009. The execution is to be carried out on Dec. 3 by the military’s first firing squad since World War II, and would be its first execution by any method since 1961.

The decision came at a particularly fraught moment for congressional Republicans, who are fighting to preserve their narrow majorities in both chambers just weeks before the midterm elections. Already burdened by voter discontent over the war with Iran and a string of controversies involving Mr. Hegseth, G. O. P. lawmakers have been struggling to distance themselves from his bellicose stance.

Instead, the idea of a livestreamed military execution thrust some of them into another politically uncomfortable debate.

“An execution shouldn’t be a live-streamed spectacle,” Representative Rob Bresnahan Jr., Republican of Pennsylvania and one of his party’s most endangered incumbents, wrote in a social media post. “The focus should be on justice for the victims and their families, not turning an execution into entertainment. Their pain deserves respect, not a public show.”

Senator John Curtis, Republican of Utah, invoked the ancient Roman philosopher Seneca to warn that turning executions into public events risked corrupting society.

“A civilization erodes when it cultivates an appetite for executions as a form of entertainment,” he wrote, adding that broadcasting Mr. Hasan’s death “diminishes us and is not an effective deterrent.”

Even Vice President JD Vance cast doubt on the idea, telling reporters on Friday that he was unsure the plan to broadcast the execution was “actually going to happen.” While he emphasized the brutality of Mr. Hasan’s attack, he added that if his execution were ultimately shown “through livestream, I’m not going to be watching.”

Mr. Hasan was convicted and sentenced to death in 2013. Mr. Trump approved his execution this week, clearing the way for the military to carry out the sentence later this year.

Mr. Hegseth, who recommended the firing squad, said the public should be able to witness the execution of Mr. Hasan to understand the consequences of attacking American service members.

“We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public,” Mr. Hegseth said in an interview with Real America’s Voice, a conservative outlet, aboard the aircraft carrier U. S. S. Abraham Lincoln on Thursday. He said he was advocating for the public execution “because people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things.”

Democrats roundly condemned the move. Senator Jack Reed of Rhode Island, the top Democrat on the Armed Services Committee, accused Mr. Hegseth of staging a publicity stunt that would give Mr. Hasan the type of martyrdom he sought.

“Livestreaming an execution is a barbaric spectacle,” Mr. Reed said in a statement. “This is a gift to anti-American terrorist recruiters.”

Still, the announcement drew praise from some of the president’s most vocal allies in Congress, including those in the most politically safe Republican territory.

“This is how every Muslim terrorist should be dealt with. We will share the stream live,” Representative Randy Fine, who represents a solidly Republican district in Florida, wrote in a social media post, adding: “Fire away!”

Representative Andy Ogles of Tennessee, who is not standing for re-election after losing his primary in August, shared the interview in which Mr. Hegseth made his announcement and called it “excellent.”

“Public execution is what this terrorist deserves,” he wrote. “We will be watching.”

Democrats raised both philosophical and legal objections.

Representative Adam Smith of Washington, the top Democrat on the Armed Services Committee, said the decision was “disturbing and makes a mockery of our legal system.”

“There is a reason why we treat the meting out of justice with the seriousness it demands,” he said in a statement. “We are a democratic country and should take the rule of law seriously, not turn it into a spectacle.”

Robert Jimison covers Congress for The Times, with a focus on defense issues and foreign policy.

Vance Says He Would Not Watch Livestreamed Execution

The New York Times October 09, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

The vice president also cast doubt on whether the public execution of Maj. Nidal Malik Hasan, the 2009 Fort Hood gunman, would go forward as Pentagon officials have planned.

By Chris Cameron

Reporting from Washington

Vice President JD Vance said he would not watch a livestream of the planned execution of the 2009 Fort Hood shooter and cast doubt on whether the Pentagon’s plan for a public execution would go forward at all.

“I see these announcements,” Mr. Vance said after casting his ballot for the midterm elections in his home state of Ohio. “I don’t know that that’s actually going to happen.”

He continued, “Now, that said, I mean, look, if it’s through livestream, I’m not going to be watching it.”

Mr. Vance also suggested that the method of the planned execution of Maj. Nidal Malik Hasan, who killed 13 people and wounded 32 others in the deadliest shooting at an American military base, was distracting from the severity of his crimes. Mr. Hasan is set to be executed by firing squad, the first soldier to be put to death by that method since World War II. The firing squad is a rare method of execution, but one that has been historically used by the military, particularly during wartime.

“This is a guy who committed, in my view, the worst terrorist attack on American soil outside of 9/11,” Mr. Vance said. “The people that he was meant to treat — the Army soldiers that he was meant to treat for mental illness and other problems — he took them at their most vulnerable and gunned down these people where they lived.”

He continued, “So whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope that people don’t forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people.”

Mr. Vance’s comments struck a markedly different tone from those of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who called the public execution a “no-brainer.”

“It hadn’t been since World War II since we’ve done that,” he told the far-right influencer Jack Posobiec in an interview, apparently referring to the last known military execution by firing squad. “Well, I kind of like the mentality we had in World War II, which was win.”

In Congress, Democrats and some G. O. P. lawmakers blasted the plan to stream the execution after Mr. Hegseth and the Pentagon announced it Thursday.

The remarks by Mr. Vance, a convert to Catholicism, came hours after top Catholic leaders in the United States condemned the planned livestream. Archbishop Paul S. Coakley, the leader of America’s Roman Catholic bishops, said the move was “a barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered.”

Mr. Vance has repeatedly clashed over U. S. policy with church leaders, including Pope Leo XIV, who he said earlier this year should stay out of American affairs.

The Catholic Church opposes all capital punishment under the reasoning that all human life is sacred. This “unconditionally pro-life” stance also undergirds the Catholic Church’s opposition to abortion, which it views as ending a life.

President Trump is a vocal advocate of the death penalty, and his administration has moved to significantly expand its use. The Pentagon said on Monday that Mr. Trump had approved Major Hasan’s execution.

Chris Cameron is a Times reporter covering Washington, focusing on breaking news and the Trump administration.
