Trump Announces White House Inquiry Into Fed Governor Cook

The New York Times October 09, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

President Trump said the White House would investigate unsubstantiated claims that Lisa D. Cook committed mortgage fraud and hold a hearing next month.

By Colby Smith and Tony Romm

Colby Smith covers the Federal Reserve. Tony Romm writes about economic policy.

President Trump said on Friday that the White House had formed a committee to investigate Lisa D. Cook, a Federal Reserve governor, and would hold a hearing to consider whether to fire her over unproven accusations that she committed mortgage fraud.

The “committee of inquiry” will look into claims that Ms. Cook made “false statements in connection with one or more mortgage instruments,” the White House said in a statement. The hearing, which called for Ms. Cook’s attendance, was scheduled for Nov. 5.

Mr. Trump asked the committee to report back on whether there were grounds for “Governor Cook’s removal” from office. While Ms. Cook was first accused by the White House of mortgage fraud more than a year ago, she has not been charged with any crime.

In a statement on Friday, lawyers for Ms. Cook said they had “grave doubts that this ‘hearing’ is a legitimate one that would conform to the law.”

“But if it is anything close to objective, the conclusion will be that Governor Cook did not commit mortgage fraud, leaving no cause to remove her from the Federal Reserve Board,” the lawyers said, adding that they had been in touch with the White House to assess whether the process “has a possibility of being a genuine one and not simply a box checking exercise.”

They said Ms. Cook “welcomes the opportunity to present the facts so she can clear her name and demonstrate there is no legal basis to fire her.”

Friday’s announcement marked the latest escalation in Mr. Trump’s efforts to fire Ms. Cook from the central bank, something a president can pursue legally only if there is “cause.” That has typically meant malfeasance or a dereliction of duty while on the job.

It came just four months after the Supreme Court ruled 5 to 4 in favor of Ms. Cook’s remaining in the job, which she can technically hold until 2038. The justices argued that Ms. Cook had not been given adequate due process before Mr. Trump announced her removal in August 2025, but they left unresolved a number of key issues, including what constitutes “cause.”

Mr. Trump, who has repeatedly sought to pressure the Fed and its members into lowering interest rates, quickly billed the ruling as a procedural setback. That paved the way for further attacks. In August, the administration then restarted the process to try to fire her, claiming that Ms. Cook was “unfit for the office in which you serve as a controlling member of the Federal Reserve.”

At the heart of the matter are allegations that Ms. Cook misled lenders in order to obtain favorable terms on a mortgage.

In 2021, Ms. Cook purchased a condominium in Atlanta and, in at least one document, referred to it as a “primary” residence despite not living there. She also maintained another home in Ann Arbor, Mich., which was also treated as a “primary” residence.

In a formal rebuttal filed to the administration in August, Ms. Cook’s lawyers described the designation on the Atlanta condo as an “entirely inadvertent oversight,” not fraud. The letter also maintained that Ms. Cook had accurately identified it as a vacation home in other records. And, in the process, Ms. Cook’s lawyers argued that Mr. Trump and his other advisers had made similar mortgage errors, pointing to a series of news reports.

The White House’s statement, which was dated Oct. 7, stipulated that Ms. Cook would be “examined by the committee, its representatives and her legal counsel, if any.” It would provide the opportunity for her to present her argument and any supporting evidence, and left open the possibility that Department of Justice personnel may conduct questioning.

The committee that will hear Ms. Cook’s case is composed of Mr. Trump’s aides and appointees including Kevin Hassett, his top economic adviser; Keith Sonderling, the acting director of the Office of Government Ethics; and Andrea Lucas, the head of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission.

Absent from the announced roster was Bill Pulte, the federal housing director, who has repeatedly attacked the Fed and originally investigated Ms. Cook over her mortgage activity. Mr. Pulte later referred his findings to the Justice Department.

Ms. Cook is not the only Fed official Mr. Trump has targeted. The president repeatedly attacked Jerome H. Powell, whose term as chair of the central bank ended in May. At one point, the Justice Department pursued a criminal investigation into Mr. Powell and his handling of costly renovations at the Fed’s headquarters in Washington.

The inquiry was dropped after a number of legal setbacks and widespread opposition by Republican senators, one of whom blocked the advancement of Mr. Trump’s pick to become the next head of the Fed. Kevin M. Warsh eventually took over in May, but Mr. Powell, instead of departing as most chairs do, opted to stay on as a governor. That term does not end until January 2028.

The Fed’s internal watchdog late last month cleared Mr. Powell of any wrongdoing associated with the nearly $2.5 billion project, even as it concluded that the renovations were poorly managed and lacked sufficient budget constraints. Still, Mr. Trump has maintained that Mr. Powell should be “forced to resign” from the board in the wake of the inspector general’s findings.

Colby Smith covers the Federal Reserve and the U. S. economy for The Times.

Tony Romm is a reporter covering economic policy and the Trump administration for The Times, based in Washington.

Zohran Mamdani’s Moral Obscenity

The New York Times October 09, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Bret Stephens

By Bret Stephens

Opinion Columnist

Zohran Mamdani, New York City’s mayor, set off a firestorm of criticism Wednesday morning with a social media post ostensibly intended to commemorate the Oct. 7, 2023, massacre of Israelis. It devoted a brief paragraph to condemning Hamas and commiserating with its victims. The rest was a much longer denunciation of Israel’s “ongoing genocide in Gaza,” a “world in which occupation and apartheid continue” and a situation in which “our federal government continues its complicity with every arms shipment.”

In response, Ammiel Hirsch, the president of the New York Board of Rabbis, said the statement was “so offensive to so many Jews that it is hard to describe how offensive it is.” In fact, it’s a moral obscenity. Let me count the ways.

It is obscene in the same way it would have been obscene if the mayor had commemorated the 25th anniversary of Sept. 11 last month with a perfunctory nod to the victims of the day, followed by a much longer denunciation of U. S. foreign policy in the Middle East. What happened on both Sept. 11 and Oct. 7 was undiluted evil, each an unprovoked visit of deliberate and maximalist violence on people who had done nothing to invite that violence other than being at the wrong place at the wrong time.

It is obscene because many of the Jews murdered on Oct. 7, living in kibbutzim with conspicuously left-leaning politics, had been at the forefront of the peace movement, volunteering, for example, to drive sick Palestinians for treatment at nearby Israeli hospitals. Hamas wasn’t just killing and terrorizing the innocent; it was eliminating the good.

It is obscene because Hamas didn’t just kill its victims in pursuit of a strategic objective. It tormented and slaughtered them like an army of serial killers who delight in the suffering of their victims. Corpses of Israeli women were described by one coroner as “shot in the crotch, intimate parts, vagina, or were shot in the breast.” Others appeared to have been raped so violently that their pelvises were broken. Parents were killed in front of their children; children were murdered in their beds. A fieldworker was beheaded with a garden hoe. I know this because Hamas filmed itself doing this and I forced myself to watch the film. I know because that same month, I visited the bedrooms where the kids had been murdered, their mattresses still soaked in blood.

It is obscene because, whatever else you may think of the war in Gaza, on the eve of Oct. 7 the border of Israel and Gaza was governed by a cease-fire. It was Hamas that chose to kick off the violence, just as the Japanese did in 1941 with the attack on Pearl Harbor. Whether in fistfights between people or wars between states, whoever throws the first punch forfeits the right to throw the last.

It is obscene because Mamdani is being misleading when he speaks as if his prime objection to Israel is what it did after Oct. 7. In fact, the mayor has been an anti-Israel zealot at least since his college days, when, as a leader of Students for Justice in Palestine, he broke off collaboration with the left-leaning Jewish group J Street, which advocates a Palestinian state, because it also recognizes the rights of a Jewish state. He’s written a rap professing “love” for five men convicted in a U. S. court of funneling money to Hamas. The day after Oct. 7, he issued a brief statement that said nothing about Hamas but immediately denounced Israel. Put simply, this is a mayor who first condemned Israel as guilty and then went about collecting evidence.

It is obscene because, however much the genocide allegation against Israel is mindlessly repeated by people too lazy or prejudiced to understand the difference between war and genocide, that allegation is as false as it is sinister. False, because genocide is about killing whole classes of people for who they are rather than for what they did — and if Israel wanted to kill Palestinians as Palestinians it never would have bothered mobilizing hundreds of thousands of its own soldiers for the war, and losing hundreds in high-intensity urban warfare. Sinister, because the political purpose of the genocide allegation is to trivialize, if not erase, the attacks of Oct. 7 by making them seem minor in comparison to the Palestinian casualties that tragically, but all-but inevitably, followed.

It is obscene because Hamas’s intentions toward Israel really are genocidal. Its leaders have often and publicly vowed to perpetrate future Oct. 7s. Had the group not been stopped by force that day, there’s no reason to think it wouldn’t have kept up its orgy of slaughter on its way to Tel Aviv and other Israeli cities. Yet one searches in vain for anything from the mayor except perfunctory, pro forma condemnations of Hamas.

It is obscene because there’s an even more wretched purpose to the genocide charge against Israel, which long predates the recent war in Gaza. It is a specimen of Holocaust erasure: not the dumb kind, which seeks to deny Nazi Germany’s murder of six million Jews, but a more sophisticated version that accuses living Jews of genocide as a way of ending the historical Jewish claim to a long and ongoing history of persecution and near-annihilation that accounts for its need for a sovereign state capable of defending its people.

Finally, it is obscene because Mamdani is the mayor for about one million Jewish New Yorkers, many with close relatives in Israel, who deserve better on a day of grief than to be offered the equivalent of an “All Lives Matter” homily. This is yet another of the double standards through which modern-day Jew hatred manifests itself: Whenever antisemitism is mentioned in progressive circles, it is inevitably accompanied by nods about Islamophobia or other bigotries.

It would be better to have a mayor who, if only on Oct. 7, can say: Jewish Lives Matter. Israeli Lives Matter. Full stop. The lectures about Gaza can come some other day.

Navi Pillay, South African Jurist, Is Awarded the Nobel Peace Prize

The New York Times October 09, 2026

2026 Nobel Prizes

Advertisement

Supported by

The choice drew condemnation from Israel over Ms. Pillay’s role leading a U. N. commission that said the country had committed genocide against Palestinians.

By Zane Irwin

A South African lawyer with a long record in human rights work, including leading a U. N. commission that said Israel had committed genocide, won the Nobel Peace Prize on Friday, a decision that drew Israel’s condemnation and underscored the country’s deep isolation on the world stage.

The lawyer, Navanethem Pillay, known as Navi, has worked for decades on human rights issues, defending anti-apartheid activists like the future president and Nobel laureate Nelson Mandela. Over the years, she has variously served as a top U. N. official and as a judge on the International Criminal Court and a tribunal investigating genocide in Rwanda.

But it was Ms. Pillay’s work last year on a U. N. commission on Israel that made the Nobel committee’s announcement on Friday an intensely political decision, as it put the prize in the middle of one of the world’s most divisive issues.

That commission said that Israel was committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza, a finding that Israel rejected.

Announcing the award, the Nobel committee did not explicitly mention Gaza, instead citing Ms. Pillay’s long career in human rights and a global shift toward “power politics” that had undermined respect for law and justice. The committee chair, Jorgen Watne Frydnes, called the award “a message to those who are attacking” international law.

Ms. Pillay, 85, is “one of the most respected international jurists of our time,” the committee said, calling her “instrumental in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide are prosecuted.”

The office of Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, quickly denounced the committee in a statement, calling its members misguided and saying it had “lost its moral compass.” It also condemned Ms. Pillay’s work, accusing her of being prejudiced against Jews.

The Israeli foreign ministry went further, calling the Nobel decision a “grotesque weaponization of an award to legitimize anti-Israel hatred and prejudice.”

After learning she had won the award, Ms. Pillay, speaking at a conference of human rights lawyers in Nuremberg, Germany, said she had tried to hew only to the law and facts in her career, not politics.

“Why would you need courage to speak the truth?” she said. “You interpret the law, you look at all the facts. So it’s an impartial, you know, impartial decision-making.”

Her work on Israel and Gaza, though, was “an important part of the reasoning why she received the prize,” Mr. Frydnes, the Nobel committee chair, told reporters.

President Trump, who has been a staunch supporter of Israel and has openly angled to win the Nobel Peace Prize himself, did not immediately address Friday’s award. He did, however, share a post on his social media platform that called Ms. Pillay “an unabashed hater of America and Israel” and said that it was Mr. Trump who deserved the prize.

After receiving the news at the conference in Nuremberg, Ms. Pillay was applauded by more than a hundred fellow attendees, a video posted by the Amnesty International head, Agnès Callamard, showed.

“If you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with Trump,” Ms. Pillay joked, apparently referring to last year’s winner, María Corina Machado, the Venezuelan opposition leader who presented her medal to the U. S. president in January.

At a brief news conference, Ms. Pillay mused that “perhaps it was meant to be” that she had received the news in Nuremberg, a city whose famous postwar trials of Nazi leaders were foundational to creating the modern international justice system.

“We are living through an era when international law and human rights are under significant political attack,” she said. Such efforts, she said, were “particularly visible with the attacks on the International Criminal Court,” which the Trump administration has vowed to dismantle “brick by brick.”

Born to a family of Indian Tamil origin, the daughter of a homemaker and a bus driver, Ms. Pillay was one of seven children who grew up in poverty in the city of Durban, on South Africa’s east coast. She came of age in a segregated city, attending a school for Indian South Africans.

As a teenager, Ms. Pillay said, she experienced apartheid’s daily injustices and witnessed the violent crackdown by police forces and vigilantes on Black South African protesters and their supporters.

“The government was oppressive, the laws were oppressive and the courts cooperated with these laws,” she said in a video published by the I. C. C. in 2017. “We had no remedies, and as a 15-year-old, I wished that we could appeal to a higher system of law, a higher institution, so that we, the victims, can get justice.”

Ms. Pillay pursued a law degree and later defended imprisoned anti-apartheid activists, including Nelson Mandela, many of whom faced terrorism charges and placed under surveillance. After the end of apartheid, Ms. Pillay became a judge on the High Court in South Africa, where she championed women’s rights and equality.

Soon, Ms. Pillay was drawn into international human rights crises. In 1995, Mr. Mandela — then South Africa’s president — appointed her as a judge at the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda.

Ms. Pillay is the fifth South African to be awarded the peace prize, after Mr. Mandela, the activist Albert Luthuli, former President F. W. de Klerk and Desmond Tutu, the cleric who helped bring down apartheid.

One of Ms. Pillay’s contributions to international law was her pioneering work on the gravity of sexual violence during the Rwanda conflict. In a trial at the tribunal, she pushed from the bench to define rape of women and children as a weapon of war.

In 1998, when the tribunal found a former Rwandan mayor guilty of genocide, it was the first time that rape had been defined as part of genocide. Sexual violence has since been integrated in international law as a potential war crime, a crime against humanity or an act of genocide.

Two decades later, in 2019, Ms. Pillay served as an ad hoc judge on the International Court of Justice in a case in which Myanmar was accused of genocide against the Rohingya Muslim minority.

Even as her work expanded beyond South Africa, she remained a prominent voice for human rights in the country, speaking out against anti-immigrant violence that flared in Durban in 2015 and chiding the South African government for having considered leaving the I. C. C. in 2016.

This year’s selection is the latest in a line of decisions by the Norwegian Nobel Committee that have carried political weight.

The year before awarding the prize to Ms. Machado, the Venezuelan opposition leader, the committee honored Nihon Hidankyo, a Japanese organization representing atomic bomb survivors, many of whom have campaigned for nuclear disarmament. In 2023, the prize went to Narges Mohammadi, Iran’s most prominent human rights activist.

Zane Irwin is an international reporter and a member of the 2026-27 Times Fellowship, a program for journalists early in their careers.

Trump Administration Hits International Criminal Court With Severe Sanctions

The New York Times October 09, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

U. S. officials announced the new, sweeping punishments just hours after the Nobel Peace Prize committee gave its annual honor to a former court judge.

By Edward Wong and Jeanna Smialek

Edward Wong reported from Athens, Greece, and Jeanna Smialek reported from Brussels. Both cover diplomacy and international news.

The Trump administration announced on Friday that it was imposing severe financial sanctions on the International Criminal Court, its latest effort to cripple the global body that seeks to prosecute those accused of war crimes, genocide and other murderous criminal acts.

The new sanctions, unveiled by Secretary of State Marco Rubio and the State Department, would prohibit transactions with the court after a grace period of six months. Any companies doing business with the court afterward could be subject to punishment by the U. S. government.

The threat of that could constrain the institution’s ability to carry out daily operations.

Although the State Department had been preparing the sanctions for months, Mr. Rubio’s announcement came just hours after a committee in Norway said it was awarding the Nobel Peace Prize to Navi Pillay, a South African lawyer who served for nine years as a judge on the International Criminal Court and worked as the top human rights official at the United Nations.

The sanctions are an intensification of the Trump administration’s push to undermine the court. In February 2025, just weeks after taking office, President Trump issued an executive order directing agencies to come up with sanctions to impose on the court.

At the time, he said the court was trying to violate American sovereignty and undermine “the critical national security and foreign policy work of the United States government and our allies, including Israel.”

Mr. Rubio said in a statement on Friday that Mr. Trump would never allow the court to prosecute Americans. “We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate,” he said.

Mr. Rubio announced in July that the United States planned to “systematically disable” the court, which Mr. Trump has long described as a threat to Americans.

The administration has imposed financial sanctions and visa bans on court judges and prosectors, but the measures announced on Friday are broader.

The I. C. C. said in a statement that the American move was “an assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order, which strikes at the simple principle that no one stands above the law.”

Many companies that have business ties with the court will be granted licenses over the next 180 days to continue their work without financial punishments, the State Department said.

During that period, the Trump administration will assess whether its concerns regarding the I. C. C. have been addressed, the department said in a statement. The administration can then adjust the licenses based on that.

The Treasury Department is helping to enact the sanctions and maintains a list of entities punished with financial restrictions.

Of nearly 200 nations in the world, 125 have signed the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court and are subject to its rulings. The United States never ratified the treaty establishing the institution, and both it and Israel are among those that are not bound by the statute.

However, given the number of countries that are members of the court — including close American allies — the prosecution of U. S. citizens could put those people at risk of arrest and extradition in many parts of the world, in theory. But experts often say that the chances of foreign officials taking those actions are low.

Mr. Rubio announced the sanctions the day after he returned from a three-nation tour of Europe during which he was trying to strengthen alliances. The three countries he visited — Iceland, Greece and Portugal — are all members of the International Criminal Court.

The court, officially established in 2002 and based at The Hague in the Netherlands, has a mission to investigate and prosecute genocide, war crimes and other serious offenses. The Trump administration has in the past pushed back on the court’s ability to look into the conduct of U. S. soldiers in Afghanistan, and has also been highly critical of the court’s actions against Israel.

In November 2024, the court issued arrest warrants for Benjamin Netanyahu, the prime minister of Israel, and Yoav Gallant, the defense minister for much of Israel’s war in Gaza. Prosecutors had investigated the officials for war crimes and crimes against humanity in operations in Gaza, where thousands of Palestinian civilians have been killed and some have starved to death. Israel carried out airstrikes and ground operations after the deadly Hamas attacks in Israel in October 2023.

The Trump administration has already sanctioned 17 of the court’s officials, including judges and prosecutors. Mr. Rubio has suggested that even more sweeping punishments were necessary because of the possibility that the court could prosecute U. S. citizens, and American service members in particular.

Such actions would “mean the death of the U. S. as a sovereign and independent nation,” Mr. Rubio wrote in an opinion essay published in The Wall Street Journal this summer.

Defenders of the court often point out that it has no police force of its own, and would be able to arrest and try U. S. citizens only if member states carry out arrests.

The Trump administration is not the first to take on the I. C. C.: Under George W. Bush, the United States also pushed back on the court’s ability to go after Americans.

Yet the Trump administration’s effort to dismantle the institution — “brick by brick, if necessary,” according to Mr. Rubio — is an escalation, from skepticism and rhetoric to outright dismemberment.

“This is incredibly disturbing,” said James A. Goldston, executive director of the legal organization the Open Society Justice Initiative, calling the sanctions a “calculated attack” on international justice.

Whether the American attack on the I. C. C. will cripple the institution will depend in part on how its member nations respond, he said, and whether they stand by the institution.

“We know that the court has been preparing for this much-rumored eventuality,” he said. “We’ll have to see.”

The European Union’s executive arm, whose 27 member countries are also members of the court, said in a statement that “The E. U. will work closely with the I. C. C. to ensure it continues to operate effectively,” and called the American move “deeply regrettable.”

The E. U. statement emphasized that the six-month delay leaves “room for dialogue.” Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands and Britain also released a joint statement in defense of the court on Friday.

The court was already in a state of turmoil. Karim A. A. Khan, the institution’s chief prosecutor, was removed earlier this year after an investigation into allegations that he sexually harassed a subordinate. Mr. Khan has denied the accusations.

In a recent interview with The New York Times that was conducted before the latest sanctions were announced, Tomoko Akane, the president of the court, said that the institution has been taking “measures to strengthen its resilience” in the face of the Trump administration’s threats.

“A permanent body like the I. C. C. must never be shut down,” she said. “The stakes extend far beyond the court itself.”

Edward Wong reports on global affairs, U. S. foreign policy and the State Department for The Times.

Jeanna Smialek is the Brussels bureau chief for The Times.

What We Know About the ICE Shooting in New York

The New York Times October 09, 2026

U. S. Immigration Crackdown

Advertisement

Supported by

A 28-year-old man was shot by a federal immigration agent in New York City on Thursday. Mayor Zohran Mamdani said agents were “terrorizing our city.”

By Emma G. Fitzsimmons

A federal agent shot and wounded a man in New York City on Thursday, heightening concerns about immigration enforcement in a city with millions of immigrants.

The man, Oscar Belgal, 28, a Dominican immigrant, was shot in the Marble Hill neighborhood as agents with Immigration and Customs Enforcement tried to arrest him while he was in a car with his 5-year-old son.

The shooting appeared to be the first by ICE in the city since 2020. It elicited swift rebukes from Gov. Kathy Hochul and Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who accused the Trump administration of “terrorizing our city.”

On Friday, the Trump administration criticized the city’s sanctuary policies and highlighted Mr. Belgal’s criminal record.

Here’s what to know about the shooting:

Mr. Belgal was shot in the neck after at least one ICE agent fired seven rounds at the car, the police said.

His son was not injured and was in the care of a family member late Thursday.

The shooting happened at around 4 p. m. on West 225th Street near Broadway in a predominantly Latino neighborhood at the edge of Manhattan and the Bronx.

The Department of Homeland Security said that the shooting had occurred as the agents tried to arrest an undocumented immigrant with a criminal record.

On Friday, the Police Department released body-worn camera footage from two police officers who had arrived at the scene. The footage showed them picking up Mr. Belgal from the ground and taking him in handcuffs to nearby NewYork-Presbyterian Allen Hospital.

A witness, Viely Herrera, said that she had heard a series of shots and saw an S. U. V. crash into concrete barriers on the street. Mr. Belgal came out of the vehicle holding his neck and shouting in Spanish. The boy was in the back seat crying.

Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, attacked the city’s sanctuary city policies at a news conference on Friday and lashed out at Mr. Mamdani.

Mr. Mullin repeatedly described Mr. Belgal as a “thug” and “the worst of the worst.” He said that ICE had sought to arrest him because the agency believe he had “indirect or direct knowledge” of a shooting that injured an off-duty customs officer in Manhattan in July 2025.

Mr. Mullin said that Mr. Mamdani’s comments condemning ICE were dangerous and that cities like New York that did not work closely with the agency made the government’s job harder.

ICE personnel were not aware that there was a young child in the vehicle, Mr. Mullin said.

Mr. Mamdani condemned the shooting at a news conference on Thursday night and called it “an outrage.”

“Tonight, a 5-year-old child sits traumatized and terrified,” the mayor said. “Tonight, millions of our neighbors are wondering whether they will be safe on our streets, in our schools, at their work sites.”

Mr. Mamdani said he had spent two hours on the phone with President Trump and Mr. Mullin, the homeland security secretary, trying unsuccessfully to negotiate the release of Mr. Belgal.

Ms. Hochul said in a statement that she had also spoken with Mr. Trump and Mr. Mullin about the shooting.

“I expressed outrage on behalf of New Yorkers and urged them to halt ICE enforcement operations in New York,” she said.

We do not know much yet about Mr. Belgal and his life in New York City.

The N. Y. P. D. video showed Mr. Belgal on the ground bleeding and looking distressed. Several men stand nearby, including one in a construction-style vest holding a long gun.

Paige Austin, a lawyer at Make the Road New York, an immigration advocacy group representing Mr. Belgal, said that he was being held in New Jersey, but his lawyers don’t know exactly where.

The police said that Mr. Belgal had pleaded guilty to fourth-degree grand larceny and received five years probation and that he was being investigated for the criminal sale of a controlled substance in 2025.

Anti-ICE demonstrators gathered at the scene of the shooting on Thursday and outside the hospital where Mr. Belgal was taken.

The Rev. Emily DeTar Birt, a Unitarian minister, said that several schools were near where the shooting happened.

“This is happening in broad daylight in front of our kids,” she said.

Late on Thursday, tensions flared outside Allen Hospital. Protesters and the police scuffled as officers tried to put up barricades to establish a clear path to and from the building’s entrance.

Protesters chanted “No justice, no peace, we want ICE off our streets.” Some hurled water bottles at the police. At least one person was taken into custody.

Nearly 40 percent of the city’s residents are immigrants, and many New Yorkers have expressed alarm over a rise in ICE activity.

Arrests by immigration agents in New York State rose from 927 in May of this year to 1,193 in June and 1,567 in July, according to federal data compiled by the Deportation Data Project, an academic group.

Emma G. Fitzsimmons is a public policy correspondent for The Times, covering New York City.

Q&A

In the documentary “Musk,” Ashley St. Clair, a former right-wing influencer and mother of one of Musk’s children, speaks about her relationship with him.

Ashley St. Clair at her home in New York. Credit... Elinor Kry for The New York Times

Supported by

By Coralie Kraft

Ashley St. Clair is sick of people asking her the same questions about Elon Musk. “People treat me like I’m some Elon psychoanalyst,” she said during a visit to The New York Times in September. “They want to know, ‘What’s it like to hang out with him?’ or they say, ‘Not many people have spent time with him one-on-one.’” She sighed. “It’s annoying and laborious.”

You can’t blame them for asking. St. Clair, a former conservative influencer, gave birth to one of Musk’s children in 2024. (At the time, she also had another child from a previous relationship.) This fall, she’s a significant figure in “Musk,” Alex Gibney’s nearly four-hour-long documentary about the world’s first trillionaire, and she has more pressing points. “This is about a deeper rot in our society, where we’ve equated capital with morality,” she said. “There’s a level of societal and individual trust that we give to people if they have money.”

Musk did not respond to requests for comment. After TMZ reported that Ashley St. Clair rejected a $40 million N. D. A., Musk responded via X, stating, “She was never offered that and has a history of making false claims.” He also condemned Gibney’s documentary with another post on X reading, “Gibney just assembled a hit list of people who either have an axe to grind or don’t even know me.”

Gibney, the Oscar-winning documentary filmmaker, first met St. Clair in December 2025. “Beyond Musk’s baby obsession, Ashley had a front-row seat during the 2024 campaign and was able to tell me things I didn’t know about Musk’s motivations,” he said in an email. Below, St. Clair shares her side of the story.

These are edited excerpts from the conversation.

Were you at all nervous about participating in the film?

No. I was familiar with some of Alex’s documentary work, like “Going Clear.” I liked that he didn’t have any fear. He has a history of treating facts and narratives with respect.

You’ve seen the film. How did you feel watching it?

What was both validating and terrifying was the way the narratives harmonized. Me, Justine [Wilson, Musk’s first wife], Sam Harris [the New Atheist philosopher] and Geoffrey Hinton [the so-called Godfather of A. I.] — there are so many similarities in our experiences with Elon. I think when you’re able to take people who have never spoken to each other and harmonize a narrative, that is the truth.

What did your life look like when you met Musk in 2023?

I worked at a conservative news site, The Babylon Bee, and I was a single mom. I also had a public persona, primarily on Twitter, where I was repeating MAGA talking points. Elon followed me on Twitter and slid into my DMs.

How did you feel when he followed you?

I don’t think people understand the number of eyeballs that were on everyone Elon interacted with at that time. I was getting “Congratulations!” texts from people in MAGA. Right away, there were people saying, “She’s going to be his next baby mama.” I was about to turn 24.

And when did you meet in person for the first time?

We’d been DMing on Twitter, and then during an interview for the Bee, he asked, “Feel like going to Providence, R. I.?” Within an hour, I was on his plane. In Providence, we shared a hotel room, and he fell asleep listening to a podcast about Kublai Khan. It was all very surreal.

Did it feel like a romantic relationship?

I would say it felt emotionally intimate. We were in contact every day. But also I was never like, “I’m the chosen one.” At the time, he was this savior of free speech, and I was very wrapped up in all of that. I’d say there was a bit of idolization going on, too.

When did you start talking about having a child together?

In January 2024, we went on vacation to St. Bart’s, and he said, “You should have 10 kids! Let’s have a kid. My only limited resource is time.”

What did that mean to you?

I wanted more children, so it meant that I would always be able to take care of my kids financially. Also, within MAGA, it was seen as a stain on your character to be a single mom. So to have this bastion of the right who is very validating of that choice — that meant so much to me.

Did you have any hesitations?

Not until I was pregnant and I watched the custody battle between Elon and Grimes [who share three children]. It made me think, “I have to protect myself.”

When did you receive the N. D. A.?

I was two months postpartum. Jared Birchall, Elon’s money manager and henchman, sent the document in a disappearing message on Signal. We didn’t have a formal financial agreement, so at that moment, getting the N. D. A. felt like, “If you would like any kind of support, sign this.”

I see. They were saying, “If you want support, sign this.” What were the terms of the N. D. A.?

I couldn’t speak about Elon or anything related to our relationship for eternity, and those terms would also apply to my heirs. I could tell our child who his father is, but I couldn’t tell my other child, or anyone else. He offered $15 million lump sum, and then $100,000 a month for 21 years.

But you decided not to sign.

For me, it was more a moral question than a legal one. I told Jared I couldn’t sign it, and he responded with, “Why? Sounds like you want to use your speech as a weapon.” I told him my children’s dignity is not a commodity.

Did Musk ever talk to you about the N. D. A.?

No.

And now you’re a significant voice in Gibney’s documentary.

People need to understand that part of the reason I’m featured prominently in the documentary is that other people cannot speak. I don’t think we should lose sight of that. I don’t want to have to speak publicly. I don’t want to be doing this interview right now. But there is a web of N. D. A. s. I feel a moral obligation to talk about my experience.

Let’s talk about your transition away from MAGA. When did that start?

It happened slowly and then all at once. There were moments where I wasn’t OK with the things I was witnessing — the misogyny, the racism — but I was a coward.

What would you say to people who think, “She’s only turning left because the right rejected her”?

I’m not dumb. I was aware what would happen when I came out against Elon, and I was OK with it. There’s a video from before I was pregnant where I say I’m not a conservative. So there were already moments where you can see these breaks from the conservative establishment.

You posted a lot of transphobic, racist and misogynistic commentary. Did other people pay the price for your public image?

I think about that all the time. Recently I got a notification about hospitals ending gender-affirming care. When I read that, I felt immensely remorseful. I know that probably would’ve happened without me, but I still feel guilt for my role.

How do you see your role today?

My only job after years of propaganda and dishonesty and being involved in MAGA for almost a decade is to be honest and set an example for my kids. My job is not to set a new narrative about myself. My only job is to be held accountable.

Coralie Kraft is a contributing writer for The New York Times Magazine.

Israel Denounces the Decision to Award the Nobel Peace Prize to Navi Pillay

The New York Times October 09, 2026

2026 Nobel Prizes

Advertisement

Supported by

Ms. Pillay, a human rights lawyer, was drawn into the international spotlight last year as chair of a commission that found that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza.

By Johnatan Reiss

Reporting from Tel Aviv

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu led Israel’s denunciations on Friday of the decision to award the Nobel Peace Prize to Navi Pillay, a human rights lawyer who was drawn into the international spotlight last year when a United Nations commission she chaired found that Israel was committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.

In a statement, Mr. Netanyahu called the decision by the Norwegian Nobel Committee misguided and said it had “lost its moral compass.” He also condemned Ms. Pillay’s work, accusing her of being prejudiced against Jews.

The Israeli foreign ministry, in a post on social media, denounced it as “the grotesque weaponization of an award to legitimize anti-Israel hatred and prejudice.”

Danny Danon, Israel’s ambassador to the United Nations, also questioned the integrity of the award. Honoring Ms. Pillay with the prize, he said through a spokesman, would damage “the credibility of the Nobel Committee,” and “tarnish the legacy of the distinguished laureates who have received this honor throughout history. Winning the Nobel Prize will not make her false conclusions about Israel any more truthful.”

While the prize’s announcement included only a brief mention of her work on the commission’s investigation into the war in Gaza, Jorgen Watne Frydnes, the chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee, said the work had played an important part in the decision.

The September 2025 finding by the panel, the U. N. Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, is among its most sweeping about the Israeli government’s conduct in the war and drew fierce criticism from Israel. The commission’s report said that some of Israel’s most senior leaders had “incited the commission of genocide.”

Last October, Ms. Pillay, a South African, said in a statement that “the actions of the Israeli government have consistently pointed toward a singular, harrowing objective — the systematic destruction of Palestinian life in Gaza.”

Israel has repeatedly rejected allegations of genocide from scholars and human rights groups.

When the commission’s findings were released, Israeli officials quickly disputed them and criticized the panel’s members. The country’s foreign ministry called the commission’s three members “notorious for their openly antisemitic positions” and “Hamas proxies,” referring to the Palestinian militant group that led the attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023. Isaac Herzog, the Israeli president, called the commission “morally bankrupt” and said it “obsesses over blaming the Jewish state.”

Ms. Pillay rebutted the criticism at the time. “I would prefer that our critics tell us: Where did we go wrong?” she said. “Which piece of that evidence is false, and why?”

Ms. Pillay brought extensive legal expertise on genocide to the inquiry. She spent eight years as part of the International Criminal Tribunal on the 1994 genocide in Rwanda, as a judge and then as the president. It was the first tribunal to interpret the definition of genocide set out in the U. N.’s 1948 Genocide Convention and the first to convict a defendant for the crime of genocide.

In June 2024, more than a year before the genocide finding against Israel, Ms. Pillay’s commission issued a report that accused members of Palestinian armed groups of committing war crimes during the Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel from Gaza, which it said involved a pattern of sexual violence.

In late 2023, South Africa, one of the most vocal critics of Israel’s war in Gaza, brought a case before the International Court of Justice, the U. N.’s top court, accusing Israel of committing genocide. Israel dismissed the claim as lacking factual or legal basis. The case remains active.

Hamas-led gunmen killed about 1,200 people in the Oct. 7 attack, according to the Israeli authorities, and took about 250 more back to Gaza as hostages, in the deadliest day of violence in the country’s history. Israel responded with a devastating war in Gaza that has killed at least 74,000 people, according to local health officials, who do not distinguish between civilians and combatants, and leveled much of the enclave.

Nick Cumming-Bruce contributed reporting.

The identity of a Scottish sailor killed in Connecticut after a skirmish during the War of 1812 long remained a mystery until two local history buffs got involved.

A Scottish sailor buried in Mystic, Conn., had an unmarked grave for more than 200 years until a local man arranged to have a marker installed. Credit... Sarah Meftah for The New York Times

Supported by

By Malia Mendez

Reporting from Mystic, Conn.

Jon Fuller kept thinking about the fallen sailor. He had just a rough sketch of the man — a crewman on a British ship, killed by a troop of scheming Yankees on the coast of Connecticut during the War of 1812, and buried in an unmarked grave. But the man’s name was lost to history.

“I was very curious,” Fuller said. “I was wondering who he was. Did he have a family? What was his history?”

Fuller, 66, works in retirement planning at a financial services firm. His Massachusetts home is cluttered with shells and cannonballs of various diameters, mostly from the Civil War, bought in antique shops or on eBay. He keeps one cannon under a table in the living room, and another by the front door. His prized swords are stored in an umbrella stand. He’s dabbled in re-enacting — wearing a replica uniform from the French and Indian War — but had to stop after getting heat stroke at a recent event.

He also has a family home in Groton Long Point, Conn., less than a mile away from the beach where the unknown sailor had died.

So when Fuller ran across an article detailing the sailor’s killing during the War of 1812, he decided to try to identify the man, and maybe even mark his grave: “I thought that would be a pretty neat thing to do.”

The exact details of what happened on that August day, two years into the war, are sometimes debated, but the consensus is that it began with a trick. A small group of local men sailed from the Mystic River into Fishers Island Sound on a vessel that appeared to be carrying valuable cargo. Militiamen lay in wait, hiding on the shoreline.

A British warship — the aptly named H. M. S. Terror, which days before had unleashed a bombardment on the nearby village of Stonington — took the bait, and dispatched a small boat to chase. Once in range, the Americans burst out from hiding and opened fire, killing a Scotsman from the British boat. They are said to have buried the enemy sailor in the northwest corner of Packer Cemetery in Mystic, underneath an apple tree.

Fuller thought he might have some luck at the Mystic Seaport Museum. But they didn’t have answers. He reached out to the British Royal Navy. They said they could make a researcher available at a cost, but the price was prohibitive. Instead, he got the help of a friend, Chris Malone, who took a slab of stone to a local garden center and paid around $200 to have it engraved: “Unknown H. M. S. Terror August 13, 1814.” An archaeologist helped him pinpoint the burial site. He recalled placing the stone there around 2019.

At least once a year, Fuller visited the grave and played “Scotland the Brave” from his phone.

“I was somewhat happy just to leave him as ‘Unknown,’” he said, “just for the sheer sake of perhaps I’d meet him in heaven someday if I’m lucky enough to go there.”

Then one day, a visitor to the gravesite changed everything.

Grace Cleere grew up near the Fort Griswold Battlefield State Park in Groton, Conn. Her family did not have much money, and vacation centered around national parks and historical sites.

“I got it in my blood early on,” she said.

Cleere worked at historical sites and societies in Connecticut before spending much of her professional career in Washington, D. C., writing for various government agencies including the Naval Observatory. But she always made room for side quests, especially those of the historical variety. Once, she said, she made hundreds of calls to return a late World War II veteran’s dog tag to his daughter.

“I never lost sight of the fact that you could bring history into anything,” she said.

After she retired, Cleere moved into an old sea captain’s home in Mystic, where shipyards once produced the whaling barks, clipper ships and schooners that powered 19th-century maritime New England. Cleere was strolling through Packer Cemetery when she came upon a gravestone which, compared to its 19th-century neighbors, was strangely austere. It had none of the usual lichen, and its lettering was inexplicably modern for markings to record the final resting place of an unknown sailor from a British ship.

“I said, ‘Terror,’” Cleere recalled. “‘That’s the ice ship that went down in 1848!’”

The New York Times

The Terror had a tumultuous history after its service in the War of 1812, during which it shelled Fort McHenry in Baltimore and its “bombs bursting in air” became part of “The Star-Spangled Banner” that immortalized American resolve.

Later refitted to forge through Arctic waters, the ship was selected by the British Admiralty to find the Northwest Passage, a trade route that would slash transit times and expand access to Asian markets.

The doomed 1845 expedition, led by Sir John Franklin, resulted in the loss of the Terror and the H. M. S. Erebus, plus all 129 crew members. The ships sank after being abandoned, their wrecks discovered just years ago.

Cleere was entranced by the mystery of the anonymous seaman.

“When there’s a puzzle anywhere,” Cleere said, “I don’t give up until I try to crack it.”

There was an emotional element to her fixation, too. Her father had been a Navy submariner. Growing up in New England, she felt close to tragedies like the U. S. S. Thresher’s sinking.

“I’ve always had a soft spot for dead soldiers and sailors,” she said, adding that she put poppies out every year on D-Day.

For years, Cleere’s research into the identity of the man in the unmarked grave did not get very far. Finally, a friend of hers named Roger Hutchins, a retired college administrator in the U. K. with a research background and an interest in genealogy, agreed to search the British Admiralty records, which are held by the National Archives in Kew, London, and cataloged online.

“I thought it was a bit of a wild-goose chase,” Hutchins said. But before long, he sent Cleere a package in the mail with a stack of photocopied archival documents.

One was an excerpt from the muster roll from the Terror. It listed the only fatality suffered during the ship’s action off the Connecticut coast in August of 1814. His name was William Adamson.

“‘My God,’” Cleere recalled saying, “‘this is our man.’”

Adamson, likely born in 1771, made his living as a sailor. In 1807, his marriage registration shows, he wed Christian Thomson at the parish church in the Scottish fishing village of Pittenweem. She was already pregnant with their first child.

Adamson shows up in the British naval records that same year. Hutchins speculates he was conscripted against his will, in part because he was newly married and building a family.

Either way, Adamson wound up a quarter gunner on the Terror.

“The emotional side of it is thinking, what extraordinary bad luck for that man,” Hutchins said. “But also there’s no doubt, and I know Grace feels this as well — there’s a feeling of real pleasure in being able to identify him.”

One mystery still remained: Who had erected the gravestone that triggered Cleere’s quest?

Then, earlier this year, Elizabeth Boucher, a collections manager at the Mystic River and Noank historical societies, texted Cleere about a monument in Groton Long Point, not far from Packer Cemetery, that appeared to reference the conflict she had been talking about.

The plaque, which adorned a large rock along East Shore Avenue, memorialized the skirmish, elevating it perhaps a bit by calling it the “Battle of Groton Long Point.” (The original article Fuller read had referred to it similarly.)

Cleere recalled contacting someone with the Groton Long Point Association, the body that governs the area; they did not know who installed the monument. But she was able to get a listing of members, with phone numbers.

Cleere started dialing and quickly reached Fuller. The commemorative rock was his work. And, he said, he was also responsible for the gravestone in Mystic. Cleere was dumbfounded.

“‘Who gave you permission?’” she recalled asking. He said no one had: “‘I just did it.’”

Having identified the dead man, Cleere set out to plan a ceremony, and to find Adamson’s family. Using various naval, census and vital records along with the genealogy websites Scotland’s People and Ancestry. com, Hutchins traced a sixth-generation Adamson descendant, Claudia Chagnon, to Lynchburg, Va.

Chagnon did not know much about Adamson beyond his name when Cleere and Hutchins found her. She was thrilled.

“How in the world did you find all this out?” she asked by email. “And connect him to an unmarked grave?”

As for attending the ceremony, she wrote: “Which cemetery and what time?”

And so it was that Chagnon found herself this past August among the estimated hundreds of people gathered in Packer Cemetery for a ceremony honoring her distant relative. A new plaque listed his name. Bagpipes, fifes and drums played into the retreating fog. People left offerings of tobacco, rum and Scottish shortbread. Fuller and local historians spoke.

Unlike the unsettled stories of the skirmish that had killed him, the day’s message to Adamson was unequivocal.

“Shipmate,” said Brian LeGare, the executive officer of the Naval Submarine Base New London, “after 212 years, you are unknown no more.”

Malia Mendez is a Culture reporter for The Times and part of the 2026-27 Times Fellowship, a program for journalists early in their careers.

What to Know About the New Elon Musk Documentary

The New York Times October 09, 2026

What to Watch

Advertisement

Supported by

A supersized portrait of the world’s richest man reveals new details and resurfaces troubling incidents from a headline-making life.

By Matthew Huff

Alex Gibney opens his documentary about the tech titan Elon Musk with a question: “How could Musk assume so much power, and why had we given it to him?”

The Oscar-winning filmmaker, whose previous subjects include Enron and Scientology, spends nearly four hours answering that question in “Musk,” tracing the rise of the Tesla chairman and chief executive from his childhood in South Africa to the I. P. O. of SpaceX in June, which made Musk the world’s first trillionaire. (The movie, in theaters, has a 10-minute intermission baked in.)

When news of Gibney’s project broke back in 2023, Musk took to Twitter (now X) to preemptively call it a “hit piece.” Combining interviews with ex-wives and former colleagues and clips from Musk’s 30-plus years in the spotlight with commentary from an A. I. version of Musk constructed from an archive of his own words, the film follows his rise from Silicon Valley start-ups to his brief tenure as the de facto head of the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE).

Here are some takeaways.

Musk’s privileged childhood was marred by violence

“Musk” paints a harrowing portrait of Elon’s youth in apartheid-era South Africa. In one interview, his wealthy businessman father, Errol Musk, claims to have shot and killed three intruders, covering the floor of their home in a “swimming pool” of blood. In another, he describes Elon riding in a car alongside the body of a family friend who had just “dropped dead.” After Elon’s mother, Maye Musk, separated from Errol, claiming physical and mental abuse (charges her former husband has denied), Elon continued to live with his father. When Elon was bullied so badly at school that he was hospitalized for a week, his father, he later said, sided with his attackers.

He’s made a habit of failing upward

Gibney suggests that Elon Musk’s business blunders have been as lucrative as his successes. After a failed bid to become the chief executive of his first start-up, Zip2, Musk was pushed out of the company but earned a $22 million buyout. Only a few years later, the entrepreneur and venture capitalist Peter Thiel pushed Musk out of PayPal with a $250 million parting gift.

More recently, according to Gibney, Twitter (now X) lost 80 percent of its value after Musk purchased it (though other estimates vary). Musk then rolled X and his A. I. start-up xAI into SpaceX for the largest I. P. O. on record to date, prompting Gibney to ask, “How can you keep screwing up and still make millions?”

Tesla is a lesson in entrepreneurial sleight of hand

While Musk claims to be a founder of Tesla, the automotive company was actually started by Martin Eberhard and Marc Tarpenning in 2003. However, Musk negotiated the title of co-founder for himself as part of a 2009 legal settlement. Later, he claimed that Tesla drivers could easily swap out their 1,000-pound car batteries, which helped him garner more than $100 million worth of environmental credits from the state of California, though he had only built a single battery swap facility in the desert.

Gibney also dedicates substantial time to Tesla’s self-driving Autopilot feature, which has been linked to deaths and injuries. In 2016, Musk oversaw the creation of a promotional video depicting a self-driving Tesla, causing the company’s stock to rise. However, it was later revealed that humans had controlled the car at certain points during filming and that the car had actually crashed.

He sees increasing the birthrate as a “national emergency”

“Musk” includes extended interviews with Justine Musk, Elon’s first wife, and Ashley St. Clair, a former conservative influencer who dated Elon from 2023 to 2025 and gave birth to one of his 14 known children. St. Clair claims to have received messages from multiple women on social media whom Musk offered to impregnate. “It’s like a Gatling gun of sperm in his DMs,” she says in one of the documentary’s more evocative lines.

Despite Musk’s preoccupation with procreating, both women suggest that Musk sustains little interest in his children or their mothers. Justine remembers Elon telling her, “I am the alpha in this relationship” at their wedding reception, and later telling her, “If you were my employee, I’d fire you.” St. Clair claims Musk openly called X Æ A-Xii (whose mother is Musk’s former partner Claire Boucher, the musician known as Grimes) his favorite and didn’t care to spend time with his other offspring.

Starlink and DOGE gave him global reach

According to Gibney, Musk has been able to consolidate political power via Starlink, the satellite arm of SpaceX, which provides internet access from space. While Musk supplied Ukrainian forces with necessary tech during their war with Russia, he’s also able to control and withhold access to it. That military bargaining chip has given Musk remarkable leverage in lucrative business deals around the world.

As part of his work with DOGE, Musk dispatched gatekeepers and regulations designed to check the A. I. industry. With those barriers removed, Gibney speculates that Musk could use A. I. to amass even more power.

The Atlantic’s Near-Record Hurricane Drought Is About to End

Wired October 07, 2026

The 2026 Atlantic hurricane season has been mercifully dull, but that’s set to change this week. Tropical Storm Isaias is forecast to become the season’s first hurricane before making landfall somewhere between Mississippi and Florida by the weekend.

El Niño has turned the Atlantic basin into a graveyard by changing winds high in the atmosphere so that they rip apart storms. That’s helped depress tropical cyclone activity to near-record-low levels and resulted in zero hurricanes. That could change imminently, though.

Isaias is churning in the Gulf of Mexico with winds of 65 mph, according to the latest update from the US National Hurricane Center. That’s just a shade below hurricane strength. The storm is forecast to pass over a patch of abnormally warm water, providing fuel for it to blossom into a hurricane. It could peak as a Category 2 storm with winds of 110 mph as it lumbers to the northeast. The storm is expected to weaken due to those aforementioned gnarly winds shortly before it makes landfall somewhere along the Gulf Coast.

The NHC has issued hurricane watches for all the coastline in Mississippi and Alabama as well as parts of the Florida Panhandle. (Tropical storm watches extend into Louisiana as well.)

Folks in that region can expect rainfall totals of up to 7 inches, though some spots in the Panhandle could see as much as 10 inches and storm surge as high as 7 feet. Tornadoes aren’t out of the question either. In other words, it’s a storm to take seriously.

Isaias could make also (or at least tie) history as the latest first Atlantic hurricane to form on record. The current record was set in 1905, when the season’s first hurricane formed on October 8. There’s still one more update scheduled for Isaias on Wednesday, so it’s possible it could just miss out on tying that mark.

Record or not, Isaias is indicative of the hurricane season that wasn’t. This year’s Atlantic hurricane season was forecast to be below average. But it’s been even quieter than expected owing to an El Niño that’s been dubbed “super,” “Godzilla,” and “supersized.” The superlatives—which meteorologists will be quick to tell you are not official designations—are indicative of the strength of this year’s event. El Niño is measured by ocean temperatures in a part of the tropical Pacific, and this year’s iteration has seen record highs throughout the summer and first part of fall.

The intensity has had a heavy hand in rearranging the atmosphere around the world, including over the Atlantic. Saharan dust has also played a role in quieting things by making the air in one of the major areas where hurricanes develop too damn dry.

For a sense of how that has impacted the Atlantic hurricane season, we can look at some averages. From 1991 to 2020, the basin saw an average of 14 named storms, seven hurricanes, and three major hurricanes—that is, storms of Category 3 or greater—annually, according to NHC data. This year has seen eight tropical storms and one soon-to-be hurricane.

Another metric to measure the season is accumulated cyclone energy (ACE for short), which takes into account not just the number and intensity of storms but how long they stick around. The ACE to date for 2026 is 10.8 units. The average for this time of year? Nearly 102, according to data maintained by Colorado State University. Most of that energy typically accumulates from mid-August through late September.

None of this is to say there might not be another surprise storm in the coming weeks. But with El Niño continuing to intensify and the peak of the season well past, the odds of this season seeing a sudden spurt of activity are minimal at best.

Shaq Got Hacked. Now He’s Pitching for a VPN

Wired October 07, 2026

At a promotional event in Times Square on Wednesday for the security company NordVPN, brand ambassador Shaquille O’Neal said he is eager to raise awareness among regular people about the importance of digital security and personal privacy.

“I have a video of me beating up Charles Barkley, and I wouldn't want the world to see that. That was a joke,” O'Neal says. “But everybody needs to have control of their own information.”

After being targeted by scammers who claimed that he was trying to buy a house and they were working on the transaction, O’Neal says, he realized he needed to learn more about cybersecurity and digital defense.

“I was hacked for the first time, not a bad hack, and I didn't know what to do,” he told reporters. “So I had to look into it. Once that happened, I really had to start paying more attention, because I would think nothing like that could ever happen to me, but it could happen to anybody.”

O'Neal, of course, is not just anybody. Still, the four-time NBA champion and media personality says that he doesn't have particularly sensitive data on his devices and tries to live a normal life as much as possible. When WIRED asked, though, whether he worries that he needs to take extra precautions to protect himself and loved ones as a result of his high profile, O'Neal said, “Yes, I think about it all the time, but I don't let it consume me, because if you let it consume you you can go crazy. But you have to be able to have great reactionary skills if something happens.”

A prolific tech investor who was early to AI, O'Neal emphasizes that the goal of his relationship with NordVPN is to inform the public and help people protect themselves. NordVPN is, well, known for its VPN. But the company has other offerings, including antivirus, threat detection, and scam-defense products that are geared toward accessibility for consumers. Marijus Briedis, the company's chief technology officer, says he was surprised by the findings of a recent NordVPN poll showing that 73 percent of Americans have an overconfidence in traditional antivirus and believe it can protect them against anything from identity theft to online tracking.

“The weakest link is between the computer and the chair, and I've been thinking so much about how to solve that problem,” Briedis told WIRED. “So the thing we are doing right now is focusing on education. It's a really interesting problem, how to do it in the best way. It's still haunting me in my dreams.”

Elon Musk’s America PAC Is Quietly Funding November’s Most Consequential Elections

Wired October 07, 2026

Elon Musk’s America PAC is focusing its war chest on the most consequential Senate races this midterm cycle—and doing so by financing attack ads on Democrats, as voters nationwide sour on the Trump administration’s agenda.

The trend of political parties and outside groups focusing on trashing their opponents is not a new phenomenon. But America PAC's approach has been unusual: for every dollar it has spent supporting GOP Senate candidates, it has spent almost three dollars attacking Democrats.

To monitor America PAC's spending ​on digital ads and mailers this cycle, our ace team at WIRED has created a live tracker that updates daily and highlights where Musk's political contributions are heading as we enter the waning years of Trump’s second term.

The political stakes are especially high for Republicans this midterms cycle because of the possibility of Democrats taking the majority in the US Senate, should the party flip four battleground races and retain three of the Senate seats it currently holds.

For Musk, the implications of a Democratic-controlled Senate would also be far-reaching, as he personally could become the target of congressional investigations, while his companies might be affected by bills related to tech and AI regulation.

For the critical Texas Senate race, America PAC has poured more than $9.4 million into ads opposing Democratic candidate James Talarico and roughly $1.8 million into ads backing Republican candidate and ​state ​attorney ​general Ken Paxton​.

The lopsided spending here is perhaps the least surprising of all of the close Senate contests. ​Paxton comes with so much personal baggage—from facing impeachment charges that were eventually dropped to having his wife (who has since endorsed him with an ad that doesn’t mention him by name) file for divorce on “biblical grounds”—that trying to boost him with ads highlighting his background is tough.

Republicans in Texas also cannot realistically do positive ads of President Donald Trump and Paxton together, since both men have terrible approval ratings.

The largest single expenditures by America PAC have been two $1.3 million digital media buys opposing Talarico. America PAC has not put any money into television ads, which is being handled by other groups, like MAGA Inc., the Trump-affiliated super PAC.

Meanwhile, the Senate Republican Conference–affiliated Texas PAC has so far booked the lion's share of television ads. Punchbowl News reported last month that Texas PAC has booked around $120 million and was looking to buy $100 million in ad slots before November 3.

In Ohio’s Senate race, America PAC has spent $3.3 million against Democrat Sherrod Brown compared to $1.6 million supporting Republican candidate Jon Husted.

Husted has been struggling to distance himself from supporting data centers at a time when voters in the state have become fed up with rising costs associated with the projects. Husted has been tagged as "the face of data centers" because of a planned Nvidia data center project in Ohio that will be leased by OpenAI, and for his past support for data centers when he served in the state government.

The effort by Brown to cast Husted as the champion of data centers has in fact been so effective that a memo by the Senate Republicans' campaign arm in August said it was tying an anchor around the neck of Husted's public polling.

At a rally this week in Ohio, despite the cratering public support for data centers, Trump could not help himself and declared to the crowd: “We want them.” Husted’s campaign quickly replied that it should be a “local decision.”

In Iowa, America PAC has spent $1.5 million hitting Democratic candidate Josh Turek, while only spending roughly $100,000 supporting the Republican candidate Ashley Hinson—the biggest disparity, according to the WIRED tracker.

To put that another way: To date, Musk's political operation has spent a staggering 14 times more attacking Turek than supporting Hinson.

This could be because Hinson has taken great pains to distance herself from Trump's agenda. She recently called on Trump to ban diesel exports and end the Iran war (after previously voting six times against the House resolution to end the conflict), after Turek called for both of those measures.

To illustrate the upside-down nature of this race, Hinson recently launched attack ads against Turek, accusing him without evidence of having “received tens of millions in support from men in the Epstein files,” a remarkable situation given that Trump has sought to tamp down any mention of the files because of the negative blowback on him personally.

Once again, pro-Republican ads are likely not helpful when the candidate is trying to run a race apart from Trump and is barely ahead in the polls in what should be a safe Republican seat. In the most recent New York Times/Siena poll, Hinson was just one single, solitary point ahead of Turek.

The Science Behind the Nobel-Winning Technology That Controls Neurons With Light

Wired October 07, 2026

The Karolinska Institute awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Medicine to researchers Karl Deisseroth of Stanford University, Peter Hegemann of Humboldt University in Berlin, and Georg Nagel of the University of Würzburg. Their discoveries led to the development of optogenetics, a technique where scientists can turn individual nerve cells on or off using beams of light.

According to Per Svenningsson, chair of the Nobel Committee for Medicine, “Optogenetics provides opportunities for mapping the brain in a way that we could once only dream of.” No other technique allows for such precise study of a living brain, helping researchers better understand the functions of our nervous systems as well as various neurological diseases and disorders.

But this prize is not just a celebration of neuroscience. It also serves as a triumphant example of what can happen when different disciplines of biology converge, as the findings that served as the basis for the development of optogenetics emerged from research in microbiology.

At the end of the last century, Peter Hegemann began a series of studies to understand how the single-celled alga Chlamydomonas is able to detect and react to light. Previous research documented that Chlamydomonas has an “eye spot,” a small orange dot on its surface that contains a light-sensing molecule called retinal.

Hegemann used tiny electrodes to measure the electrical signals generated by the alga and to expand our understanding of this structure’s rapid response. The scientist discovered that the organism was capable of producing an electrical impulse about 0.5 milliseconds after receiving light. This response time is 20 times faster than that of the human eye, whose light detection process takes at least 10 milliseconds.

Hegemann suggested that light detection in the alga must be the result of a much simpler process than that identified in the human eye. In the early 1990s, he proposed that the eye spots contained a protein that both detected the light and responded to it, likely opening as a channel to let ions through. At the time, this hypothesis sparked controversy. Many ion channels had been documented up to that point, but none could respond to light on their own.

To test his theory, the scientist attempted to isolate the light-sensitive proteins from the eye spot. However, when removed from their natural environment, these proteins became unstable. Later, a group of Japanese researchers sequenced the complete DNA of Chlamydomonas, which allowed Hegemann’s team to identify two genes that would create proteins with the expected characteristics of a possible light-sensing channel.

Georg Nagel took the next step of verifying the function of the genes. He introduced copies of each of the identified genes separately into different groups of frog eggs. The eggs began to produce the corresponding proteins, which eventually localized to the cell membranes. Nagel then turned on the lights.

Both proteins functioned as ion channels that opened when exposed to light. He named the genes channelrhodopsin-1 and channelrhodopsin-2. Further experiments showed the protein produced by this second gene—called ChR2 for short—opened especially quickly, the flow of ions occurring in just 0.2 milliseconds. It explained the extraordinary speed of the light reaction originally observed in Chlamydomonas.

When the researchers introduced the gene into mammalian cells—which do not normally respond to light—the cells generated an electrical signal when illuminated. This is what got the neuroscientists particularly excited.

Ion channels are important across many types of cells, but they do some especially heavy lifting in our nervous systems. The electrical impulses that neurons use to communicate with one another, as well as other tissues in our body, are mediated by the flow of ions in and out of the cell. If you can control the ion channels, you can control the neuron.

This is where Karl Deisseroth comes in. Deisseroth was searching for a method that would allow him to toggle the activity of specific nerve cells in a living brain. In his view, this tool could expand our understanding of brain functions and open new avenues for treating conditions such as depression and schizophrenia.

Following the discovery of ChR2, he asked Nagel for the DNA sequence so he could introduce it into rat nerve cells. The neurons, growing in dishes, produced ChR2 and, when illuminated with blue light, reacted immediately—sending an electrical impulse that propagated to other neurons. This result, obtained in 2005, was decisive in establishing ChR2 as a tool for neuroscience.

In the following years, Deisseroth, Hegemann, and Nagel collaborated to identify other proteins capable of activating or deactivating neurons using different wavelengths of light. With this toolkit, researchers can now design experiments where one group of neurons is turned on by one wavelength of light and another set of neurons is controlled by a different wavelength.

The term optogenetics was coined in 2006 and has since been implemented in a variety of studies. “Using optogenetics, researchers have been able to reveal neural circuits governing specific memories, feelings, and behaviors relevant for neurological and psychiatric disorders. In clinical medicine, researchers are using the method in attempts to restore sight in people with visual impairment,” the Nobel Assembly at the Karolinska Institute stated in a press release.
